Let every man be persuaded in his own mind. He who regards the day regards it unto the Lord; he who eats, eats unto the Lord and gives God thanks; and he who eats not, eats not unto the Lord and gives God thanks.

section: Romans 14:1–6 — Strong and Weak Believers; Royal Family Honor Code; Essential vs. Non-Essential
text: Romans 14 addresses the relationship between strong and weak believers in the royal family of God — how their differences in doctrinal maturity produce divergent standards, and how those differences must be navigated within the royal family honor code rather than through controversy, judgment, or maligning. This chapter introduces three major applications of the honor code: to privacy (vv. 1–12), to controversy (vv. 13–17), and to royal family interaction (vv. 18–23). The present chapter orients the reader to the foundational distinction between the strong and the weak believer, and to the governing principle of essential versus non-essential.

section: I. The Royal Family Honor Code as the Governing Standard
text: I. The Royal Family Honor Code as the Governing Standard

section: I. The Royal Family Honor Code as the Governing Standard
text: The subject of Romans 14 is the application of the royal family honor code. The honor code governs believer-to-believer relationships precisely because believers occupy different stations of doctrinal maturity and therefore operate from different norms and standards. The code does not eliminate those differences; it provides the framework within which they can coexist without becoming the occasion for sin.

section: I. The Royal Family Honor Code as the Governing Standard
text: The honor code includes morality but exceeds it. In some respects it supersedes morality as a category, because morality operates on the level of conduct whereas the honor code operates on the level of motivation and orientation to God's plan. The honor code makes an issue of essentials and is deliberately flexible about non-essentials. It recognizes the privacy of every believer functioning as a royal priest. It respects the righteousness imputed to every member of the royal family. It understands the difference between personal and impersonal love — personal love directed toward a few, impersonal love extended to all. It is inflexible about doctrine and very flexible about the application of doctrine to circumstance.

section: I. The Royal Family Honor Code as the Governing Standard
text: The three-part outline of Romans 14 that emerges from the text is as follows:

section: I. The Royal Family Honor Code as the Governing Standard
text: 1. Application of the honor code to privacy — Romans 14:1–12 2. Application of the honor code to controversy — Romans 14:13–17 3. Application of the honor code to royal family interaction — Romans 14:18–23

section: II. Definition of the Strong Believer
text: II. Definition of the Strong Believer

section: II. Definition of the Strong Believer
text: The strong believer is that member of the royal family of God who has attained maturity adjustment to the justice of God through maximum doctrine resident in his soul. He is not merely an older or more experienced believer — he is a mature believer in the technical sense, having cracked the maturity barrier through sustained intake of Bible doctrine under the filling of God the Holy Spirit.

section: II. Definition of the Strong Believer
text: The strong believer has constructed his norms and standards of conscience on doctrine, not on a false system of morality, self-righteousness, or legalism. He operates under the royal family honor code in full understanding of its provisions. He distinguishes between his function as a royal ambassador — productive service — and his blessing received as a royal priest — grace bestowed by the justice of God.

section: II. Definition of the Strong Believer
text: The strong believer has received what may be identified as the sixth imputation: blessing from the justice of God in five operational categories — spiritual blessing, temporal blessing, blessing by association, historical impact, and undeserved suffering. These blessings flow through the grace pipeline from the justice of God to the righteousness of God resident in the believer. The strong believer is therefore under divine blessing in the full sense, whereas the believer advancing toward maturity operates under logistical grace — adequate support for life and continued spiritual advance, but not yet the full expression of mature blessing.

section: A. Logistical Grace Versus Mature Blessing
text: A. Logistical Grace Versus Mature Blessing

section: A. Logistical Grace Versus Mature Blessing
text: The distinction between logistical grace and mature blessing is critical for understanding the structure of God's provision. While a believer is advancing toward maturity, every material provision — transportation, food, clothing, shelter, relationships — constitutes logistical grace. Such provision sustains the believer in life and in the learning process, but it does not of itself indicate divine blessing in the technical sense. One believer may have more material resources than another; this variation reflects logistical grace dispensed according to God's sovereign design for each life, not a differential in divine approval or blessing.

section: A. Logistical Grace Versus Mature Blessing
text: Mature blessing is reserved for the believer who has cracked the maturity barrier. Only at that point does the justice of God begin to impute blessing in categories that exceed logistical support. The weak believer remains under logistical grace. The strong believer is under both logistical grace and mature blessing simultaneously.

section: B. The Strength That Does Not Appear Strong
text: B. The Strength That Does Not Appear Strong

section: B. The Strength That Does Not Appear Strong
text: One of the most frequently misunderstood features of the strong believer is that his strength does not manifest as external assertiveness. The strong believer knows when to remain silent. When controversy arises over a non-essential, the strong believer backs down — not because he lacks conviction, but because he possesses sufficient doctrinal discernment to recognize that the issue does not warrant engagement. To the observer whose norms and standards have not been formed by doctrine, this restraint looks like weakness or vacillation. In reality it is the expression of moral courage functioning from a stable doctrinal base.

section: B. The Strength That Does Not Appear Strong
text: Conversely, the weak believer who takes a rigid public stand on a non-essential may appear strong. The external posture of inflexibility mimics strength, but its source is arrogance and doctrinal ignorance rather than conviction shaped by truth. The determining factor in every case is Bible doctrine resident in the soul — not visible conduct, not public posture, not the intensity with which a position is held.

section: III. Moral Courage as the Distinguishing Characteristic of the Strong Believer
text: III. Moral Courage as the Distinguishing Characteristic of the Strong Believer

section: III. Moral Courage as the Distinguishing Characteristic of the Strong Believer
text: The capacity that distinguishes the strong believer is moral courage. Moral courage must be carefully distinguished from physical courage, which is the form of courage most readily recognized and most commonly admired. The two are not equivalent, and the failure to distinguish between them produces chronic misreading of who is strong and who is weak — in military history, in ordinary life, and in the Christian community.

section: III. Moral Courage as the Distinguishing Characteristic of the Strong Believer
text: Physical courage is the capacity to act under physical threat without being controlled by fear of injury or death. It is often stimulated by emotion, adrenaline, or group momentum. It requires no evaluation of alternatives, no imaginative grasp of consequences, and no deliberate decision-making under uncertainty. It is frequently associated with individual heroism and attracts public recognition. Physical courage is a genuine and honorable quality, but it is categorically below moral courage.

section: III. Moral Courage as the Distinguishing Characteristic of the Strong Believer
text: Moral courage is the capacity to make and sustain difficult decisions in full awareness of the alternatives and their costs — and to do so without requiring external validation or the approval of observers. It demands imagination, integrity, and the willingness to bear the weight of being misunderstood. It is not born with a person. For the unbeliever it is developed through integrity and the discipline of sustained thinking. For the believer it is developed through doctrine — specifically through the accumulation of Bible doctrine in the soul that forms the norms and standards of the conscience and produces a relaxed mental attitude grounded in the faith-rest technique.

section: III. Moral Courage as the Distinguishing Characteristic of the Strong Believer
text: The stability of a military force depends far more on the moral courage of its senior officers than on the physical courage of its individual soldiers. A unit whose members all perform their assigned function without spectacular individual displays is the product of officers with moral courage. Individual heroism, paradoxically, is sometimes the symptom of organizational failure — one man doing what the entire unit should have done. The greatest armies generate few individual decorations precisely because excellence is the institutional norm.

section: III. Moral Courage as the Distinguishing Characteristic of the Strong Believer
text: Moral courage includes physical courage where circumstance demands it. A man of moral courage does not shrink from violence that is professionally and ethically required. But moral courage also recognizes when violence is not the solution — when engagement would escalate the problem rather than resolve it, when backing away from a confrontation is the intelligent and principled response. At that point moral courage looks like cowardice to those who can only evaluate conduct through the lens of physical assertiveness. It is not cowardice. It is the recognition that force without wisdom creates greater damage than the problem it was meant to address.

section: III. Moral Courage as the Distinguishing Characteristic of the Strong Believer
text: Controversy does not solve problems; controversy creates problems. This is a principle that most people do not understand, but it is the operating assumption of the strong believer. When factions form and sides are chosen, the original issue is quickly subsumed by the dynamic of the conflict itself — maligning, gossip, and escalating grievance displace the substantive question entirely. The strong believer, possessing moral courage from doctrine, declines to be drawn into conflicts over non-essentials precisely because he can see this dynamic operating and knows that engagement will not produce resolution.

section: IV. Definition of the Weak Believer
text: IV. Definition of the Weak Believer

section: IV. Definition of the Weak Believer
text: The weak believer must not be confused with the new believer. A new believer is a spiritual infant — ignorant of doctrine because he has recently come to faith and has not yet had the opportunity to learn. Given positive volition toward doctrine, the new believer will grow. His ignorance is circumstantial, not dispositional.

section: IV. Definition of the Weak Believer
text: The weak believer, by contrast, is ignorant of doctrine because he has rejected, remained indifferent to, or grown apathetic toward doctrine. His ignorance is the product of sustained negative volition. He may have been a believer for many years; length of time in the Christian life does not determine maturity. Only doctrine does.

section: IV. Definition of the Weak Believer
text: The weak believer operates on a false system rather than under the royal family honor code. He has distorted the grace of God in one of two antithetical directions: toward legalism and self-righteousness on the one side, or toward antinomianism and license on the other. Both are expressions of weakness, and both result from the same root failure — the absence of doctrine as the governing standard of the soul. The legalist parlays good into evil by making non-essentials the measure of spiritual status. The antinomian parlays sin into evil by implying that God approves of his conduct. The end result in both cases is evil.

section: IV. Definition of the Weak Believer
text: The strong believer advancing on the road toward maturity is attacked from both sides simultaneously. The legalist accuses him of compromise; the antinomian accuses him of being insufficiently oriented to grace. The strong believer does not deviate in either direction. Doctrine keeps him on the road. This requires moral courage, because it means being misunderstood, maligned, and judged by both camps — while maintaining a position that appears to neither side as sufficiently bold.

section: A. Characteristics of the Weak Believer
text: A. Characteristics of the Weak Believer

section: A. Characteristics of the Weak Believer
text: The weak believer fails to distinguish between the functions of the royal priesthood and the royal ambassadorship. He attempts to earn divine blessing through his behavior — functioning as a spiritual entrepreneur rather than understanding that blessing flows through adjustment to the justice of God and not through meritorious performance. He is either legalistic or antinomian, both of which are expressions of the same underlying arrogance: the rejection of God's authority in favor of his own standards.

section: A. Characteristics of the Weak Believer
text: The weak believer is a reversionist, operating in some stage of the reversionist cycle: the frantic search for happiness, operation boomerang, emotional revolt of the soul, negative volition toward doctrine, blackout of the soul, scar tissue of the soul, or reverse process reversionism. He carries grudges, seeks revenge, and is implacable toward those he perceives as having wronged him. His mental sins are expressed verbally through maligning, judging, and the public putting-down of others.

section: A. Characteristics of the Weak Believer
text: The weak believer is inflexible about non-essentials and flexible about essentials — the precise inversion of the strong believer's orientation. He makes an issue of social problems, ceremonial observances, dietary practices, and personality conflicts, while remaining indifferent to the doctrinal content that alone constitutes the essential. He sees everything in binary categories of black and white, and the nuanced distinctions required for doctrinal maturity are inaccessible to him precisely because he has not built the doctrinal framework that makes those distinctions intelligible.

section: B. Essential Versus Non-Essential
text: B. Essential Versus Non-Essential

section: B. Essential Versus Non-Essential
text: The governing analytical distinction throughout Romans 14 is the distinction between essential and non-essential. The essential is doctrine — the content of Scripture as accurately exegeted and systematically presented. On the essential, the strong believer is inflexible. He cannot and does not compromise doctrinal truth.

section: B. Essential Versus Non-Essential
text: The non-essential encompasses the vast range of personal practices, social positions, ceremonial preferences, and circumstantial choices that do not constitute doctrinal truth in themselves. On the non-essential, the strong believer is flexible. This flexibility is not indifference — it is the expression of a mature understanding that these matters do not belong in the same category as doctrine, and that making an issue of them is the characteristic error of the weak believer.

section: B. Essential Versus Non-Essential
text: When the strong believer declines to press a point on a non-essential, he may appear weak or unprincipled to observers who lack the doctrinal framework to assess what they are seeing. In reality, his flexibility on the non-essential is the product of the same doctrinal strength that makes him inflexible on the essential. The two postures are inseparable — the capacity to hold the essential firmly requires the capacity to release the non-essential graciously.

section: V. Historical Illustration: The War Between the States
text: V. Historical Illustration: The War Between the States

section: V. Historical Illustration: The War Between the States
text: The principles of Romans 14 — the errors of strong and weak believers in relation to one another, the danger of making non-essentials the occasion for controversy, and the destruction that follows when fanaticism forecloses rational discussion — find a stark historical illustration in the period leading to the War Between the States.

section: V. Historical Illustration: The War Between the States
text: The abolitionists represent, at the level of social history, a version of the weak believer's error: the inflexible pursuit of a position on a non-essential (a social and political institution) through methods — burning copies of the Constitution, inflammatory public denunciation, anti-constitutional agitation — that were destructive of the legal and social framework within which the problem might otherwise have been resolved. Their fierce rhetoric foreclosed the possibility of tempered discussion and provoked the resentment of those in the South who might have been persuaded by patient argument. Their unreasoning denunciation was the mirror image of the weak believer's inability to distinguish between the force required for essentials and the grace required for non-essentials.

section: V. Historical Illustration: The War Between the States
text: Among those in the South who possessed doctrine and understood the issues, two postures stand out as representative of the honorable path. Robert E. Lee, writing as a colonel in the United States Army, acknowledged slavery as a moral and political evil while insisting that its resolution must come through the slow, sure influence of Christian doctrine rather than through storms of controversy — and he freed his own slaves before the war. Thomas J. Jackson, though not a slave owner, devoted sustained personal effort to teaching Bible doctrine to the enslaved, holding a weekly prayer meeting and Sunday instruction with the same seriousness he brought to every other endeavor. Both men demonstrate the principle that the resolution of social problems lies not in controversy but in the patient communication of doctrine.

section: V. Historical Illustration: The War Between the States
text: The war that followed was not inevitable. Had the principle of Romans 14 been understood and applied by believers on both sides of the Mason-Dixon Line — had the strong remained strong by staying on the road of doctrine, and had the weak been guided by doctrine rather than inflamed by controversy — the political and moral conditions for a different outcome existed. Controversy does not solve problems. It creates them, and then perpetuates them. This is as true in a local congregation as it is in the history of a nation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventeen
text: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventeen

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventeen
text: 1. The strong believer is defined by maturity adjustment to the justice of God, not by external conduct or public posture. Strength in the royal family is determined by the quantity and quality of Bible doctrine resident in the soul, and by the degree to which that doctrine has shaped the believer's norms, standards, and decision-making.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventeen
text: 2. The strong believer operates under the royal family honor code, which includes but exceeds morality. The honor code makes an issue of essentials, recognizes the privacy of every royal priest, respects the imputed righteousness of every believer, and distinguishes between personal love for a few and impersonal love for all.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventeen
text: 3. The strong believer has received mature blessing through the justice of God; the advancing believer operates under logistical grace. All material provision during the advance toward maturity is logistical grace — adequate and faithful, but not yet the full expression of the mature blessing that flows to the believer who has cracked the maturity barrier.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventeen
text: 4. The strength of the strong believer is expressed as moral courage, which is categorically superior to physical courage. Moral courage requires imagination, integrity, and the capacity to make difficult decisions in full awareness of alternatives and costs. It is developed through doctrine. Physical courage requires none of these qualities and is not a reliable indicator of spiritual strength.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventeen
text: 5. Moral courage produces flexibility on non-essentials and inflexibility on essentials. The strong believer backs down from non-essential controversies not out of weakness but out of doctrinal discernment. This posture will be misread as weakness by observers who lack the doctrinal framework to evaluate what they are seeing.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventeen
text: 6. The weak believer must not be confused with the new believer. The new believer is a spiritual infant whose ignorance is circumstantial. The weak believer's ignorance is dispositional — the product of sustained rejection of, or indifference to, doctrine. Length of time in the Christian life does not produce maturity; only doctrine does.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventeen
text: 7. The weak believer inverts the strong believer's orientation: inflexible on non-essentials, flexible on essentials. This inversion is the signature of reversionism. The weak believer makes an issue of social problems, ceremonial differences, and personality conflicts, while remaining indifferent to the doctrinal content that constitutes the only genuine essential.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventeen
text: 8. Controversy does not resolve problems; it creates and perpetuates them. The principle of Romans 14 is that believers with differing levels of doctrinal maturity must relate to one another through the honor code, not through controversy, maligning, or public judgment. This principle applies within the local congregation, within the larger Christian community, and within the social and political life of a nation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Seventeen
text: 9. Romans 14 divides into three applications of the honor code: to privacy (vv. 1–12), to controversy (vv. 13–17), and to royal family interaction (vv. 18–23). Each section addresses a different arena in which the strong and weak believer interact, and each prescribes the application of the honor code appropriate to that arena.

section: Glossary
text: The operational standard governing relationships within the royal family of God — Church Age believers as a category distinct from Old Testament believers. section: Glossary
text: Maturity adjustment

section: Glossary
text: The third and progressive category of adjustment to the justice of God, achieved through sustained daily intake of Bible doctrine over time. Distinguished from salvation adjustment (instantaneous, once only) and rebound adjustment (instantaneous, repeated as needed). Maturity adjustment culminates in supergrace and ultra-supergrace, at which point the justice of God begins to impute mature blessing.

section: Glossary
text: Logistical grace

section: Glossary
text: God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical existence and continued spiritual advance during the period prior to cracking the maturity barrier. All material provision — food, shelter, transportation, relationships — constitutes logistical grace for the advancing believer. Variation in material resources does not indicate differential divine blessing; it reflects God's sovereign logistical design for each life.

section: Glossary
text: Mature blessing

section: Glossary
text: Blessing imputed by the justice of God through the righteousness of God resident in the mature believer, in five categories: spiritual blessing, temporal blessing, blessing by association, historical impact, and undeserved suffering. Mature blessing is distinct from logistical grace and is received only after the believer has cracked the maturity barrier.

section: Glossary
text: Moral courage

section: Glossary
text: The capacity to make and sustain difficult decisions in full awareness of alternatives and their costs, without requiring external validation or the approval of observers. For the believer, moral courage is produced by Bible doctrine resident in the soul and is the practical expression of the faith-rest technique functioning at the level of the will. It is categorically superior to physical courage and is the distinguishing characteristic of the strong, mature believer.

section: Glossary
text: Essential

section: Glossary
text: In the context of Romans 14, that which belongs to the category of doctrine — the content of Scripture as accurately exegeted and systematically applied. On the essential the strong believer is inflexible. The weak believer, characteristically, is flexible about the essential while being rigidly inflexible about non-essentials.

section: Glossary

section: Glossary
text: Personal practices, social positions, ceremonial preferences, dietary choices, and circumstantial matters that do not constitute doctrinal truth in themselves. On the non-essential the strong believer is flexible. Making a non-essential into an issue of principle is the characteristic error of the weak believer and the occasion for the controversies addressed in Romans 14.

section: Glossary

section: Glossary
text: Retroactive spiritual regression — the condition of the believer who has turned away from doctrine and reverted to the thinking and values of the old sin nature. The reversionist cycle passes through identifiable stages: frantic search for happiness, operation boomerang, emotional revolt of the soul, negative volition toward doctrine, blackout of the soul, scar tissue of the soul, and reverse process reversionism.

The weak believer fails to distinguish between these functions and attempts to earn blessing through ambassadorial activity, which is a category confusion.

section: Romans 14:1 — The Weak and Strong Believer; pistis; Royal Family Honor Code
text: Romans 14:1 — The Weak and Strong Believer; pistis; Royal Family Honor Code

section: Romans 14:1 — The Weak and Strong Believer; pistis; Royal Family Honor Code
text: Romans 14:1 “As for the one who is weak in faith, welcome him, but not to quarrel over opinions.” (ESV)

section: Romans 14:1 — The Weak and Strong Believer; pistis; Royal Family Honor Code
text: Corrected translation: Now receive that one who is weak in the doctrine, not for the purpose of getting into quarrels about opinions.

section: Romans 14:1 — The Weak and Strong Believer; pistis; Royal Family Honor Code
text: Romans 14 opens the final major paraenetic section of the epistle. Paul has established the doctrinal foundation of the Protocol Plan of God across chapters 1–11 and has applied it to the life of the royal family in chapters 12–13. He now addresses a concrete pastoral crisis in the Roman congregation: the conflict between weak and strong believers over non-essential matters — food, wine, and the observance of special days. The resolution he brings is not a verdict on the disputed practices themselves but a sustained application of the Royal Family Honor Code, and specifically the principle of the privacy of the royal priesthood.

section: I. The Weak Believer Defined — Romans 14:1a
text: I. The Weak Believer Defined — Romans 14:1a

section: The Participle astheneō
text: The Participle astheneō

section: The Participle astheneō
text: The verse opens with a present active participle from the verb astheneō (ἀσθενέω), meaning to be weak, to be deficient, or to be powerless. The present tense is a retroactive progressive present: the condition of weakness began in the past — through sustained negative volition toward Bible doctrine — and continues into the present. The active voice indicates that the weak believer himself produces this condition. The participle is circumstantial. The definite article functions as a demonstrative pronoun: that one. The corrected translation of this phrase is: now that one who is weak.

section: The Locative of Sphere: en tē pistei
text: The Locative of Sphere: en tē pistei

section: The Locative of Sphere: en tē pistei
text: The following phrase, en tē pistei (ἐν τῇ πίστει), is a locative of sphere. The noun pistis (πίστις) carries three distinct but related connotations: (1) faith — non-meritorious trust or confidence in the active sense; (2) faithfulness — as an attribute of reliability; and (3) doctrine — that which is believed, the body of belief in the passive sense. The third connotation governs here, as it does throughout Hebrews 11 and in many other Pauline passages. The generic use of the definite article treats Bible doctrine as a category distinct from all other categories of knowledge. The corrected translation of the full phrase is: now that one who is weak in the doctrine.

section: The Weak Believer Distinguished from the New Believer
text: The Weak Believer Distinguished from the New Believer

section: The Weak Believer Distinguished from the New Believer
text: A critical distinction must be maintained. The new believer is also deficient in doctrine, but his deficiency is a function of time and positive volition. He is moving forward; he will crack the maturity barrier through consistent daily intake of Bible doctrine. The weak believer, by contrast, is deficient in doctrine as a result of sustained negative volition. He has been saved for years, yet doctrine holds no high priority in his scale of values. His norms and standards have been formed not by the Word but by his background: his pre-salvation environment, his academic formation, his emotional attachments, and the opinions of those he admires. The weak believer is therefore properly classed as a reversionist — not necessarily in the terminal sense, but as one who has reversed the priority structure that spiritual advance requires.

section: II. The Two Categories of Weak Believers at Rome
text: II. The Two Categories of Weak Believers at Rome

section: II. The Two Categories of Weak Believers at Rome
text: The Roman congregation contained two distinct groups whose background had produced two distinct forms of weakness.

section: II. The Two Categories of Weak Believers at Rome
text: The first group consisted of Jewish believers whose formation under the Mosaic economy inclined them toward legalism. They retained the observance of the Sabbath, the Passover, Unleavened Bread, First Fruits, and the other calendrical landmarks of Israel's covenant life. Their application of these practices was not necessarily malicious, but it was anchored in background rather than in the doctrine of the Church Age dispensation.

section: II. The Two Categories of Weak Believers at Rome
text: The second and larger group consisted of Gentile believers who had come out of the polytheism of the Roman world. Their reaction to their former religious life had produced a strong set of taboos: they refused to eat meat that had been offered to idols and then sold in the public markets, and they refused to drink wine associated with pagan sacrifice. The food in question was often of the highest quality — comparable to the premier crus of any great wine-producing region — but its association with idolatry made it intolerable to those whose consciences were still calibrated by their former life. Their application was running ahead of their doctrine: inflexible on the taboo, indifferent to the essential.

section: II. The Two Categories of Weak Believers at Rome
text: Every generation produces its own version of this conflict. The specific taboos change across eras and cultural settings; the underlying dynamic does not. In each case, the weak believer is dogmatic about what is non-essential and flexible — often dismissive — about what is essential, namely the daily perception of Bible doctrine.

section: III. The Command to the Strong Believer — Romans 14:1b
text: III. The Command to the Strong Believer — Romans 14:1b

section: The Imperative proslambano
text: The Imperative proslambano

section: The Imperative proslambano
text: Paul addresses the strong believer with a present middle imperative from proslambano (προσλαμβάνω), meaning to take to oneself, to take as a companion, to receive or accept into one's society. The customary present denotes what is reasonably expected to occur when the Royal Family Honor Code is operational. The indirect middle emphasizes that the agent — the strong believer — is himself the one producing the action of reception. The imperative mood is a command. The definite article governing the participle is in the accusative case as direct object: now accept that one. Full corrected translation of this clause: now receive that one who is weak in the doctrine.

section: The Limiting Clause: mē eis diakriseis dialogismōn
text: The Limiting Clause: mē eis diakriseis dialogismōn

section: The Limiting Clause: mē eis diakriseis dialogismōn
text: The command is qualified by a negative clause: the particle mē (μή) followed by the prepositional phrase eis diakriseis dialogismōn (εἰς διακρίσεις διαλογισμῶν). The particle mē — as distinct from ou (οὐ), which denies fact — denies the idea. The noun diakriseis (διακρίσεις) means differentiation or quarrel; dialogismōn (διαλογισμῶν) is a genitive of reference plural, meaning about opinions — that is, about non-essentials. The corrected translation of the limiting clause is: not for the purpose of getting into quarrels about opinions. The strong believer is to receive the weak believer into the fellowship of the royal family without making an issue out of his erroneous views, and without inviting the weak believer to challenge his own liberty.

section: IV. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: IV. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Privacy of the Royal Priesthood

section: IV. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: The resolution of the weak-strong conflict does not lie in adjudicating whose opinions are correct. It lies in the consistent application of the Royal Family Honor Code, and specifically in recognizing the privacy of the royal priesthood as an inviolable principle of congregational life.

section: IV. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: Every Church Age believer is simultaneously a royal priest and an ambassador of Jesus Christ. The priesthood means that each believer approaches God directly, without human mediation, and that the business transacted between a believer's soul and the Lord is a matter of private jurisdiction. No other believer — whether stronger in doctrine or weaker — has the standing to intrude upon that jurisdiction. The weak believer's false opinions, his taboos, his legalistic application: these are matters between him and the Lord. The strong believer's liberty in the non-essentials is equally his own affair. Neither party has the authority to impose his norms on the other.

section: IV. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: Patience, properly understood, is not passive tolerance of whatever anyone does. It is the disciplined restraint of the strong believer's impulse to correct the weak believer directly when non-essentials are the issue. The strong believer may be right in his views. He is nonetheless wrong if he bypasses the ordained means of correction — the consistent teaching of Bible doctrine from the pulpit of the local church — in favor of personal confrontation. Such confrontation violates the privacy of the priesthood, creates subjective strife in the congregation, and replaces objective doctrine intake with the noise of competing opinions.

section: IV. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: Conversely, the weak believer who judges the strong, who maligns his liberty, who uses the strong believer's freedom as a rationalization for his own disobedience or bitterness, is equally in violation of the honor code. The command of this verse runs in both directions, though it is formally addressed to the strong.

section: V. The Framework: Three Laws of the Spiritual Life
text: V. The Framework: Three Laws of the Spiritual Life

section: V. The Framework: Three Laws of the Spiritual Life
text: Paul's treatment of the weak-strong relationship in Romans 14 cannot be properly understood apart from the three-law framework developed earlier in the Corinthian correspondence and implicit here.

section: V. The Framework: Three Laws of the Spiritual Life
text: The law of liberty governs the mature believer's freedom in the non-essential areas of life. Where the Word of God has not spoken prescriptively, the believer with maximum doctrine resident in the soul is free to exercise his own judgment without guilt and without apology. This liberty is the fruit of maturity — of having cracked the maturity barrier through sustained perception of doctrine — and it is not to be surrendered to the demands of weaker believers as a permanent policy.

section: V. The Framework: Three Laws of the Spiritual Life
text: The law of expediency supersedes the law of liberty in the context of evangelism. When the strong believer is in a position to communicate the gospel to an unbeliever, he may voluntarily set aside certain liberties — not because they are wrong, but because removing potential stumbling blocks clears the channel for the communication of saving doctrine. This is Paul's principle of becoming all things to all men (1 Corinthians 9:22).

section: V. The Framework: Three Laws of the Spiritual Life
text: The law of love supersedes the law of liberty in the context of the weak believer within the congregation. Impersonal love — love oriented toward the integrity of the subject rather than the merit of the object — does not lower its standards to match the weak believer's misconceptions. It does, however, refuse to make those misconceptions the occasion for strife, judgment, or the intrusion of personal correction. The strong believer backs away from the non-essential controversy, not because the weak believer is right, but because making doctrine the issue is more important than winning the argument.

section: V. The Framework: Three Laws of the Spiritual Life
text: A fourth law, the law of supreme sacrifice, supersedes the law of liberty in the context of undeserved suffering — the condition Paul describes when he says he knows both how to be abased and how to abound. This is the trajectory of the mature believer moving from supergrace blessing in time toward the ultimate imputation of blessing and reward at the judgment seat of Christ.

section: VI. The Local Church as the Classroom for Doctrine
text: VI. The Local Church as the Classroom for Doctrine

section: VI. The Local Church as the Classroom for Doctrine
text: The practical implication of the weak-strong principle is that the local church must be maintained as an environment in which Bible doctrine can be taught and received objectively. This requires several conditions.

section: VI. The Local Church as the Classroom for Doctrine
text: First, the pastor-teacher bears the primary responsibility for both teaching the Word and enforcing the conditions under which it can be received. The congre­gation is not a debating society. Two believers expressing opposite opinions — whether simultaneously in a quarrel or sequentially in a debate — do not produce doctrine intake. They produce subjectivity, strife, and the displacement of authority by the loudest voice.

section: VI. The Local Church as the Classroom for Doctrine
text: Second, the privacy of the royal priesthood means that every believer — regardless of his current spiritual condition, his background, his opinions, or his sins — has an equal right to receive Bible doctrine in an environment free from intrusion. The congregation is not the appropriate forum for spiritual bullying in any direction. The strong believer's duty is to permit the Word, taught consistently and accurately, to correct the weak believer's false opinions over time. The correction that comes through the ministry of the Holy Spirit applied to accurate teaching is permanent and genuine. The correction imposed by personal pressure is neither.

section: VI. The Local Church as the Classroom for Doctrine
text: Third, the believer who gossips, maligns, judges, or bullies other believers within the congregation has moved from the category of opinion — which is private — into the category of overt offense against the honor code. At that point, the privacy of the offender does not protect the offense, because the offense has itself violated the privacy of others.

section: VI. The Local Church as the Classroom for Doctrine
text: The justice of God remains the reference point throughout. Divine blessing flows from the justice of God to the righteousness of God imputed at salvation. No form of production — legitimate or legalistic — can penetrate that pipeline and become the basis for receiving blessing. The capacity for blessing is built up solely through the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception: the consistent intake and metabolization of Bible doctrine under the filling of the Holy Spirit. Strife and bickering between weak and strong believers destroy the academic discipline through which that capacity is formed.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: 1. The weak believer is defined by negative volition toward doctrine. He is not simply ignorant; he is ignorant because doctrine does not hold a high priority in his scale of values. His norms and standards are formed by background, environment, and emotional attachment rather than by the Word of God. The retroactive progressive present of astheneō indicates a condition that has accumulated over time through sustained negative volition.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: 2. The weak believer must not be confused with the new believer. The new believer is also minus doctrine, but he is positively oriented toward learning and will advance through the maturity barrier in due course. The weak believer, by contrast, has been saved for years and remains doctrinally deficient by choice, not by circumstance.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: 3. The locative of sphere en tē pistei identifies the arena of weakness as doctrine itself. The passive connotation of pistis — that which is believed, the body of doctrine — governs here. The weak believer's deficiency is not in sincerity or in effort; it is in accurate information about the Word of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: 4. The strong believer is commanded to receive the weak believer without making an issue of his erroneous opinions. The present middle imperative of proslambano is a command addressed to the mature believer. Reception does not imply endorsement of false views; it means refusing to make those views the occasion for quarrel or intrusion.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: 5. The limiting clause excludes quarrels about opinions from the reception of the weak. The genitive of reference dialogismōn identifies the content of the prohibited quarrels as opinions — non-essentials. The non-essentials are precisely the arena in which the weak believer is most dogmatic and the strong believer is most tempted to correct him.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: 6. The weak believer is a consistent violator of the Royal Family Honor Code in three ways. He intrudes on the privacy of the royal priesthood by inserting himself into the business of others. He attempts to obtain blessing from God through production rather than through the justice-to-righteousness pipeline. And he has no functional understanding of impersonal love, substituting emotional reaction for the integrity of the subject.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: 7. The law of love supersedes the law of liberty in relation to the weak believer. The strong believer does not lower his doctrinal standards to accommodate the weak believer's misconceptions. He does, however, decline to make those misconceptions the occasion for personal confrontation, recognizing that the ordained means of correction is consistent Bible teaching from the pulpit.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: 8. Patience in this context means keeping the non-essentials from displacing the essential. It is not passive tolerance of false doctrine. It is the deliberate refusal to allow the strong believer's correct views on non-essentials to create an atmosphere of strife that prevents the essential — Bible doctrine — from reaching every soul in the congregation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: 9. The privacy of the royal priesthood is the foundational principle governing congregational life. Every believer — regardless of spiritual condition, background, opinions, or sins — has an equal right to receive Bible doctrine in an environment free from intrusion, bullying, or the imposition of another believer's norms and standards. Correction of false opinions belongs to the Word of God, applied through the ministry of the Holy Spirit to consistently taught doctrine.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: 10. Strife between weak and strong believers destroys the academic discipline of the local church. The local church is the classroom in which the Grace Apparatus for Perception functions. Quarreling and debating replace objectivity with subjectivity, displace authority with the loudest opinion, and make it impossible for doctrine to reach the right lobe where spiritual growth occurs.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Eighteen
text: 11. All divine blessing flows through the justice-to-righteousness pipeline and is received only through capacity built by doctrine. No form of production — legitimate or legalistic — can penetrate the encapsulation of that pipeline. The only means of building the capacity for the imputation of divine blessing is the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception: consistent, objective intake of Bible doctrine under the filling of the Holy Spirit.

section: Romans 14:2 — Strong and Weak Believers; Food Taboos; Flexibility in Application; the Royal Family Honor Code
text: Romans 14:2 — Strong and Weak Believers; Food Taboos; Flexibility in Application; the Royal Family Honor Code

section: Romans 14:2 — Strong and Weak Believers; Food Taboos; Flexibility in Application; the Royal Family Honor Code
text: Romans 14:2 “One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.” (ESV)

section: Romans 14:2 — Strong and Weak Believers; Food Taboos; Flexibility in Application; the Royal Family Honor Code
text: Corrected translation: On the one hand, the one — the mature believer — believes, is convinced, holds the opinion that he may eat all things; on the other hand, that one — the weak believer — because of weakness, eats only vegetables.

section: Romans 14:2 — Strong and Weak Believers; Food Taboos; Flexibility in Application; the Royal Family Honor Code
text: Romans 14 continues Paul's extended treatment of the relationship between strong and weak believers within the Roman congregation. Chapter 13 established the believer's obligations under divine institutions and toward governing authorities. Now Paul turns to a more delicate interior problem: the collision between mature believers exercising their doctrinal freedom and immature believers who have erected food and beverage taboos as tests of spirituality. Verse 2 introduces the two categories in formal classical Greek construction, and the morphological and syntactical precision of Paul's language repays careful analysis.

section: I. Inflexibility and Flexibility: The Organizing Principle
text: I. Inflexibility and Flexibility: The Organizing Principle

section: I. Inflexibility and Flexibility: The Organizing Principle
text: The governing distinction of Romans 14 is not between what is permitted and what is forbidden, but between what is essential and what is non-essential in the Christian way of life. Doctrine itself is the domain of inflexibility: the essential content of Scripture does not bend to circumstance, personality, or cultural background. Application, however — the translation of doctrinal principle into behavior in specific situations — is the domain of flexibility. The failure to maintain this distinction in the correct direction is the root of most practical failures in the royal family of God.

section: I. Inflexibility and Flexibility: The Organizing Principle
text: Inflexibility applied to doctrine produces stability, courage, and precision of discernment. Inflexibility applied to application produces legalism, bullying, and a chronic violation of the privacy of the royal priesthood. Conversely, flexibility applied to doctrine produces apostasy and relativism; flexibility applied to application produces the mature sensitivity that Paul is commending in this passage. The mature believer has learned to be hard in the right place and yielding in the right place — a combination that requires sustained doctrine resident in the soul.

section: I. Inflexibility and Flexibility: The Organizing Principle
text: This combination may superficially resemble inconsistency to an observer who lacks the doctrinal framework to distinguish the essential from the non-essential. Paul uses the term finesse to describe the mature believer's capacity to read a situation and act accordingly: pressing forward when doctrine requires it, stepping back when sensitivity toward a weaker brother makes withdrawal the stronger move. The man who can only attack and the man who can only retreat are both deficient. The royal family honor code demands both capabilities, deployed in the right circumstances.

section: II. The Classical Greek Structure of Verse 2
text: II. The Classical Greek Structure of Verse 2

section: A. The Correlative Particles: Men and De
text: A. The Correlative Particles: Men and De

section: A. The Correlative Particles: Men and De
text: Paul opens verse 2 in Attic Greek with the classical correlative affirmative particles men (μέν) and de (δέ). Men — on the one hand — introduces the strong believer. De — on the other hand — introduces the weak believer, carrying its characteristic adversative connotation. This is not the common Koine idiom; it is the formal rhetoric of classical Attic prose, and its appearance here is intentional. Paul, when theologically excited or doctrinally precise, reverts to classical constructions — a pattern already observed in Romans 5 and elsewhere in the epistle.

section: B. The Relative Pronoun Used as a Demonstrative
text: B. The Relative Pronoun Used as a Demonstrative

section: B. The Relative Pronoun Used as a Demonstrative
text: There is no word for 'for' (γάρ, gar) in the opening clause. Instead, Paul uses the nominative singular of the relative pronoun hos (ὅς) as a demonstrative pronoun, designating a specific category of believer. This usage reaches back to Sanskrit, where the relative pronoun yas was originally demonstrative. Homeric Greek preserves this double function: Homer uses hos alternately as a relative and as a demonstrative. Attic prose retained the construction selectively, and Paul employs it here to signal a categorizing move — he is not simply speaking of 'a person who' but pointing to a defined class: the mature believer as a type. The translation 'one' captures the demonstrative force.

section: C. The Strong Believer: Grammatical Analysis
text: C. The Strong Believer: Grammatical Analysis

section: C. The Strong Believer: Grammatical Analysis
text: The verb governing the strong believer's position is the present active indicative of pisteuō (πιστεύω), meaning to believe, to be convinced of, to hold a settled opinion. This is a customary present tense, denoting what habitually characterizes the mature believer — not a momentary judgment but a stable conviction formed through sustained doctrine intake. The active voice indicates that the mature believer himself produces this action; the declarative indicative affirms it as historical reality.

section: C. The Strong Believer: Grammatical Analysis
text: The object of this conviction is expressed by the aorist active infinitive of esthiō (ἐσθίω), to eat — with the accusative neuter plural direct object panta (πάντα), all things. The constative aorist contemplates the action of eating in its entirety — from the point of doctrinal sufficiency forward through all subsequent stages of maturity, supergrace A, supergrace B, and ultra-supergrace. The word broma (βρῶμα), which will recur throughout this chapter, encompasses all food and beverage: meat, vegetables, fish, and drink. When only drinking is specifically in view, the separate verb pinō (πίνω) is used; its absence here confirms that food and beverage are treated together.

section: C. The Strong Believer: Grammatical Analysis
text: The mature believer's conviction is not libertinism. It is the result of having learned and stored in the soul the pertinent doctrines: that the earth is the Lord's and the fullness thereof; that food was designed by God to sustain the physical body; that an idol has no real existence; that no food or drink commends or disqualifies a person before God (1 Corinthians 8:4, 8). This is the inflexible doctrinal base from which flexible application proceeds.

section: D. The Weak Believer: Grammatical Analysis
text: D. The Weak Believer: Grammatical Analysis

section: D. The Weak Believer: Grammatical Analysis
text: The adversative particle de introduces the second category. The definite article functions again as a demonstrative pronoun, now pointing to the weak believer as a class. The causal participle is the present active participle of astheneō (ἀσθενέω), to be weak. The retroactive progressive present denotes a condition that began in the past and continues into the present: this believer has had no doctrine — or insufficient doctrine — in the past, and the deficiency persists. The active voice indicates that the weak believer himself produces the action of being weak; the causal participle makes weakness the ground for the main verb. The translation: on the other hand, that one, because of weakness.

section: D. The Weak Believer: Grammatical Analysis
text: The main verb is again esthiō in the present active indicative — a descriptive or pictorial present, bringing before the mind the ongoing scene of what the weak believer does. The direct object is the accusative plural of lachanos (λάχανον), derived from the verb lachainō (λαχαίνω), to dig in a garden — hence, what is dug out of the garden: vegetables. The translation 'herbs' found in older versions is a mistranslation. The correct rendering is eats only vegetables.

section: III. The Nature of the Food Taboo
text: III. The Nature of the Food Taboo

section: III. The Nature of the Food Taboo
text: Paul identifies two forms of legalism in view in this passage, both of which manifest as food and beverage restrictions. The first is an ascetic taboo against eating any kind of animal flesh — a stance associated with various forms of Stoic or ascetic religiosity that had influenced some Jewish and Gentile converts in Rome. The second is a taboo specifically against eating food that had been offered to idols and subsequently sold in temple markets or restaurants — the most common and often the highest-quality provisions available in a Roman city. Paul treats this problem at length in 1 Corinthians 8:4–8, establishing that an idol has no real existence, that all food belongs to the Lord, and that eating such food neither advantages nor disadvantages the believer before God.

section: III. The Nature of the Food Taboo
text: In the Roman context, the background of Jewish dietary law under the Mosaic code — the Levitical prohibitions against pork, shellfish, and animals not properly slaughtered — would have contributed an additional layer of restriction for Jewish believers who had not yet worked through the doctrinal implications of the Church Age. The Mosaic code was given to Israel as a national and ceremonial system; it is not operative in the Church Age. Nevertheless, a Jewish believer whose entire background was saturated with these restrictions would not abandon them quickly or easily, and the pastoral response to such a believer is not ridicule or pressure but patience and doctrinal instruction over time.

section: III. The Nature of the Food Taboo
text: The parallel on the positive side — the observation of special days — will be developed in the following verses. One category of legalism is negative: you cannot do this and be spiritual. The other is positive: you must observe this day to be spiritual. Both represent the same underlying failure: the substitution of background and taboo for doctrine resident in the soul.

section: IV. The Soul Structure of Correct Application
text: IV. The Soul Structure of Correct Application

section: IV. The Soul Structure of Correct Application
text: The mature believer's capacity for correct application is not simply a matter of willingness or temperament. It depends on the actual structure of the soul — on whether doctrine has been received, stored, and integrated through the various faculties of the inner man. At salvation, eternal life is imputed to the human spirit; at physical birth, human life is imputed to the soul. Both require orientation. In the soul, doctrine must be resident in the frame of reference, the memory center, the vocabulary storage, and the conscience — the norms and standards of the soul — before it can govern application through self-consciousness, emotion, volition, and the left lobe.

section: IV. The Soul Structure of Correct Application
text: When doctrine is present in both the human spirit and the soul, and when it has been organized into stable categories, it becomes an inflexible base — not a rigid reflex, but a secure platform from which the believer can assess any situation with accuracy and respond with precision. This is what Paul describes as the strong believer's conviction: not a preference or a habit, but a settled theological judgment formed by years of consistent doctrine intake.

section: IV. The Soul Structure of Correct Application
text: The weak believer, by contrast, lacks this structure. In the absence of doctrine, the soul defaults to its background: the cultural environment, the family inculcation, the pre-salvation religious framework. These fill the space that doctrine should occupy. They produce strong opinions — often rigidly held — but opinions with no doctrinal foundation. The weak believer is inflexible in the wrong column: fixed in application where he should be flexible, and lacking the doctrinal substance that would give him anything solid to be inflexible about. The result is legalism.

section: V. The Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: V. The Privacy of the Royal Priesthood

section: V. The Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: A recurring theme of the royal family honor code, which this passage develops in detail, is the privacy of the royal priesthood. Every Church Age believer is a priest, with direct access to God through Jesus Christ. This priesthood is individual and private; no believer has the authority to impose his personal standards — however correct they may be in principle — on another believer's private devotional or dietary decisions. The violation of this privacy through superimposition, whether by criticism, social pressure, or doctrinal intimidation, is a form of bullying and a direct breach of the honor code.

section: V. The Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: Freedom, privacy, and property form an inseparable package. Just as no one would walk up to another person and take money from his pocket — a violation of both property and privacy — no believer has the right to walk up to another and demand conformity to his personal taboos. The only legitimate superimposition within the local church context is the enforcement of the privacy rule itself: the protection of each believer's freedom to receive doctrine without interference.

section: V. The Privacy of the Royal Priesthood
text: Parents are a valid exception within the family structure: children under parental authority are obligated to obey parental standards while under that roof, regardless of their own developing convictions. Integrity and obedience in that context are themselves doctrinal applications, not violations of freedom.

section: VI. Correct Translation of Romans 14:2
text: VI. Correct Translation of Romans 14:2

section: VI. Correct Translation of Romans 14:2
text: On the one hand, the one — the category of the mature believer — believes (pisteuō), is convinced, holds the settled opinion that he may eat all things (panta, πάντα). On the other hand, that one — the weak believer — because of weakness (astheneō), eats only vegetables (lachanos, λάχανον).

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen
text: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen
text: 1. Doctrine is the domain of inflexibility; application is the domain of flexibility. The mature believer maintains this distinction precisely. Errors occur when inflexibility migrates from doctrine into application, producing legalism, or when flexibility migrates from application into doctrine, producing relativism.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen
text: 2. The classical Attic structure of verse 2 is deliberate. Paul's use of the correlative particles men and de, and his use of the relative pronoun hos as a demonstrative, signal a formal categorical distinction between two defined classes of believer. This is not casual Koine; it is the rhetoric of precision.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen
text: 3. The strong believer's conviction is doctrinal, not temperamental. The customary present tense of pisteuō indicates a stable, habitual conviction formed by sustained doctrine intake through advancing and mature stages of the spiritual life.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen
text: 4. The weak believer is weak through lack of doctrine, not through moral failure. The retroactive progressive present of astheneō describes a condition of doctrinal deficiency that began in the past and continues. This believer's taboos are the product of background, not of evil volition; the pastoral response is instruction, not condemnation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen
text: 5. Lachanos means vegetables, not herbs. The term derives from the verb meaning to dig in a garden and refers to garden produce generally. The ascetic taboo against animal flesh is the referent, not some narrow herbal restriction.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen
text: 6. Broma encompasses food and beverage together. The word is not limited to solid food. When only drink is specifically in view, Paul uses the separate verb pinō; its absence here confirms that the issue of food taboos includes beverage restrictions of all kinds.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen
text: 7. Two forms of legalism appear in this passage. The first is a negative taboo: prohibition against eating certain foods or drinking certain beverages. The second (developed in the following verses) is a positive requirement: the mandatory observation of special days. Both substitute background and tradition for doctrine as the basis for application.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen
text: 8. Self-righteousness is the characteristic accompaniment of ascetic reversionism. The weak believer derives a sense of spiritual superiority from his abstentions. This stimulation of arrogance, mistaken for piety, intensifies the social pressure he exerts on others and is incompatible with the royal family honor code.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen
text: 9. The privacy of the royal priesthood is a basic tenet of the honor code. Freedom, privacy, and property form an inseparable unit. Superimposing personal standards — even correct ones — on another believer's private decisions violates the priesthood and constitutes a form of spiritual bullying.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Nineteen
text: 10. Only the believer advancing toward or having attained maturity fulfills the privacy doctrine. The honor code requires both the inflexibility of doctrine and the flexibility of application. Neither is achievable without doctrine resident in the soul through consistent, positive volition toward the teaching of the word of God.
