section: Romans 14:3 — The Royal Family Honor Code: Strong and Weak Believers
text: Romans 14:3 — The Royal Family Honor Code: Strong and Weak Believers

section: Romans 14:3 — The Royal Family Honor Code: Strong and Weak Believers
text: Romans 14:3 “Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.” (ESV)

section: Romans 14:3 — The Royal Family Honor Code: Strong and Weak Believers
text: Corrected translation: Let not him who eats despise him who does not eat, and let not him who does not eat judge him who eats, for God has received him.

section: Romans 14:3 — The Royal Family Honor Code: Strong and Weak Believers
text: Romans 14 continues the extended application of the Royal Family Honor Code to situations in which mature and immature believers hold conflicting opinions on non-essential matters. Verses 1 and 2 established the basic categories: the strong believer, who is convinced in doctrine that all foods are permissible, and the weak believer, who abstains from meat on grounds of religious scruple. Verse 3 now turns to the mental and verbal failures that each party commits toward the other, and to the theological principle that resolves both.

section: I. Review of Romans 14:1–2 and the Two Categories
text: I. Review of Romans 14:1–2 and the Two Categories

section: I. Review of Romans 14:1–2 and the Two Categories
text: Romans 14:1 established the foundational command: receive the one who is weak in doctrine, but not for the purpose of generating quarrels about opinions. The exegesis developed there requires that the mature believer distinguish consistently between essentials and non-essentials — inflexible with respect to the former, fully flexible with respect to the latter. The same passage required a working understanding of the distinction between personal love and impersonal love, which was developed in the closing verses of Romans 13.

section: I. Review of Romans 14:1–2 and the Two Categories
text: Verse 2 introduced the specific instance: the strong believer holds the conviction — based on adequate doctrinal content in the soul — that he may eat all things. The weak believer, because of doctrinal deficiency, restricts himself to vegetables. The food taboo is representative, not exhaustive; it stands for the entire class of non-essential religious observances that divide believers with different backgrounds.

section: A. The Strong Believer Defined
text: A. The Strong Believer Defined

section: A. The Strong Believer Defined
text: The strong believer is positive toward doctrine. Through the daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP), Bible doctrine accumulates in the right lobe of the soul and becomes the basis for application. Because his standards are doctrinal, his application is flexible. He does not run about taking stands on inconsequential matters. The firm stand he takes is for doctrine itself; in every area of application, he is adaptable.

section: A. The Strong Believer Defined
text: This flexibility is consistently misread by the weak believer as weakness or compromise. In reality, the capacity to refrain from taking a public stand on a non-essential — especially under social pressure — requires a quality of moral courage that the weak believer does not yet possess.

section: B. The Weak Believer Defined
text: B. The Weak Believer Defined

section: B. The Weak Believer Defined
text: Two types of believer may be called weak. The first is simply the younger believer who has not yet accumulated sufficient doctrine to navigate complex applications — he is in the process of growth and is not the primary subject of Romans 14. The second, who is the central figure in this passage, is the reversionistic believer: one who has rejected sustained doctrine intake and fallen back upon pre-conversion standards, whether those standards derive from a Jewish background governed by Levitical dietary law or from a Gentile background governed by the moral codes of heathenism.

section: B. The Weak Believer Defined
text: The weak believer is negative toward doctrine. Having no adequate doctrinal content in the soul, he must rely on human viewpoint thinking — the background standards he carried into the Christian life. These standards reside in the conscience as false norms, and because the norms are false, the applications derived from them are also false. Inflexibility about non-essentials is not strength; it is the inflexibility of ignorance.

section: II. The Principle of Impersonal Love and Privacy
text: II. The Principle of Impersonal Love and Privacy

section: II. The Principle of Impersonal Love and Privacy
text: The Royal Family Honor Code, which governs intra-family relationships among Church Age believers, rests on the distinction between personal love and impersonal love. Personal love emphasizes the object: it is selective, reserved for a limited circle — the Lord Jesus Christ as the primary object, right man or right woman as the secondary object, and close friends and family as the tertiary objects. The norms and standards of personal love flow from the subject's doctrinal content, but the orientation is toward the object.

section: II. The Principle of Impersonal Love and Privacy
text: Impersonal love — the love commanded toward all members of the royal family — emphasizes the subject. The subject with doctrinal content in the soul applies those standards consistently regardless of who the object is or how the object behaves. This means that when the weak believer maligns, judges, bullies, or condemns the strong believer, the strong believer does not retaliate. He tolerates. He grants the weak believer his privacy. He leaves the matter in the Lord's hands. To counterattack is to lower oneself to the weak believer's standards — an expression of the old sin nature rather than the doctrinal content of the soul.

section: II. The Principle of Impersonal Love and Privacy
text: By the same principle, impersonal love toward the brethren means granting the weak believer the privacy of his priesthood. The strong believer makes an issue of doctrine — not of the weak believer's dietary practices or calendar observances. He leaves the weak believer in a state of objectivity toward doctrine, neither arguing him out of his taboos nor mocking them. Doctrine is the issue; personal taboos are not.

section: III. Exegetical Introduction to Romans 14:3
text: III. Exegetical Introduction to Romans 14:3

section: III. Exegetical Introduction to Romans 14:3
text: Before proceeding to the word-by-word exegesis of verse 3, several preliminary observations establish the doctrinal context.

section: A. The Nature of the Weak Believer's Abstinence
text: A. The Nature of the Weak Believer's Abstinence

section: A. The Nature of the Weak Believer's Abstinence
text: The weak believer in Romans 14 refuses to eat meat not on the basis of dietary preference or medical judgment, but on the basis of religious legalism. His abstinence is a bid for divine approbation — a false assumption that God is more pleased with vegetarians than with those who eat freely. This is the theological error. Vegetarianism as a personal choice, a matter of health, or a dietary preference carries no moral weight in either direction; Scripture assigns it none. But vegetarianism adopted as a mechanism for gaining divine favor, and then enforced upon the rest of the royal family, is a compound error: it is theologically false and socially tyrannical.

section: B. The Arrogance of the Weak Believer's Conscience
text: B. The Arrogance of the Weak Believer's Conscience

section: B. The Arrogance of the Weak Believer's Conscience
text: The weak believer possesses what may be described as a subjective, self-righteous, hypersensitive, and arrogant conscience. Its standards are legalistic and reversionistic — not the norms of Bible doctrine. The issue in relationship to the Lord is adjustment to His justice; the issue in fellowship with other believers is the Royal Family Honor Code. Neither relationship requires conformity to dietary or calendrical taboos. The weak believer's conscience introduces a false standard into both relationships.

section: B. The Arrogance of the Weak Believer's Conscience
text: Arrogance is the specific mechanism by which private taboos become public tyranny. Every believer has the right under privacy of the royal priesthood to maintain personal standards of conduct. Arrogance takes those private standards and attempts to superimpose them on every other believer in the community. When the weak believer does this, he has moved from the exercise of his own priesthood into an assault on the priesthood of others.

section: C. The Two Directions of Failure in Verse 3
text: C. The Two Directions of Failure in Verse 3

section: C. The Two Directions of Failure in Verse 3
text: Verse 3 identifies a specific failure mode for each category. The strong believer's occupational hazard is contempt: he looks down on the weak believer with disdain, treating his scruples as beneath serious consideration. The weak believer's failure mode is judicial condemnation: he pronounces the strong believer's freedom as sin and treats himself as the appointed enforcer of divine standards. Both attitudes violate the Royal Family Honor Code. The command of verse 3 addresses both simultaneously.

section: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community
text: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community

section: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community
text: The following nine principles organize the doctrinal content of this passage and provide the framework for the exegesis of verse 3 and the verses that follow.

section: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community
text: 1. The weak believer who refuses to eat meat has become a vegetarian on the basis of religious legalism, not dietary judgment. If he wishes to observe this practice privately under the priesthood, that is his right. The error begins when he seeks to make all believers conform to his practice and persecutes those who do not comply.

section: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community
text: 2. Vegetarianism adopted for dietary reasons is entirely permissible and morally neutral. Vegetarianism adopted as a means of gaining divine approbation is theologically false; and when it is enforced on others, it constitutes a violation of the privacy of the royal priesthood.

section: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community
text: 3. The subjective, self-righteous, hypersensitive, and arrogant conscience of the weak believer operates on legalistic and reversionistic standards. These standards are not the issue in the believer's relationship to the Lord, nor are they the basis of fellowship with other believers.

section: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community
text: 4. Christian fellowship allows for both the privacy of the priesthood and genuine differences of opinion on non-essential matters. The weak believer violates this allowance when he becomes a bully — seeking to superimpose his legalistic opinions on the entire community.

section: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community
text: 5. Ascetic taboos — dietary restrictions, the observance of special days, abstinence from certain activities — are not prerequisites for Christian fellowship. Doctrine is the basis of fellowship; lifestyle conformity is not. Inflexibility about doctrine is essential; inflexibility about application is a mark of immaturity.

section: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community
text: 6. Agreement on lifestyle, diet, or the observance of days is not required for Christian fellowship. The Royal Family Honor Code becomes essential precisely because believers will always differ in their applications of doctrine to the circumstances of daily life.

section: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community
text: 7. Because strife is generated by both the strong and the weak believer in their clash of opinions, Scripture identifies the specific failure of each: the mental attitude failure of contempt in the strong believer, and the verbal failure of judicial condemnation in the weak believer. Both must be corrected.

section: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community
text: 8. Disagreement on non-essentials must never be permitted to destroy Christian fellowship. Non-essentials are defined precisely by the fact that they fall outside the realm of doctrinal absolutes. The strong believer has no right to react with contempt to the weak believer's scruples, and the weak believer has no right to condemn the strong believer's freedom.

section: IV. Nine Principles Governing the Strong and Weak Believer in Community
text: 9. Non-essentials arise from either legalistic or antinomian distortions of doctrine. The strong believer is not a legalist because he refuses antinomianism, and he is not an antinomian because he refuses legalism. He takes a firm stand on doctrine and moves with complete flexibility through its applications — misunderstood by both camps simultaneously, but correct before the Lord.

section: V. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Life Lived Unto the Lord
text: V. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Life Lived Unto the Lord

section: V. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Life Lived Unto the Lord
text: Since no believer in this life achieves sinless perfection — a fact established by 1 John 1:8, which states that anyone who claims to be without sin deceives himself and has no truth in him — the royal family of God requires an operational code that makes community life workable among imperfect members. Resurrection will bring perfection; the present Church Age requires an honor code.

section: V. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Life Lived Unto the Lord
text: The Royal Family Honor Code functions on the same principle as impersonal love: the subject with doctrinal content applies consistent standards regardless of the object's behavior. The strong believer tolerates the weak believer's scruples. The weak believer — when he advances in doctrine — will come to grant the strong believer his freedom. Until that advance occurs, the strong believer's task is to make doctrine the issue and to refuse to make the weak believer's opinions an occasion for contempt or retaliation.

section: V. The Royal Family Honor Code and the Life Lived Unto the Lord
text: The expression 'as unto the Lord' that appears in verse 6 and governs the entire passage establishes the ultimate orientation: every practice, whether eating or abstaining, whether observing a day or treating all days alike, is evaluated not by community consensus but by the believer's accountability before the Lord. This vertical orientation — life lived before the Lord — is the only stable basis on which horizontal differences of opinion can be tolerated without destroying fellowship.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty
text: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty
text: 1. The two categories of verse 2 remain in force through verse 3. The strong believer operates from doctrinal content and is flexible in application. The weak believer operates from reversionistic or legalistic background standards and is inflexible about non-essentials. Verse 3 identifies the specific sin that each category commits in the conflict.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty
text: 2. The strong believer's occupational hazard is contempt. When the mature believer looks down on the weak believer's scruples with disdain, he has allowed his doctrinal confidence to become arrogance toward a person for whom Christ died. The command 'let not him who eats despise him who does not eat' directly prohibits this attitude.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty
text: 3. The weak believer's occupational hazard is judicial condemnation. When the legalistic believer pronounces the strong believer's freedom to be sin, he has appointed himself a judge in a matter that belongs to the Lord. The command 'let not him who does not eat judge him who eats' directly prohibits this verdict.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty
text: 4. Private taboos become tyranny when superimposed on the royal family. Every believer has the right under privacy of the royal priesthood to maintain personal standards of conduct in non-essential areas. Arrogance is the mechanism by which private convictions are converted into demands upon others. Spiritual bullying — the attempt to compel conformity to one's personal taboos — violates both the privacy of the priesthood and the Royal Family Honor Code.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty
text: 5. Inflexibility about non-essentials is not a mark of spiritual strength. It is the inflexibility of ignorance — the same structure as the inflexibility that produces physical courage without moral courage. The strong believer's flexibility in application is consistently misread as weakness. In reality it requires a higher quality of character than the rigid enforcement of personal taboos.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty
text: 6. Doctrine, not lifestyle conformity, is the basis of Christian fellowship. Believers may differ widely in their personal applications — in diet, in the observance of days, in any number of cultural practices — and still maintain full fellowship on the basis of shared doctrinal content. Agreement on non-essentials is never a prerequisite for fellowship; agreement that doctrine is the essential always is.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty
text: 7. Impersonal love provides the operational mechanism for tolerating disagreement. Because impersonal love emphasizes the subject — the believer's own doctrinal standards — rather than the object, it remains stable regardless of how the weak believer behaves. The strong believer grants the weak believer his privacy, refuses retaliation, leaves judgment to the Lord, and continues to make doctrine the issue.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty
text: 8. The antinomian error is as destructive as the legalistic error. Both represent a failure to distinguish essentials from non-essentials. The legalist enforces private taboos on the community; the antinomian abandons doctrinal standards in the name of grace. The strong believer is inflexible about doctrine and flexible about application — occupying the middle position that is attacked from both sides and is correct before the Lord.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty
text: 9. The theological resolution of the conflict is the phrase 'God has received him.' The strong believer who eats has been accepted by God on the basis of faith in Christ and adjustment to the justice of God. No secondary observance — dietary or calendrical — either adds to or subtracts from that acceptance. The weak believer's condemnation of the strong believer's freedom is therefore a judgment against a person whom God Himself has received.

Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One

section: Romans 14:3 — Occupational Hazards of the Strong and the Weak Believer
text: Romans 14:3 — Occupational Hazards of the Strong and the Weak Believer

section: Romans 14:3 — Occupational Hazards of the Strong and the Weak Believer
text: Romans 14:3 “Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.” (ESV)

section: Romans 14:3 — Occupational Hazards of the Strong and the Weak Believer
text: Corrected translation: He who eats — the strong believer — let him stop regarding with contempt that one who does not eat — the weak believer. Furthermore, he who does not eat — the weak believer — stop judging that one who keeps on eating everything — the strong believer.

section: Romans 14:3 — Occupational Hazards of the Strong and the Weak Believer
text: Romans 14 continues Paul's treatment of the strong and the weak believer within the Roman congregation. The presenting issue is food — specifically, whether a believer may eat all things or must restrict himself to vegetables, a practice rooted in legalistic taboos carried over from pre-conversion backgrounds. Verse 3 identifies the occupational hazard on each side: the strong believer tends toward contempt; the weak believer tends toward judgment. Both failures are expressions of arrogance, and Paul commands each party to cease and desist.

section: I. The Verb Structure of Romans 14:3
text: I. The Verb Structure of Romans 14:3

section: I. The Verb Structure of Romans 14:3
text: The verse opens with the articular present active participle of the verb ἐσθίω (esthiō), meaning to eat or to consume, used here to encompass food and beverage alike. The customary present tense denotes habitual action: the strong believer characteristically operates under the law of liberty. He is not constrained by the self-righteous taboos of the legalist, nor has he swung to the opposite error of antinomianism. He eats freely because he understands his standing before God.

section: I. The Verb Structure of Romans 14:3
text: The verb translated despise is the third person singular present active imperative of exoutheneō (ἐξουθενέω): to treat with contempt, to reject with disdain. The negative here is mē (μή), which combined with the present imperative carries the force of a prohibition against ongoing action: stop doing what you are already doing. The strong believer in Rome had already fallen into this pattern, and Paul commands him to discontinue it.

section: I. The Verb Structure of Romans 14:3
text: The second imperative in the verse governs the weak believer. The articular present active participle of ἐσθίω with the negative μή designates the one who habitually abstains. The verb translated judge is

section: I. The Verb Structure of Romans 14:3
text: krinō (κρίνω): to judge, to evaluate adversely, to pass sentence. Again the negative mē with the present imperative means stop judging — the action is already in progress and must be discontinued. The direct object is the demonstrative pronoun that one, emphasizing the category being judged: the mature believer who eats without restriction.

section: I. The Verb Structure of Romans 14:3
text: There is no coordinating conjunction

section: I. The Verb Structure of Romans 14:3
text: kai (καί) linking the two clauses. Instead, Paul uses the post-positive conjunctive particle de (δέ), which marks the superaddition of a clause — best rendered furthermore. The shift signals that the second command is not merely coordinate with the first but adds a distinct and equally serious concern.

section: II. The Occupational Hazard of the Strong Believer
text: II. The Occupational Hazard of the Strong Believer

section: II. The Occupational Hazard of the Strong Believer
text: The strong or mature believer is characterized by maximum orientation to Bible doctrine. He understands the distinction between essential and non-essential. Doctrine is the essential; the application of doctrine to daily life demands flexibility. Where essentials are concerned, the strong believer is inflexible. Where non-essentials are concerned — dietary customs, food taboos, matters of indifference — he is appropriately flexible.

section: II. The Occupational Hazard of the Strong Believer
text: The occupational hazard emerges precisely from this strength. After repeated correct and flexible applications of doctrine, the mature believer encounters a weak believer mired in self-righteous legalism. The weak believer is easy to identify: his arrogance is conspicuous, his taboos are baseless, his inflexibility about non-essentials is a spiritual failure that is plain to anyone with doctrinal orientation. At this point the strong believer is tempted to make an inflexible application to the weak believer — to respond with contempt, snobbishness, and intolerance. In doing so, he departs from his own norms and standards.

section: II. The Occupational Hazard of the Strong Believer
text: This is the internal logic of the problem: when a person retaliates against an antagonist, he does not maintain his own standards — he adopts the antagonist's. The very quality the strong believer despises in the weak believer, namely rigid and petty inflexibility, he immediately replicates in a different form. His inflexibility is directed not at doctrine but at a person. His intolerance of the legalist is itself a violation of the royal family honor code, specifically of the principle of impersonal love, which requires the mature believer to maintain consistent, non-retaliatory conduct toward all categories of people regardless of their failures.

section: III. The Occupational Hazard of the Weak Believer
text: III. The Occupational Hazard of the Weak Believer

section: III. The Occupational Hazard of the Weak Believer
text: The weak believer is not always in reversionism, but in this context that is the primary emphasis. He has either failed to advance beyond the early stages of spiritual growth, or he has regressed from a point of greater maturity. Either way, his thinking is governed by false norms and standards derived from pre-conversion background rather than from Bible doctrine. He is inflexible precisely where flexibility is required — in the realm of non-essentials — and flexible precisely where inflexibility is required — in the realm of doctrine.

section: III. The Occupational Hazard of the Weak Believer
text: His characteristic failure is judging. The weak believer uses the food observance as a measuring rod of spirituality. Those who abstain are righteous; those who do not are suspect. The mature believer who eats freely becomes the target of malicious evaluation: he is criticized, maligned, and subjected to the vindictive scrutiny of the legalist. This is spiritual bullying. The weak believer is self-righteous, arrogant, petty, implacable, and inflexible. He majors in peripheral concerns while remaining blind to the central realities of the spiritual life.

section: III. The Occupational Hazard of the Weak Believer
text: The source of this judging is arrogance compounded by jealousy. The legalist has invested considerable effort in the maintenance of his taboo system, and he has derived from that effort a pride of accomplishment. When he observes the mature believer living freely, the pride is threatened, and the response is aggressive judgment. His arrogance does not look the same as the arrogance of the strong believer, but it is arrogance nonetheless. The problem in both directions is pride operating in different spheres.

section: IV. The Symmetry of the Two Failures
text: IV. The Symmetry of the Two Failures

section: IV. The Symmetry of the Two Failures
text: Paul's construction is deliberate and symmetrical. Each command mirrors the other. Each addresses an ongoing action that must be stopped. Each targets a specific form of arrogance that is characteristic of a specific stage of spiritual development. This symmetry carries a critical pastoral implication: neither the strong nor the weak believer is exempt from the possibility of arrogance. The form differs; the root is identical.

section: IV. The Symmetry of the Two Failures
text: The strong believer's arrogance is rooted in knowledge — the accumulation of Bible doctrine that rightly distinguishes essential from non-essential but then wrongly applies that capacity as a weapon against a fellow believer. The weak believer's arrogance is rooted in performance — the self-generated satisfaction of maintaining a taboo system that has nothing to do with spiritual reality but which he has elevated to the status of divine requirement.

section: IV. The Symmetry of the Two Failures
text: What Paul commands in both directions is the cessation of the arrogance, not the cessation of the underlying convictions. He does not tell the strong believer to stop eating. He does not tell the weak believer to start eating. He tells each party to stop weaponizing his position against the other. The mature believer is to maintain his norms and standards without descending into contempt. The legalistic believer is to refrain from subjecting the mature believer to his own standard of evaluation. Each is to honor the privacy of the royal priesthood and the independence of each believer's standing before God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One
text: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One
text: 1. The occupational hazard of the mature believer is arrogance related to superior knowledge of doctrine. After many correct and flexible applications from doctrine, the strong believer may succumb to spiritual snobbishness, regarding with contempt the weak believer who operates on false norms and standards derived from his background.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One
text: 2. The verb exoutheneō (ἐξουθενέω) carries the specific force of contemptuous rejection. The present imperative with the negative mē (μή) demands that the strong believer stop an action already in progress: he is currently treating the weak believer with contempt and must immediately cease.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One
text: 3. The strong believer's flexibility in application is a strength that can become a failure. He is rightly flexible about non-essentials, but when he encounters the weak believer's legalism, he applies his inflexibility to a person rather than to a doctrine — reproducing the very rigidity he despises.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One
text: 4. When a believer retaliates against an antagonist, he does not maintain his own standards — he adopts the antagonist's. The strong believer who responds to the legalist with contempt has accepted the legalist's framework of judgment, merely reversing the direction of the verdict.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One
text: 5. The occupational hazard of the weak or legalistic believer is judging the mature believer. The weak believer is the worst spiritual bully: self-righteous, arrogant, petty, implacable, and inflexible in peripheral matters while indifferent to the central realities of the spiritual life.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One
text: 6. The verb krinō (κρίνω) with the negative mē in the present imperative commands the weak believer to stop judging — an action already in progress. The present tense indicates continuous action; the imperative mood of prohibition demands its immediate cessation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One
text: 7. The arrogance of the strong believer and the arrogance of the weak believer differ in expression but share a common root. The strong believer's arrogance is intellectual — superiority of doctrinal knowledge wielded as contempt. The weak believer's arrogance is performative — pride of accomplishment in a taboo system elevated to the status of divine requirement.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One
text: 8. Paul's commands are symmetrical: neither party is exempted from correction, and neither is commanded to change his dietary practice. The issue is not what each believer eats but how each believer treats the other. Both are commanded to honor the privacy of the royal priesthood and to cease using personal conviction as an instrument of coercion.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One
text: 9. The royal family honor code requires impersonal love — consistent, non-retaliatory regard for all believers regardless of their doctrinal condition. Contempt on the part of the strong believer is a violation of this principle, just as judging on the part of the weak believer is a violation of the privacy of the priesthood.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-One
text: 10. Doctrinal maturity does not eliminate the possibility of arrogance; it shifts the form arrogance takes. The remedy in both cases is the same: continued residence and function under the filling of the Holy Spirit, with maximum Bible doctrine in the soul controlling the believer's evaluation of and conduct toward others.

Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two

section: Romans 14:3–4 — Friendship with God, the Royal Family Honor Code, and the Household Slave
text: Romans 14:3–4 — Friendship with God, the Royal Family Honor Code, and the Household Slave

section: Romans 14:3–4 — Friendship with God, the Royal Family Honor Code, and the Household Slave
text: Romans 14:3–4 “Let not the one who eats despise the one who abstains, and let not the one who abstains pass judgment on the one who eats, for God has welcomed him. Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another? It is before his own master that he stands or falls. And he will be upheld, for the Lord is able to make him stand.” (ESV)

section: Romans 14:3–4 — Friendship with God, the Royal Family Honor Code, and the Household Slave
text: Corrected translation: He who eats — the mature or strong believer — let him stop regarding with contempt that one who does not eat — the weak believer. Furthermore, he who does not eat — the taboo weak believer — stop judging that one — the mature believer — who keeps on eating everything. For the God has admitted him into friendship. You there — who are you, the one who keeps judging a house slave belonging to another?

section: Romans 14:3–4 — Friendship with God, the Royal Family Honor Code, and the Household Slave
text: Romans 14 continues Paul's sustained treatment of the two categories of believers in the Roman congregations: the mature or strong believer, who understands that Christian freedom in non-essential matters rests on doctrine, and the weak believer, whose norms and standards derive from environment, background, and legalistic influence rather than from Bible doctrine. Verse 3 closes with a theologically decisive phrase — 'for God has admitted him into friendship' — and verse 4 opens with a direct, personal address to the weak believer, grounding the prohibition against judging in the social and legal norms governing the household slave in the Roman Empire.

section: I. The Two Occupational Hazards: Contempt and Judging (Romans 14:3)
text: I. The Two Occupational Hazards: Contempt and Judging (Romans 14:3)

section: I. The Two Occupational Hazards: Contempt and Judging (Romans 14:3)
text: Each of the two categories in Romans 14 carries a characteristic besetting sin. The mature believer is tempted to regard the weak believer with contempt. The weak believer is tempted to judge and bully the mature believer. These are not symmetric failures; they arise from opposite orientations to doctrine and application.

section: A. The Weak Believer: Inflexible in Application, Flexible in Doctrine
text: A. The Weak Believer: Inflexible in Application, Flexible in Doctrine

section: A. The Weak Believer: Inflexible in Application, Flexible in Doctrine
text: The weak believer may be weak for either of two reasons: he is reversionistic — he has regressed from whatever doctrinal ground he once occupied — or he is simply a new believer who has not yet accumulated sufficient doctrine to form a doctrinal frame of reference. In either case, his norms and standards are not derived from Bible doctrine but from environment, background, academic training, and the influence of other believers who may themselves be legalistic or antinomian.

section: A. The Weak Believer: Inflexible in Application, Flexible in Doctrine
text: The defining characteristic of the weak believer is his inversion of the correct relationship between doctrine and application. The mature believer is inflexible with regard to doctrine and flexible with regard to application: doctrine is fixed, and application varies with circumstances. The weak believer reverses this. He is inflexible in application — his taboos and non-essential standards are non-negotiable — but he is flexible, even indifferent, toward doctrine itself. This inversion makes him appear strong on the surface while rendering him spiritually weak at the core.

section: B. The Strong Believer: The Occupational Hazard of Contempt
text: B. The Strong Believer: The Occupational Hazard of Contempt

section: B. The Strong Believer: The Occupational Hazard of Contempt
text: The mature believer, sustained by years of doctrine intake and familiar with the freedom that doctrinal understanding confers, faces a different temptation. When subjected to the judging and bullying of the weak believer, the natural response is contempt — a looking down on the legalistic or antinomian critic as beneath serious engagement. This attitude violates the principle of impersonal love, which is the strong believer's obligation under the royal family honor code.

section: II. 'For the God Has Admitted Him into Friendship' — Exegesis of Romans 14:3b
text: II. 'For the God Has Admitted Him into Friendship' — Exegesis of Romans 14:3b

section: A. The Conjunction and Its Function
text: A. The Conjunction and Its Function

section: A. The Conjunction and Its Function
text: The explanatory clause is introduced by the post-positive conjunctive particle gar (γάρ), used here in its explanatory function: what follows gives the ground for the double prohibition of contempt and judging. The nominative singular subject is ho theos (ὁ θεός), with the generic use of the definite article. The generic article comprehends a category as a single whole and distinguishes it from all other categories; the translation 'the God' is therefore precise: the God, as opposed to all other claimants to divine authority.

section: B. Proslambanō: Admitted into Friendship
text: B. Proslambanō: Admitted into Friendship

section: B. Proslambanō: Admitted into Friendship
text: The verbal form is the aorist middle indicative of proslambanō (προσλαμβάνω), a compound of pros (πρός, toward, into) and lambanō (λαμβάνω, to take, to receive). The verb carries the sense of admitting someone into one's circle, receiving into friendship or fellowship. The aorist tense here is constantive: it gathers the entire action into a single whole and refers to the fact that the mature believer has crossed the maturity barrier and entered into the status of friend of God. The indirect middle voice indicates that the God produces the action of admitting without participating in the results; the action originates entirely with God.

section: B. Proslambanō: Admitted into Friendship
text: The direct object is the intensive pronoun auton (αὐτόν), accusative singular. Koine Greek possesses no third-person personal pronoun; the intensive pronoun autos (αὐτός) fills that function. The referent is the mature or strong believer — not every believer indiscriminately.

section: B. Proslambanō: Admitted into Friendship
text: The corrected translation of the clause is therefore: 'For the God has admitted him — the strong believer — into friendship.' The indicative mood is declarative, asserting a dogmatic statement of doctrine: the mature believer is the friend of God.

section: C. 'Friend of God' as a Technical Term
text: C. 'Friend of God' as a Technical Term

section: C. 'Friend of God' as a Technical Term
text: Friendship with God is not a general description of the divine-human relationship available to every believer regardless of spiritual condition. It is a technical designation for the mature believer — one who has cracked the maturity barrier through sustained intake of Bible doctrine and has thereby come to share the thinking of Christ.

section: C. 'Friend of God' as a Technical Term
text: The scriptural precedent is Abraham. Three passages establish the technical connotation of the term:

section: C. 'Friend of God' as a Technical Term
text: 2 Chronicles 20:7 — Abraham is called the friend of God in the context of God's covenant faithfulness to Israel, appealed to by Jehoshaphat in prayer. The designation is not casual; it reflects Abraham's long history of doctrinal orientation and faith response.

section: C. 'Friend of God' as a Technical Term
text: James 2:23 — 'Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness — and he was called a friend of God.' The connection between imputed righteousness and the designation 'friend' confirms that friendship is a post-salvation status attained through doctrinal advance, not a benefit of salvation itself.

section: C. 'Friend of God' as a Technical Term
text: Exodus 33:11 — Moses is said to have spoken with the Lord 'face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.' Moses as a mature believer, saturated with doctrine and deeply oriented to the divine plan, qualifies for the designation.

section: C. 'Friend of God' as a Technical Term
text: The concept of friendship in the ancient world carried the connotation of intimacy of mind — the capacity to sit at table with another and share thought, perspective, and counsel. Friendship with God means possessing the thinking of Christ, which is Bible doctrine resident in the soul and human spirit, to such a degree that genuine communication with God is possible. The believer who lacks doctrine in the soul has no frame of reference from which to engage God's thinking and therefore does not qualify for the designation.

section: C. 'Friend of God' as a Technical Term
text: The reversionistic believer, by contrast, is described in Philippians 3:18 as an enemy of the cross of Christ, and in James 4:4 friendship with the world is identified as enmity toward God. The weak believer retains his eternal relationship with God — that relationship is secured by the imputation of eternal life to the human spirit, which nothing can reverse — but he is not God's friend. He is saved and in a permanent relationship with God, but the qualitative intimacy of friendship is absent.

text: A. Human Life and the Soul

section: A. Human Life and the Soul
text: At physical birth, human life is imputed by God to its divinely prepared home, the human soul. This imputation is permanent and irrevocable. No sin, no act of the will, no external force — not even physical death — can remove human life from the soul. Physical death is the departure of the soul from the body; it is not the removal of human life from the soul. The soul with its human life continues to exist after physical death, in either positive or negative eternal states.

section: A. Human Life and the Soul
text: This permanence of human life in the soul is the foundation for understanding both logistical grace and eternal security. Logistical grace — God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical life — rests on the fact that God has placed His gift of human life in the soul and is committed to sustaining the vessel that houses it.

section: B. Eternal Life and the Human Spirit
text: B. Eternal Life and the Human Spirit

section: B. Eternal Life and the Human Spirit
text: At salvation, the Holy Spirit creates the human spirit — regeneration — and eternal life is imputed to this newly created home. Before salvation the individual is dichotomous: body and soul. At salvation he becomes trichotomous: body, soul, and spirit. Eternal life in the human spirit is equally irrevocable. Nothing the believer does or fails to do can remove eternal life from the human spirit. The doctrine of eternal security rests on the same structural logic as the permanence of human life in the soul: the imputation is divine, permanent, and not conditional on human performance.

section: B. Eternal Life and the Human Spirit
text: Ignorance of imputation is one of the root causes of weak-believer theology. The weak believer does not understand that his relationship with God is secured by divine act, not by doctrinal knowledge or moral performance. This misunderstanding generates both the fear of losing salvation and the compensatory legalism that expresses itself in judging others.

section: C. Doctrine in the Soul and Spirit: The Mechanism of Advance
text: C. Doctrine in the Soul and Spirit: The Mechanism of Advance

section: C. Doctrine in the Soul and Spirit: The Mechanism of Advance
text: Spiritual advance is not a function of external religious activity — witnessing, giving, moral behavior — but of doctrine resident in the soul and human spirit. The soul has two lobes: the left lobe, which processes information at the level of cognition and can reproduce doctrine in parrot fashion, and the right lobe — the heart — where the conscience resides and from which doctrinal application to life is made. Only doctrine transferred from the left lobe to the right lobe, through the Grace Apparatus for Perception under the filling of the Holy Spirit, can be applied to life.

section: C. Doctrine in the Soul and Spirit: The Mechanism of Advance
text: Doctrine in the human spirit constructs the edification complex — the interior structure of spiritual maturity described in Ephesians. The norms and standards that govern a believer's application to life derive from doctrine resident in the human spirit, not from environment, background, or the opinions of other believers. The weak believer, lacking doctrine in both soul and spirit, operates his human life on pre-doctrinal norms and standards, producing the characteristic behaviors of legalism, antinomianism, judging, and bullying.

section: D. The Filling of the Holy Spirit
text: D. The Filling of the Holy Spirit

section: D. The Filling of the Holy Spirit
text: The spiritual status of the individual depends on two factors. First, the Holy Spirit who permanently indwells the body must control the soul — the condition called the filling of the Spirit. This is a binary condition: the believer is either filled or not filled. The Holy Spirit is never lost; the command is not to be indwelt but to be filled — to walk by means of the Spirit. Second, doctrine must be resident in the right lobe and the human spirit. Both factors together determine where the believer stands on the continuum from weakness to maturity.

section: IV. Romans 14:4 — 'You There: Who Do You Think You Are?'
text: IV. Romans 14:4 — 'You There: Who Do You Think You Are?'

section: A. The Proleptical Personal Pronoun
text: A. The Proleptical Personal Pronoun

section: A. The Proleptical Personal Pronoun
text: Verse 4 opens with the vocative singular of the personal pronoun su (σύ), placed in the proleptical position — before the main verb and its object — for maximum rhetorical emphasis. The proleptical pronoun functions as a direct, personal address that interrupts the flow of argument to confront the weak believer personally: 'You there.' The effect in the Greek syntax is to force the inattentive weak believer to attention before the indictment is delivered.

section: B. The Interrogative Pronoun: 'Who Do You Think You Are?'
text: B. The Interrogative Pronoun: 'Who Do You Think You Are?'

section: B. The Interrogative Pronoun: 'Who Do You Think You Are?'
text: The nominative singular interrogative pronoun tis (τίς) follows: 'You there — who are you?' In context this is an idiom of indignant challenge equivalent to 'Who do you think you are?' The interrogative is not a request for biographical information; it is a challenge to the weak believer's assumed authority to judge another believer.

section: C. The Articular Participle: Habitual Judging
text: C. The Articular Participle: Habitual Judging

section: C. The Articular Participle: Habitual Judging
text: The participial phrase is built on the articular present active participle of krinō (κρίνω), to judge. The definite article functions as a reality pronoun, identifying the participle with the known activity of the weak believer. The present tense is descriptive, indicating linear, ongoing action: 'the one who keeps judging.' The active voice confirms that the weak believer is the one producing this action.

section: D. The House Slave: Allotrion Oiketēn
text: D. The House Slave: Allotrion Oiketēn

section: D. The House Slave: Allotrion Oiketēn
text: The direct object is accusative singular from the adjective allotrios (ἀλλότριος), meaning 'belonging to another,' modifying the accusative singular noun oiketēs (οἰκέτης), which denotes specifically a house slave — a domestic servant — as distinct from the field hand (doulos, δοῦλος). The choice of oiketēs rather than the more generic doulos is exegetically significant and carries a precise social reference.

section: D. The House Slave: Allotrion Oiketēn
text: The full phrase: 'You there — who are you, the one who keeps judging a house slave belonging to another?'

section: V. The Roman Household Slave and the Ethics of Criticism
text: V. The Roman Household Slave and the Ethics of Criticism

section: A. The Social Code of the Roman Imperial Household
text: A. The Social Code of the Roman Imperial Household

section: A. The Social Code of the Roman Imperial Household
text: One of the most firmly established norms of Roman imperial social etiquette was the prohibition against criticizing another person's domestic slaves. In the social structure of the Roman Empire, the household slave — the oiketēs — occupied a position of considerable dignity and often of extraordinary intellectual attainment. To criticize such a slave directly, rather than addressing any complaint to the slave's master, was considered a gross breach of manners — evidence of low breeding and social ignorance. The critic was regarded as placing himself far below the slave he presumed to censure.

section: B. Categories of the Roman Household Slave
text: B. Categories of the Roman Household Slave

section: B. Categories of the Roman Household Slave
text: The Roman imperial household included several distinct categories of domestic slave, each with recognized status and function:

section: B. Categories of the Roman Household Slave
text: First, the paedagogus — the educated Greek slave who served as tutor and educator for the children of the household. These individuals were often among the most intellectually accomplished persons in the empire, equivalent in learning to university professors. They constituted what might be called the peripatetic university of the Roman household.

section: B. Categories of the Roman Household Slave
text: Second, domestic slaves responsible for the maintenance of the household — cleaning, organization, and the daily operation of the physical premises.

section: B. Categories of the Roman Household Slave
text: Third, the body servant — the personal valet or lady's maid — who attended to the physical needs and presentation of the master or mistress.

section: B. Categories of the Roman Household Slave
text: Fourth, the kitchen staff: the head chef, under-chefs, those who served at table, and — regarded as one of the most important of all household domestics — the wine steward. The wine steward was expected to possess extensive knowledge of vintages, grape varieties, aging, and regional production. Such slaves were highly educated in their discipline and commanded respect commensurate with their expertise.

section: B. Categories of the Roman Household Slave
text: In the time of the emperor Claudius — immediately preceding the composition of Romans — certain freed household slaves had risen to positions of imperial administration, effectively governing the empire. The house slave of the Roman imperial period was therefore not a figure of contempt but of dignity, competence, and often of genuine authority.

section: C. The Theological Application
text: C. The Theological Application

section: C. The Theological Application
text: Paul's use of the household slave image is precise. Every believer is a domestic slave of the Lord Jesus Christ. The master is Christ; the household is the royal family of God. When the weak believer judges the strong believer, he is doing precisely what Roman social etiquette prohibited: criticizing another person's house slave directly, without going to the master. The proper recourse for any complaint is the master — that is, prayer and the application of doctrine, not personal judgment and public criticism.

section: C. The Theological Application
text: The strong believer, as the friend of God, is God's house slave of highest standing. To judge him is not merely a social impropriety; it is an assault on the master's household and an implicit challenge to the master's judgment in admitting this particular slave into friendship. The weak believer who judges the strong believer is, in effect, judging God.

section: C. The Theological Application
text: The principle extends to the entire royal family. No believer has been authorized to serve as judge over another believer in the non-essential matters of application. Two exceptions exist: parents bear the responsibility of judging their minor children as an inseparable part of training and authority, and the pastor-teacher bears a carefully bounded responsibility to judge and, when necessary, to remove from the congregation those who violate the privacy of the priesthood and disrupt the environment of doctrinal learning. Outside these two categories, the prohibition is absolute.

section: VI. The Royal Family Honor Code: Two Violations, Two Principles
text: VI. The Royal Family Honor Code: Two Violations, Two Principles

section: VI. The Royal Family Honor Code: Two Violations, Two Principles
text: Romans 14:3–4 identifies two distinct violations of the royal family honor code, one characteristic of each category of believer.

section: A. The Weak Believer: Violation of the Privacy of the Priesthood
text: A. The Weak Believer: Violation of the Privacy of the Priesthood

section: A. The Weak Believer: Violation of the Privacy of the Priesthood
text: Every Church Age believer is a royal priest. Royal priesthood carries with it the right of privacy in the believer's relationship with God. No other believer has standing to intrude upon that private relationship by judging, maligning, gossiping, or criticizing the manner in which another believer exercises his priestly function before God. The weak believer's habitual judging of the strong believer in matters of non-essential application is a direct violation of this privacy.

section: A. The Weak Believer: Violation of the Privacy of the Priesthood
text: The weak believer's judging arises from arrogance — the mental attitude sin that places his own norms and standards above those of every other person and above the freedom that doctrine confers. From arrogance comes implacability, from implacability comes the persistent campaign of maligning and bullying that characterizes the legalistic or antinomian weak believer.

section: B. The Strong Believer: Violation of Impersonal Love
text: B. The Strong Believer: Violation of Impersonal Love

section: B. The Strong Believer: Violation of Impersonal Love
text: The strong believer's occupational hazard is contempt — the attitude that regards the weak believer as beneath engagement, unworthy of serious consideration, or simply stupid. This attitude violates the principle of impersonal love.

section: B. The Strong Believer: Violation of Impersonal Love
text: Impersonal love, as the term is used in this commentary's theological framework, is love in which the subject — the one loving — is emphasized rather than the object. The standard for impersonal love is derived from the norms and standards resident in the believer's own conscience, formed by doctrine. In personal love, by contrast, the object is emphasized: personal love for Christ (category one), for the right man or right woman (category two), or for close friends and family (category three) is responsive to the qualities of the object. Impersonal love is not responsive to the qualities of the object and therefore can be extended to the disagreeable, the ignorant, and the hostile — including the weak believer who is actively maligning the strong believer.

section: B. The Strong Believer: Violation of Impersonal Love
text: The strong believer is not required to approve of the weak believer's behavior, to pretend that the legalism is harmless, or to refuse to resist the bullying. He is required to resist without contempt — maintaining the integrity of his own doctrinal orientation while extending impersonal love toward the one attacking him.

section: VII. Doctrine as the Remedy, Not the Cause
text: VII. Doctrine as the Remedy, Not the Cause

section: VII. Doctrine as the Remedy, Not the Cause
text: A persistent error of the weak believer is the association of sin with doctrine — the implicit or explicit claim that exposure to Bible teaching somehow causes or enables sinful behavior. This error rests on a failure to understand the doctrine of the old sin nature.

section: VII. Doctrine as the Remedy, Not the Cause
text: The old sin nature — the sin capacity inherited at physical birth through the male genetic line — is the sole source of personal sin. Doctrine comes from God. God cannot sin, cannot be tempted, and cannot solicit to sin. Therefore doctrine cannot be the cause of sin. Doctrine restrains sin; it does not produce it.

section: VII. Doctrine as the Remedy, Not the Cause
text: The observation that believers who take in doctrine continue to commit sins is not evidence against doctrine; it is evidence that believers continue to possess old sin natures. The remedy for the old sin nature's influence is more doctrine, not less — specifically, rebound (the naming of known sins to God, restoring fellowship with the Holy Spirit) and sustained doctrinal intake that progressively transforms the norms and standards of the right lobe.

section: VII. Doctrine as the Remedy, Not the Cause
text: The weak believer's antagonism toward doctrine, when he cannot be separated from it by apathy, becomes the mechanism by which negative volition operates: if the weak believer can be convinced that doctrine is the problem, he will separate himself from the only means of his own advance. This is the pattern of reversionism.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 1. The weak believer's occupational hazard is judging and bullying the mature believer. This judging arises from a set of norms and standards derived from environment, background, and legalistic or antinomian influence rather than from Bible doctrine. The weak believer is inflexible in application and flexible in doctrine — the precise inversion of the mature believer's orientation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 2. The strong believer's occupational hazard is contempt. Having advanced to maturity through sustained doctrine intake, the strong believer is tempted to regard the weak believer's ignorance and bullying with utter contempt. This violates the principle of impersonal love, which the royal family honor code demands. The strong believer may resist the bullying of legalism without the attitude of contempt.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 3. The phrase 'for the God has admitted him into friendship' is technically precise. The aorist middle indicative of proslambanō (προσλαμβάνω) refers to the completed action of God's admitting the mature believer into the status of friend — a status attained by cracking the maturity barrier through sustained doctrinal advance. The generic article with theos (θεός) distinguishes the God of Scripture from all other claimants to divine authority.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 4. 'Friend of God' is a technical term for the mature believer. It is not a general description of the divine-human relationship available to every believer. Abraham (2 Chronicles 20:7; James 2:23) and Moses (Exodus 33:11) are designated friends of God because they were mature believers. The reversionistic or immature believer is not the friend of God; Philippians 3:18 and James 4:4 describe such a believer as an enemy of the cross and of God respectively.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 5. The weak believer who judges the strong believer is judging the friend of God. The theological overtones are significant: the strong believer being maligned is God's domestic slave of highest standing. To judge him is implicitly to challenge the master's judgment and to intrude upon a relationship the master has deliberately established.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 6. Human life in the soul and eternal life in the human spirit are both permanent imputations. Nothing the believer does can remove human life from the soul or eternal life from the human spirit. Physical death is the departure of the soul from the body, not the removal of life from the soul. The doctrine of eternal security rests on the irrevocable nature of divine imputation, not on human performance.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 7. Before salvation the individual is dichotomous; at salvation he becomes trichotomous. The Holy Spirit creates the human spirit at regeneration — the divinely prepared home for eternal life. The Holy Spirit permanently indwells the body of every believer and is never lost. The command to the believer is not to be indwelt but to be filled — to walk by means of the Spirit.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 8. Spiritual advance depends on doctrine resident in the right lobe of the soul and in the human spirit. The left lobe processes doctrinal information at the cognitive level; application can only be made from the right lobe, where the conscience resides. Doctrine in the human spirit constructs the edification complex and provides the norms and standards from which the believer applies doctrine to life.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 9. The choice of oiketēs (οἰκέτης) rather than doulos (δοῦλος) is exegetically deliberate. The house slave carried specific social dignity in the Roman imperial world. To criticize another person's house slave directly — rather than addressing the master — was a recognized breach of etiquette that marked the critic as socially inferior to the slave he criticized. Every believer is a domestic slave of Christ; no believer has standing to judge another believer's slave.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 10. The proleptical personal pronoun su (σύ) at the opening of verse 4 is a direct personal confrontation. Paul addresses the weak believer personally and emphatically — 'You there' — before delivering the indictment: 'Who do you think you are, the one who keeps judging a house slave belonging to another?' The present active participle of krinō (κρίνω) indicates habitual, ongoing action.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 11. Two violations of the royal family honor code are present in Romans 14:3–4, one for each category. The weak believer violates the privacy of the royal priesthood by intruding upon the strong believer's private relationship with God through judging, maligning, and bullying. The strong believer violates the principle of impersonal love by responding with contempt. Each has failed a different principle in the same code.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 12. Doctrine is from God and cannot be the cause of sin. God cannot sin, cannot be tempted, and cannot solicit to sin. The old sin nature — not doctrine — is the source of personal sin. Believers who take in doctrine continue to sin because they continue to possess old sin natures. The weak believer's confusion of doctrine with sin is evidence of doctrinal ignorance and is one of the primary mechanisms by which negative volition sustains reversionism.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 13. Two exceptions to the prohibition against judging exist. Parents bear the God-given responsibility to judge their minor children as an inseparable part of authority and training. The pastor-teacher bears a bounded responsibility to judge those who violate the privacy of the congregation's priesthood, in order to maintain the environment of grace perception. Outside these two categories, the prohibition against judging other believers is absolute.
