section: Romans 15:15 — Grace, Spiritual Gift, and Logistical Support
text: Romans 15:15 — Grace, Spiritual Gift, and Logistical Support

section: Romans 15:15 — Grace, Spiritual Gift, and Logistical Support
text: Romans 15:15 “But on some points I have written to you very boldly by way of reminder, because of the grace given me by God” (ESV)

section: Romans 15:15 — Grace, Spiritual Gift, and Logistical Support
text: Corrected translation: In fact, I have written you more boldly — with greater alertness and audacity — in part, that is, in some parts of Romans, in such a way as to remind you again and again, because of that grace which has been given to me from the God.

section: Romans 15:15 — Grace, Spiritual Gift, and Logistical Support
text: Romans 15:15 stands within the concluding section of the epistle, where Paul transitions from doctrinal exposition to personal apostolic statement. Having developed the theme of strength through flexibility across the preceding verses, Paul now identifies the twin foundations of his ministry: the spiritual gift of apostleship that authorizes his communication, and the logistical grace that sustains both the communicator and the recipients. The verse crystallizes the relationship between grace received and doctrine imparted — the axis on which the entire epistle turns.

section: I. Boldness, Alertness, and the Purpose of Repetition
text: I. Boldness, Alertness, and the Purpose of Repetition

section: I. Boldness, Alertness, and the Purpose of Repetition
text: The opening phrase — 'in fact, I have written you more boldly in part' — identifies two qualities in Paul's writing: boldness and alertness. The Greek construction underlying the corrected translation conveys an audacity of expression and a sharpness of focus. Paul is not apologizing for the directness of certain passages in Romans; he is explaining it.

section: I. Boldness, Alertness, and the Purpose of Repetition
text: The phrase 'in part' specifies that this heightened register is not uniform throughout the epistle but appears in select passages where the doctrinal stakes are highest. Paul's stated purpose is to remind — not merely to inform for the first time. The repetition is deliberate and pedagogically essential.

section: I. Boldness, Alertness, and the Purpose of Repetition
text: The analogy to military training is instructive here. A soldier does not profit from combat experience as such; he profits from what he learned before entering the combat situation. The repeated drilling of fundamentals — weapons familiarization, tactical responses, command protocols — produces trained reflexes that function instinctively under extreme pressure. Paul's repeated doctrinal emphasis across Romans functions identically. The Roman believers are learning doctrine in a period of relative prosperity. The Neronian persecution will constitute their 'combat experience.' They will not profit from that experience per se; they will profit from what they have internalized beforehand.

section: I. Boldness, Alertness, and the Purpose of Repetition
text: This is the principle behind the injunction to study and teach doctrine systematically and repeatedly. Doctrine resident in the soul operates instinctively when crisis arrives. The believer who has cracked the maturity barrier does not need to reason through each disaster from first principles; the correct assessment, the right decision, the appropriate response, arise from structured doctrine already internalized. This is what Paul means by reminding 'again and again.'

section: II. 'Because of That Grace' — Grammatical Analysis
text: II. 'Because of That Grace' — Grammatical Analysis

section: II. 'Because of That Grace' — Grammatical Analysis
text: The phrase dia tēn charin (διὰ τὴν χάριν) — 'because of that grace' — is governed by dia plus the accusative singular of charis (χάρις), the standard New Testament term for grace. The construction expresses causal ground: Paul's bold, repeated teaching is grounded in and warranted by grace.

section: II. 'Because of That Grace' — Grammatical Analysis
text: The presence of the definite article is exegetically significant. Paul does not write simply 'because of grace' as an abstract principle. The article functions as a demonstrative pronoun, pointing to two specific, identifiable realities: (1) the spiritual gift of apostleship given to Paul, which authorizes and empowers his communication; and (2) the logistical grace by which God sustains Paul and the Roman believers so that the communication can be received and appropriated. Both are in view simultaneously.

section: A. Grace as Spiritual Gift
text: A. Grace as Spiritual Gift

section: A. Grace as Spiritual Gift
text: Paul's apostolic gift is the primary personal referent of 'that grace.' The gift of apostleship is a grace gift — not earned, not merited, not produced by superior personal character or effort. Paul received it at salvation and it was further defined at his commissioning. It carries with it extraordinary communicative authority: the ability to transmit and explain divine revelation with apostolic weight. This gift is why Paul can write with 'greater alertness and audacity in part' — the authority is not his own but is grace-derived.

section: A. Grace as Spiritual Gift
text: The same principle applies to the gift of pastor-teacher in the present Church Age. The spiritual gift of communication is a grace provision, not a human achievement. Authority in the local church is therefore grace-derived authority. It does not depend on the personal superiority of the individual who holds it, but on the divine appointment conveyed through the gift. When that authority is exercised under grace principles, it does not become tyranny; a double grace — grace-given authority used in a grace manner — cannot produce tyranny.

section: B. Grace as Logistical Support
text: B. Grace as Logistical Support

section: B. Grace as Logistical Support
text: The second specific referent of 'that grace' is logistical grace: the full system of divine provision by which God sustains the believer's physical existence from salvation to physical death or the Rapture. The term is borrowed from military science, where logistics denotes the supply, movement, and sustainment operations that support troops in every tactical situation — advance, retreat, exploitation, pursuit. For every soldier in combat, ten to twenty support personnel maintain the logistical chain that makes combat effectiveness possible. The combat soldier may be inclined to undervalue logistics until the moment the supply line fails.

section: B. Grace as Logistical Support
text: Divine logistics operates on an incomparably larger scale. God provides everything necessary for the believer's continued existence so that doctrine can be learned and applied. The components of logistical grace include:

section: B. Grace as Logistical Support
text: Life support: God sustains physical life according to His sovereign timetable. The believer remains alive because God wills it, and that continuation of life is itself a statement of divine purpose.

section: B. Grace as Logistical Support
text: Security: The believer's security does not rest on financial resources, social position, or human provision. The very fact of continued existence under divine sustenance is the foundation of security. Logistical support constitutes real security; human institutional arrangements are derivative and contingent.

section: B. Grace as Logistical Support
text: Time: God provides the duration of life necessary for the believer to advance spiritually. This includes the full material provision — food, shelter, clothing, transportation, a stable environment — required to sustain life while doctrine is being learned.

section: B. Grace as Logistical Support
text: Doctrinal provision: God provides the written Word, the local church as a teaching institution, and the right pastor-teacher with the spiritual gift of communication. The local church is not primarily a social organization; it is a classroom. Its function is the systematic transmission of Bible doctrine so that believers are equipped for every situation that will arise in the course of their lives.

section: B. Grace as Logistical Support
text: Freedom: The laws of divine establishment — including the protection of life, property, and privacy — create and maintain the conditions under which doctrine can be freely communicated and received. Military victory by client nations preserves the freedom that makes doctrinal teaching possible. The believer who rejects authority in the home, in the military, or in civil life will consistently reject the authority of the pastor-teacher and will therefore fail to advance spiritually.

section: B. Grace as Logistical Support
text: The supporting texts for logistical grace as a category include 1 Peter 3:18 — 'grow by means of grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior' — where charis refers to the logistical provision that makes spiritual momentum possible; and 1 Peter 5:12, 'I have written to you briefly, exhorting and testifying that this is the true grace of God — stand fast in it,' where stability itself is the fruit of logistical grace internalized through doctrine. Similarly, Hebrews 12:28 — 'since we have received an unshakable kingdom, let us keep holding grace, through which we render acceptable service to God with reverence and respect toward doctrinal teaching' — frames logistical grace as the basis for stable, God-honoring function.

section: III. Grace Received and Grace Expressed
text: III. Grace Received and Grace Expressed

section: III. Grace Received and Grace Expressed
text: The final clause of the verse — tēs dotheisēs moi (τῆς δοθείσης μοι) — 'which has been given to me' — employs the aorist passive participle of didōmi (δίδωμι), the standard term for giving as divine bestowment. The aorist tense here functions as a constative aorist, viewing the entire span of Paul's reception of grace — from his salvation through the moment of writing — as a single complete act. The passive voice identifies Paul as the recipient: the action originates with God and is directed toward Paul. The dative singular indirect object moi (μοι) — 'to me' — specifies that the grace was provided in Paul's interest. The prepositional phrase apo tou theou (ἀπὸ τοῦ θεοῦ) — 'from the God' — with the definite article on theos emphasizes the specific identity of the divine source.

section: III. Grace Received and Grace Expressed
text: Paul has been on the receiving end of grace from the moment of his salvation. In writing Romans he is on the giving end. Every passage of heightened alertness and doctrinal urgency in the epistle is the expression of grace received being transmitted to others. This is the pattern the Royal Family Honor Code makes explicit: believers who are the beneficiaries of divine grace are called to express grace toward others — not because they have earned the right to do so, but because grace received and understood naturally expresses itself in grace extended.

section: III. Grace Received and Grace Expressed
text: The believer who operates under the Royal Family Honor Code does not respond to provocation with retaliation, does not answer insult with injury, and does not leverage superior position to crush those who cannot defend themselves. This is not weakness; it is the highest expression of strength. Flexibility grounded in doctrine is strength. Flexibility without doctrine is instability. The grace-based response in a conflict situation — stepping back, absorbing an undeserved slight, declining to retaliate — requires more inner strength than any aggressive counter-response. It requires doctrine resident in the soul operating instinctively.

section: III. Grace Received and Grace Expressed
text: The Roman believers, well taught and approaching spiritual maturity, are about to enter a period of sustained historical pressure. They will face it not because of the combat experience itself but because of what they have already internalized. The principle is not unique to them. Every believer who advances through consistent doctrine intake — cracking the maturity barrier, moving through supergrace toward ultra-supergrace — builds the same reserve of structured truth from which instinctive, God-honoring decisions can be drawn under any pressure.

section: IV. The Corrected Translation in Full
text: IV. The Corrected Translation in Full

section: IV. The Corrected Translation in Full
text: The corrected translation of Romans 15:15 reads: 'In fact, I have written you more boldly — with greater alertness and audacity — in part, that is, in some parts of Romans, in such a way as to remind you again and again and again, because of that grace which has been given to me from the God.'

section: IV. The Corrected Translation in Full
text: The verse thus identifies grace as the single causal ground for everything Paul has written in Romans: the doctrinal architecture of chapters 1–8, the historical argument of chapters 9–11, the applied ethics of chapters 12–15, and the concluding personal section. All of it flows from grace — the gift that authorized the communication, and the logistical support that sustained both writer and readers so that the communication could take place and be received.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Five
text: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Five

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Five
text: 1. The definite article in 'because of that grace' is exegetically decisive. It points to two specific realities: the spiritual gift of apostleship that authorizes Paul's communication, and the logistical grace that sustains both the communicator and the recipients. Abstract appeals to 'grace' miss the specificity Paul intends.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Five
text: 2. Repetition in doctrinal teaching is not redundancy — it is pedagogy. Paul explicitly states that his purpose in writing with heightened boldness in certain passages is to remind the Roman believers 'again and again.' Doctrine must be drilled to become instinctive, exactly as tactical responses must be drilled before combat to function under pressure.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Five
text: 3. The believer profits from crisis not because of the experience itself but because of what was internalized beforehand. Combat experience benefits soldiers who were trained before entering battle. Disaster reveals what doctrine is resident in the soul, not what the experience itself teaches. The Roman believers facing Neronian persecution will draw on what they learned in the present period of prosperity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Five
text: 4. Logistical grace is the totality of divine provision that sustains the believer from salvation to physical death. It encompasses life support, security, time, material provision, the written Word, the local church as a teaching institution, the right pastor-teacher, and the freedom guaranteed by the laws of divine establishment. None of these provisions are earned; all are grace.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Five
text: 5. Spiritual gift authority is grace-derived authority and therefore does not depend on the personal superiority of the one who holds it. The pastor-teacher's communicative authority is a divine provision, not a human achievement. When that authority is exercised under grace principles, it cannot become tyranny. The Roman believers at the honor-roll level of maturity — including many women named in chapter 16 — reached that level precisely by accepting the authority structure God established.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Five
text: 6. Grace received must become grace expressed. Paul received grace from salvation through the moment of writing Romans; his writing is the expression of that grace toward others. The Royal Family Honor Code is not a system of rules imposed from outside; it is the natural crystallization of grace internalized through doctrine. Believers who understand what they have received on the receiving end must learn to extend it on the giving end.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Five
text: 7. The constative aorist passive of didōmi in 'which has been given to me' views Paul's entire reception of divine grace as a complete, unified act. The divine source is emphasized by the article on theos: the grace comes specifically from the God. Paul's bold writing is therefore not self-generated audacity but the output of a grace-sustained instrument.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Five
text: 8. Flexibility grounded in doctrine is strength; flexibility without doctrine is instability. The believer who has cracked the maturity barrier responds to pressure with instinctive, doctrinally shaped decisions — not because the pressure itself teaches him, but because structured truth in the soul automatically generates the correct assessment and response. This is the spiritual analogue of the trained military officer who categorizes and responds to combat stimuli automatically because of prior systematic training.

section: Romans 15:16 — Leitourgos, the Doctrine of Communication, and the Minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles
text: Romans 15:16 — Leitourgos, the Doctrine of Communication, and the Minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles

section: Romans 15:16 — Leitourgos, the Doctrine of Communication, and the Minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles
text: Romans 15:16 “to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.” (ESV)

section: Romans 15:16 — Leitourgos, the Doctrine of Communication, and the Minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles
text: Corrected translation: that I should be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles.

section: Romans 15:16 — Leitourgos, the Doctrine of Communication, and the Minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles
text: Romans 15:16 opens a purpose clause initiated by the Greek preposition eis with the accusative definite article, followed by a present active infinitive. The clause expresses the contemplated result of the grace given to Paul described in verse 15 — namely, his apostolic appointment as communicator of doctrine to the Gentiles. The governing noun of this verse is leitourgos, a term of rich semantic range that draws together the concepts of servant, government official, Levitical priest, and sacrificial minister. This chapter examines the word in its grammatical setting, traces the history of doctrinal communication from Moses through the present age, and defines the spiritual gift of pastor-teacher in relation to the other communication gifts of Ephesians 4:11.

section: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 15:16a
text: I. Grammatical Analysis of Romans 15:16a

section: The Purpose Clause: eis to with the Infinitive
text: The Purpose Clause: eis to with the Infinitive

section: The Purpose Clause: eis to with the Infinitive
text: The construction eis to (εἰς τό) followed by an infinitive introduces a purpose clause. Its function is to express the aim of the action denoted by the main verb of verse 15. This aim may reflect a deliberate design, a general direction, or — as here — a contemplated result. Grammarians sometimes call this a final clause, noting that it can exhibit shades of meaning ranging from strict purpose to intended result. The translation is: that I should be.

section: The Purpose Clause: eis to with the Infinitive
text: The accusative of general reference from the personal pronoun ego serves as the subject of the infinitive. The infinitive itself is drawn from the verb einai.

section: The Purpose Clause: eis to with the Infinitive
text: The present tense of einai (εἶναι) is a historical present, employed when a past event is viewed with the vividness of a present occurrence. The active voice indicates that Paul produces the action through the grace ministry of God — specifically through the Holy Spirit's provision of his spiritual gift. The infinitive of intended result is used when a result indicates or fulfills a deliberate objective, blending purpose and result: that I should be.

section: The Purpose Clause: eis to with the Infinitive
text: Whatever God intends for the believer to be, He guarantees complete logistical support. The same principle governed the Apostle Paul. Grace is in total support of what God intends.

section: Leitourgos: Semantic Range of the Word
text: Leitourgos: Semantic Range of the Word

section: Leitourgos: Semantic Range of the Word
text: The accusative singular noun leitourgos (λειτουργός) carries several related meanings: (1) a servant; (2) a government official — the term reflects the principle of divine establishment, under which government officials are servants, not masters; (3) a Levitical priest functioning at the altar, as the word is used in Hebrews 8:2; and (4) a communicator of Bible doctrine — in Paul's era designated apostle, in the present church age designated pastor-teacher.

section: Leitourgos: Semantic Range of the Word
text: The genitive of relationship that follows identifies the principal: Christ Jesus. The proper noun Christos emphasizes Christ's appointment and office; Iesous emphasizes His humanity. The prepositional phrase eis plus the accusative plural of ethnos — eis ta ethne — completes the commission: to the Gentiles.

section: Leitourgos: Semantic Range of the Word
text: That the smartest Jew who ever lived outside of the Lord should be appointed minister to the Gentiles is consistent with the pattern already established in Romans 15:12 from Isaiah 11:10, where Christ Himself is declared minister to the Gentiles. Paul is not greater than his Master; the same commission applies. While the dispensation of Israel emphasized the Jewish people, the dispensation of the Church emphasizes the Gentiles — without excluding Jewish believers, who hold exactly the same privileges as members of the royal family of God and the body of Christ. Because of the baptism of the Holy Spirit, unique to the Church Age, Jew and Gentile are one in Christ.

section: II. The Doctrine of Communication
text: II. The Doctrine of Communication

section: Definition and Scope
text: Definition and Scope

section: Definition and Scope
text: The appointment of Paul as leitourgos is the occasion for an examination of the doctrine of communication — the divinely authorized system by which Bible doctrine has been transmitted to believers in every dispensation since Moses.

section: Category One: The Old Testament Communicator — The Prophet
text: Category One: The Old Testament Communicator — The Prophet

section: Category One: The Old Testament Communicator — The Prophet
text: Prior to Moses, the question of who communicated doctrine is, strictly speaking, a matter of historical inference. The book of Genesis was written by Moses. Certain men prior to Moses are described as knowing doctrine — Noah, Adam, Abel, Seth — but none are explicitly designated as official communicators in the institutional sense. There is evidence that angels served as teachers in this period: Moses himself was taught by angels before he committed the Law to writing under the ministry of the Holy Spirit.

section: Category One: The Old Testament Communicator — The Prophet
text: Abraham was a receiver of doctrine and a witness, but not primarily an official communicator. Isaac, Jacob, and Joseph — however significant their roles in redemptive history — are not described as communicators in the sense of the Hebrew nabi. It is not until Moses that an official human communicator whose sole function is the transmission of doctrine appears in history.

section: Category One: The Old Testament Communicator — The Prophet
text: Moses was uniquely qualified: the crown prince of Egypt, adopted son of Hatshepsut, military hero, architectural and engineering genius, administrator whose systems outlasted his own era. He told God he was not eloquent; God assigned Aaron as spokesman. Moses eventually set Aaron aside and became, by general assessment, the world's greatest communicator of doctrine in the Old Testament period. He held both the office and the gift of prophet, and he communicated constantly.

section: Category One: The Old Testament Communicator — The Prophet
text: After Moses, two sub-categories of prophets appear throughout the dispensation of Israel: (1) those who held the office of prophet — official, full-time communicators of doctrine; and (2) those who held the gift of prophecy as one of several functions — Daniel, David, Solomon are examples. Both sub-categories received direct revelation from God and produced canonical Scripture or canonical-quality communication, yet their roles differed.

section: Category One: The Old Testament Communicator — The Prophet
text: The three sources available to the Old Testament prophet were: (1) direct communication — the voice of God; (2) the teaching ministry of angels; and (3) previously written Scripture, beginning with the writings of Moses.

section: Category Two: The Apostle — Pre-Canon Church Age (circa AD 30–96)
text: Category Two: The Apostle — Pre-Canon Church Age (circa AD 30–96)

section: Category Two: The Apostle — Pre-Canon Church Age (circa AD 30–96)
text: The Apostle Paul is the representative figure of this period. His two sources of doctrinal content were direct communication from God and the previously written Old Testament Scriptures. From these two sources he became the primary doctrinal voice of the New Testament, though John, Peter, James the half-brother of the Lord, Jude, Luke, and others also contributed to the canon.

section: Category Two: The Apostle — Pre-Canon Church Age (circa AD 30–96)
text: The apostolic gift carried the highest level of authority ever granted in the spiritual realm during the Church Age. Twelve apostles are recognized — Judas replaced by Matthias, and Paul added as the twelfth by direct divine appointment. The term apostle is also used in a secondary sense for certain missionaries who carried apostolic authority. No one has heard the voice of God directly since AD 96, when the canon of the New Testament was completed. Any claim to have heard the voice of God since that date is without biblical warrant.

section: Category Three: The Pastor-Teacher — Post-Canon Church Age
text: Category Three: The Pastor-Teacher — Post-Canon Church Age

section: Category Three: The Pastor-Teacher — Post-Canon Church Age
text: After the closing of the canon, the system of communication shifts to a single authorized form: the pastor-teacher. His two sources are the completed written Word of God and the training received from his own pastor-teacher. No direct revelation, no angelic instruction, no prophetic office supplements the written Word. The canon is sufficient.

section: Category Three: The Pastor-Teacher — Post-Canon Church Age
text: The spiritual gift of pastor-teacher is sovereignly bestowed by the Holy Spirit at the moment of salvation. It is not earned, surrendered for, or discovered through a vision or an auditory experience. It is discovered through two convergent means: (1) spiritual growth under consistent Bible teaching, through which the gift becomes apparent; and (2) a pattern of providential discipline that closes off other vocational options and directs the gifted individual toward his calling.

section: Category Three: The Pastor-Teacher — Post-Canon Church Age
text: The gift provides both authority and ability — not natural eloquence, charm, or platform presence, but the capacity to communicate doctrine in such a way that the congregation understands. The gift is compatible with a wide range of personalities, including those who are by temperament reserved or initially inarticulate.

section: The Sacrificial Character of the Communicator's Calling
text: The Sacrificial Character of the Communicator's Calling

section: The Sacrificial Character of the Communicator's Calling
text: The term leitourgos carries the connotation of altar sacrifice. The calling of a communicator of doctrine involves a genuine sacrifice: the deliberate foregoing of success in other fields for which the gifted man may be naturally qualified. The demands of consistent doctrine intake and consistent communication preclude the kind of normal professional and social life available to others. Paul himself — an ultra-supergrace believer who knew both abundance and deprivation — illustrates this principle. Historical obscurity is the general rule for the faithful communicator of doctrine. This is not unhappiness, but it is sacrifice.

section: Communication in the Tribulation
text: Communication in the Tribulation

section: Communication in the Tribulation
text: After the Church is removed, the dispensation of Israel resumes. The communication system in the Tribulation reverts to a form consistent with the Old Testament: 144,000 sealed Jewish witnesses, the two prophets Moses and Elijah returned, and angels communicating directly. Moses represents the greatest of the writing prophets; Elijah represents the greatest of the non-writing prophets. Their return provides continuity with the age of Israel and signals the resumption of that dispensation prior to the second advent of Christ.

section: III. The Five Communication Gifts of Ephesians 4:11
text: III. The Five Communication Gifts of Ephesians 4:11

section: III. The Five Communication Gifts of Ephesians 4:11
text: Ephesians 4:11–16 defines the purpose and ordering of the communication gifts given to the Church. Four gifts are listed in order of institutional priority.

section: 1. Apostle — Highest Authority
text: 1. Apostle — Highest Authority

section: 1. Apostle — Highest Authority
text: The apostle held the highest spiritual authority given to any communicator in the Church Age. The office required direct appointment by the risen Christ, direct revelation, and eyewitness qualification (in the case of the Twelve). The gift and office of apostle ceased with the closing of the canon. There are no apostles in the present era.

section: 2. Prophet — Carryover from the Dispensation of Israel
text: 2. Prophet — Carryover from the Dispensation of Israel

section: 2. Prophet — Carryover from the Dispensation of Israel
text: The gift of prophecy in the early Church Age was a carryover from the dispensation of Israel, serving the transitional period before the New Testament canon was completed. It, too, ceased at the closing of the canon. There are no prophets in the present era.

section: 3. Evangelist — Specialist in Gospel Communication
text: 3. Evangelist — Specialist in Gospel Communication

section: 3. Evangelist — Specialist in Gospel Communication
text: The gift of evangelism is a permanent communication gift for the duration of the Church Age. The evangelist possesses a unique capacity to present the gospel to unbelievers in such a way that they will listen and respond — regardless of setting, demographic, or cultural context. This is not the same as witnessing, which every believer is commanded to do. Witnessing is a function; evangelism is a gift.

section: 3. Evangelist — Specialist in Gospel Communication
text: The evangelist is listed before the pastor-teacher in Ephesians 4:11 because the pastor-teacher requires an audience of believers. Without the conversion of unbelievers, there is no congregation to teach. The evangelistic gift is the prerequisite for the pastoral gift in terms of church formation — both at home and on the mission field.

section: 3. Evangelist — Specialist in Gospel Communication
text: The gift of evangelism is designed to operate outside the local church assembly, in the sphere where unbelievers are found. Conducting evangelistic campaigns inside a church building, directed primarily at the existing congregation, inverts the design of the gift. The evangelist belongs on neutral or hostile ground, among those who have not yet believed.

section: 3. Evangelist — Specialist in Gospel Communication
text: The evangelist is frequently undertrained in doctrine — this is a historical pattern, not a design feature. The gift does not compensate for doctrinal ignorance; it operates in spite of it, because God honors the gift. But an evangelist who combines the gift with rigorous doctrinal training is far more effective and accurate. The appropriate response to an evangelist's doctrinal imprecision is not public criticism; it is recognition that the gift is sovereign and that God the Holy Spirit uses it to produce genuine conversion.

section: 4. Pastor-Teacher — Permanent Gift for the Church Age
text: 4. Pastor-Teacher — Permanent Gift for the Church Age

section: 4. Pastor-Teacher — Permanent Gift for the Church Age
text: The gift of pastor-teacher is designated in the New Testament by five distinct Greek terms, each highlighting a different dimension of the calling:

section: 4. Pastor-Teacher — Permanent Gift for the Church Age
text: (1) Presbuteros (πρεσβύτερος) — translated 'elder' in most English versions, but better rendered 'old man' in the sense of commanding officer. The term denotes authority, not age. There is one presbuteros per congregation; the concept of a rotating plurality of elders sharing preaching responsibility is without New Testament warrant and contrary to the principle of unity of command.

section: 4. Pastor-Teacher — Permanent Gift for the Church Age
text: (2) Poimenas (ποιμένας) — shepherd. Connotes both authority and provision. Used in combination with didaskalos (διδάσκαλος) to form the compound designation pastor-teacher. Those under the pastor's teaching are students under strict academic discipline.

section: 4. Pastor-Teacher — Permanent Gift for the Church Age
text: (3) Episkopos (ἐπίσκοπος) — overseer, guardian of the system. Administrative in the sense of policy-making. Because of intensive doctrine intake, the pastor is aware of what is doctrinally correct and incorrect, and therefore functions as the policy maker and guardian of the local church. The English word 'episcopal' derives from this term.

section: 4. Pastor-Teacher — Permanent Gift for the Church Age
text: (4) Diakonos (διάκονος) — servant, originally a table waiter. Emphasizes the servant function of the communicator in serving spiritual food to the congregation.

section: 4. Pastor-Teacher — Permanent Gift for the Church Age
text: (5) Leitourgos (λειτουργός) — minister, one who performs sacrificial service. As used by Paul in Romans 15:16, it combines the concepts of servant, government official, Levitical priest, and sacrificial minister — the full range of what it means to communicate doctrine as a calling.

section: The Purpose of the Pastor-Teacher: Ephesians 4:12–16
text: The Purpose of the Pastor-Teacher: Ephesians 4:12–16

section: The Purpose of the Pastor-Teacher: Ephesians 4:12–16
text: Ephesians 4:12 states the purpose of the pastor-teacher: training and equipping the saints for the angelic conflict. Verse 13 identifies the goal: that the entire royal family attain spiritual maturity — full knowledge of the Son of God, the standard of the fullness of Christ. This goal requires consistency of doctrine intake over time; irregular or occasional attendance cannot produce the maturity that the passage envisions.

section: The Purpose of the Pastor-Teacher: Ephesians 4:12–16
text: Verse 14 identifies what maturity prevents: doctrinal instability — being tossed by waves and carried by every wind of false doctrine, by the cunning methods of those who employ deception in the service of error.

section: The Purpose of the Pastor-Teacher: Ephesians 4:12–16
text: Verses 15–16 describe the mature outcome: teaching doctrine in the sphere of love — impersonal love operating through the royal family honor code — causing growth up into Christ, the absolute chief, from whom the whole body is joined and taught categorically through every joint of supply. The pastor is the joint of supply. Each member of the body functions according to the measure of operational power allotted to it, producing growth that results in the edification complex belonging to itself in love.

section: The Purpose of the Pastor-Teacher: Ephesians 4:12–16
text: The chain of dependence is direct: no evangelist, no converts; no converts, no congregation; no congregation, no pastor; no pastor, no edification complex; no edification complex, no maturity adjustment; no maturity adjustment, no fulfillment of the Protocol Plan of God at the individual or national level.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six
text: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six
text: 1. Leitourgos carries a range of meaning that encompasses servant, government official, Levitical priest, and sacrificial minister. Paul uses it of himself in Romans 15:16 to capture the full weight of his apostolic commission as a communicator of doctrine to the Gentiles. All five New Testament terms for the communicator — presbuteros, poimenas, episkopos, diakonos, leitourgos — describe different dimensions of a single office.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six
text: 2. Whatever God intends the believer to be, He provides complete logistical support for that calling. The grace that appointed Paul as minister to the Gentiles (verse 15) is the same grace that underwrites his function as leitourgos in verse 16. The principle applies universally: God's logistical grace is coextensive with His intended purpose for each believer.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six
text: 3. The appointment of the smartest Jew outside of Christ as minister to the Gentiles is consistent with the pattern of Romans 15:12. Christ Himself was declared minister to the Gentiles (Isaiah 11:10); Paul follows his Master. The Church Age does not exclude Jewish believers — it includes them with full equality in the royal family of God, the body of Christ, united by the baptism of the Holy Spirit.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six
text: 4. The doctrine of communication identifies three successive systems of doctrinal transmission since Moses. The Old Testament prophet received doctrine from three sources: the voice of God, the teaching of angels, and previously written Scripture. The New Testament apostle received it from two: direct divine communication and the Old Testament. The post-canon pastor-teacher receives it from two: the completed written Word and his own pastor-teacher. No one has heard the voice of God since AD 96.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six
text: 5. Moses and Paul are the two supreme communicators of their respective dispensational periods. Moses was the first official human communicator of doctrine in history and is unique to Israel as Paul is unique to the Gentile mission of the Church Age. Neither began as a communicator; both were prepared by divine providence through extended prior training in other fields.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six
text: 6. The spiritual gift of pastor-teacher is sovereignly bestowed by the Holy Spirit at salvation and is not earned, surrendered for, or confirmed by an auditory or visionary experience. It is discovered through spiritual growth and providential discipline. The gift provides both authority and ability independent of natural temperament or native eloquence. There is one pastor-teacher per congregation; the concept of a rotating plurality of elders sharing the teaching function is without New Testament warrant.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six
text: 7. The gift of evangelism is a permanent communication gift for the duration of the Church Age and is listed ahead of the pastor-teacher in Ephesians 4:11 because it is the prerequisite for the formation of a congregation. Without conversion there is no congregation; without a congregation there is no pastoral teaching ministry. The gift is designed to operate outside the church assembly among unbelievers. Doctrinal imprecision in an evangelist does not nullify the gift; God honors the gift. Public criticism of the evangelistic gift is contrary to the recognition that the Holy Spirit sovereignly distributes it.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six
text: 8. Spiritual maturity — the goal stated in Ephesians 4:13 — requires consistency of doctrine intake under a single right pastor-teacher. Irregular or eclectic exposure to teaching cannot produce maturity. The maturity barrier is cracked through sustained, consistent doctrine under the GAP (Grace Apparatus for Perception), leading to supergrace and ultimately ultra-supergrace. No believer advances in the Protocol Plan of God apart from this system.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six
text: 9. The calling of the communicator involves genuine sacrifice in the leitourgos sense — altar sacrifice. The demands of consistent doctrine intake and consistent communication foreclose extended engagement in other professional or social activities for which the gifted man may be naturally qualified. Historical obscurity is the normal result for the faithful communicator. This is not deprivation but the shape of the calling itself.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Six
text: 10. The purpose clause of Romans 15:16a — eis to einai me leitourgon — blends purpose and intended result. Paul's apostolic appointment to the Gentiles is simultaneously God's deliberate design and the contemplated result of the grace given in verse 15. Logistical grace and spiritual gift are not separable: the one sustains the other throughout the communicator's ministry.

Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven

section: Romans 15:16 — Priestly Ministry and the Communication of Doctrine
text: Romans 15:16 — Priestly Ministry and the Communication of Doctrine

section: Romans 15:16 — Priestly Ministry and the Communication of Doctrine
text: Romans 15:15b–16 “…because of the grace given me by God to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel of God, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit.” (ESV)

section: Romans 15:16 — Priestly Ministry and the Communication of Doctrine
text: Corrected translation: …because of the grace which has been given to me from God, that I should be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, ministering as a priest the good news of God, in order that the offering consisting of the Gentiles might be acceptable, having been sanctified by the Holy Spirit.

section: Romans 15:16 — Priestly Ministry and the Communication of Doctrine
text: Romans 15 continues Paul's extended personal statement begun in verse 15, where he defends the audacity of his letter by appealing to the grace commission entrusted to him. Having established that he is a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, the text moves deeper into the character of that ministry. Verse 16 introduces a Greek participle that reframes the entire discussion: Paul does not merely preach — he officiates as a priest, presenting the Gentiles themselves as a living offering to God. This chapter examines the meaning of that priestly service, its relationship to the communication of doctrine, and its application to any believer equipped and motivated to teach.

section: I. The Participle: Ministering as a Priest
text: I. The Participle: Ministering as a Priest

section: I. The Participle: Ministering as a Priest
text: The key word in verse 16 is the present active participle translated 'ministering' in most English versions. The Greek term is

section: I. The Participle: Ministering as a Priest
text: hierourgounta (ἱερουργοῦντα), the present active participle of the verb hierourgeō (ἱερουργέω), a compound of hieros (ἱερός, sacred, holy) and ergazomai (ἐργάζομαι, to work, to perform). The compound means to perform sacred rites — specifically the ritual functions of a priest at the altar.

section: I. The Participle: Ministering as a Priest
text: The present tense is progressive: the priestly action is continuous, linear, and sustained. Paul is not describing a single act of proclamation but an ongoing mode of ministry. The participle modifies his role as a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles and specifies the manner in which that ministry is executed.

section: I. The Participle: Ministering as a Priest
text: In the Levitical system, the priest did not merely speak — he acted visibly before the congregation. He placed the animal on the altar, explained its significance, transferred the worshiper's sins symbolically through the laying on of hands, and executed the sacrifice. Every step was a training aid. The blood, the fire, the aroma, the grain — all of it communicated doctrine in a form the observer could see, smell, and remember. The priest also renewed the table of showbread, tended the menorah, and maintained every article of the tabernacle and later the temple — each item a visual embodiment of a doctrinal reality.

section: I. The Participle: Ministering as a Priest
text: Paul's use of this participle signals that his ministry among the Gentiles had this same character. He did not restrict himself to verbal exposition alone. He took the Levitical institutions — the burnt offering, the food offering, the peace offering, the sin offering, the trespass offering — and laid them open before Gentile audiences who had never encountered Judaism. By means of these inherited training aids, he made propitiation, reconciliation, the person of Christ, and the rebound principle concrete and memorable.

section: II. The Direct Object: The Gospel of God
text: II. The Direct Object: The Gospel of God

section: II. The Direct Object: The Gospel of God
text: The phrase translated 'the gospel of God' consists of the possessive genitive singular of theos (θεός, God) governing the accusative singular direct object euangelion (εὐαγγέλιον). In its general, non-technical sense euangelion means simply good news. In its technical and restricted sense it refers to the gospel of salvation — faith in Christ as the sole basis of justification before God. Both meanings are in view here. Paul ministers the specific saving message, but the vehicle of that ministry is the entire wealth of revealed doctrine, the full good news of God's redemptive plan as disclosed through the Old Testament institutions and fulfilled in Christ.

section: II. The Direct Object: The Gospel of God
text: Similarly, the word apostle (

section: II. The Direct Object: The Gospel of God
text: apostolos, ἀπόστολος) carries both a technical and a general sense. In its technical sense it refers to the unique office held by the Twelve (with Judas replaced) and by Paul — individuals directly commissioned by the risen Christ and bearing foundational authority for the Church Age. In its general sense it can describe a missionary, one sent out with a specific message. Paul operates under the technical sense here, but the ministry he describes — priestly communication of the good news — extends beyond that office to any qualified, motivated believer.

section: III. The Purpose Clause: The Offering of the Gentiles
text: III. The Purpose Clause: The Offering of the Gentiles

section: III. The Purpose Clause: The Offering of the Gentiles
text: The conjunction introducing the purpose clause is

section: III. The Purpose Clause: The Offering of the Gentiles
text: hina (ἵνα), which governs a semi-final clause expressing the aim and anticipated result of the priestly ministry. The subject of the purpose clause is the nominative singular prosphora (προσφορά), meaning the act of bringing or presenting an offering. The offering in view is the Gentiles themselves — not an offering made by the Gentiles but an offering consisting of the Gentiles, expressed by the appositional genitive plural of ethnos (ἔθνος, nation, Gentile people).

section: III. The Purpose Clause: The Offering of the Gentiles
text: Paul casts his entire Gentile ministry in sacrificial terms. Every Gentile believer brought to faith and grounded in doctrine is, in Paul's imagery, a living sacrifice presented to God. The priest's labor — sustained, visual, explanatory — produces an offering. The offering is the congregation he has built. The completion of this purpose clause (that the offering might be acceptable, having been sanctified by the Holy Spirit) will be taken up in the following section of verse 16; the present chapter focuses on the nature of the priestly function itself.

section: III. The Purpose Clause: The Offering of the Gentiles
text: What made the Gentiles a striking offering was precisely their distance from Israel's heritage. They had no prior exposure to the tabernacle, the priesthood, the Levitical calendar, or the sacrificial system. When Paul introduced these things, the effect was immediate and powerful. The Galatians, for example, responded with the enthusiasm of children encountering something entirely new. Their lack of familiarity was not an obstacle to understanding; it was the condition for fresh wonder. The training aids of Israel, explained by a skilled priest-communicator to audiences who had never seen them, produced exactly the kind of doctrinal retention for which those aids had been designed.

section: IV. Prophet and Priest — Two Modes of Communication
text: IV. Prophet and Priest — Two Modes of Communication

section: IV. Prophet and Priest — Two Modes of Communication
text: The Old Testament distinguished the prophet from the priest along functional lines that remain instructive for the Church Age. The prophet was the verbal communicator par excellence: he stood before the people and declared the word of God with direct propositional force. The priest was the visual communicator: he performed, demonstrated, and enacted the realities the prophet declared. Both functions were necessary, and neither was superior to the other.

section: IV. Prophet and Priest — Two Modes of Communication
text: In the Church Age, the gift of pastor-teacher corresponds to the prophetic mode: the male believer with this gift is responsible for the authoritative, systematic exposition of Scripture to the assembled congregation. The priestly mode, however, belongs to the entire royal family of God. Every Church Age believer is a priest — a member of the royal priesthood — and therefore every believer who has acquired sufficient doctrine and is motivated by that doctrine may function as a priest-communicator in the appropriate context.

section: IV. Prophet and Priest — Two Modes of Communication
text: This distinction has direct bearing on the question of who may teach doctrine to children. The pastor-teacher's gift is not in view when a believer uses visual materials, flannel boards, object lessons, or other training aids to communicate doctrinal realities to young learners. That is priestly function, open to men and women alike, requiring doctrine, motivation, and the absence of spiritual arrogance but not the specific gift of pastor-teacher.

section: V. Training Aids and the Principle of Doctrinal Retention
text: V. Training Aids and the Principle of Doctrinal Retention

section: V. Training Aids and the Principle of Doctrinal Retention
text: The Levitical system was the ancient world's most sophisticated curriculum. Its genius lay in the fact that it did not require its students to be literate. A worshiper who watched the burnt offering year after year could not avoid learning propitiation. A family that observed the peace offering understood reconciliation experientially before they could articulate it theologically. The training aids did not replace verbal instruction; they embedded it at a level deeper than cognition alone could reach.

section: V. Training Aids and the Principle of Doctrinal Retention
text: This principle governs effective communication of doctrine in any dispensation. When the priest-communicator introduces a visual element — an object, a demonstration, a model, a map, a living illustration — the student's attention engages at a different level than it does during purely verbal instruction. The visual element creates a frame of reference to which subsequent verbal teaching can be attached. The doctrine then travels with the image and is recalled when the image is recalled.

section: V. Training Aids and the Principle of Doctrinal Retention
text: Flexibility in the choice of training aids is not a concession to intellectual weakness but a mark of skilled priestly ministry. The Levitical system itself employed a range of media: fire, blood, grain, oil, incense, woven fabric, hammered gold, acacia wood, linen, animal skins. No two offerings were identical in their materials or their emphasis. This variety was deliberate. Different sensory and conceptual registers were engaged by different offerings, ensuring that no single doctrinal truth was taught through only one medium. The priest who understood this variety did not insist on a single approved method; he selected from the full range of available aids the one most suited to his audience and occasion.

section: V. Training Aids and the Principle of Doctrinal Retention
text: Effective priestly communication also requires the absence of arrogance — on two counts. First, the priest-communicator must not be so attached to a particular method that he refuses to adopt one better suited to his students. Second, he must not be so self-conscious about appearing undignified that he withholds aids his students need. Children in particular require the priest-communicator to meet them where they are, not where the communicator is comfortable.

section: VI. The Levitical Offerings as Doctrinal Training Aids
text: VI. The Levitical Offerings as Doctrinal Training Aids

section: The Burnt Offering and Propitiation
text: The Burnt Offering and Propitiation

section: The Burnt Offering and Propitiation
text: The burnt offering (

section: The Burnt Offering and Propitiation
text: olah, עֹלָה) was wholly consumed on the altar — nothing was retained by the offerer or the priest. The entire animal ascended as a pleasing aroma to God. This total consumption illustrated the substitutionary character of Christ's work: his humanity was fully offered to the justice of God in judgment for human sin. Propitiation is satisfied justice — the justice of God fully met by the penalty paid in the humanity of Christ. The burnt offering made this abstract truth visible and sensory.

section: The Food Offering and the Person of Christ
text: The Food Offering and the Person of Christ

section: The Food Offering and the Person of Christ
text: The food or grain offering (

section: The Food Offering and the Person of Christ
text: minchah, מִנְחָה) illustrated the person of Christ in the hypostatic union. Fine flour without leaven (a type of sin) represented the sinless humanity of Christ. Oil pressed into the flour represented the indwelling Spirit. Salt, which preserves and prevents corruption, represented the incorruptibility of the divine nature. The priest-communicator who explained these details to Gentile audiences was making Christology concrete.

section: The Peace Offering and Reconciliation
text: The Peace Offering and Reconciliation

section: The Peace Offering and Reconciliation
text: The peace offering (

section: The Peace Offering and Reconciliation
text: shelamim, שְׁלָמִים) was the only offering in which the offerer ate a portion. God received his portion on the altar; the priest received his portion; the offerer and his household ate their portion. This shared meal across the altar depicted reconciliation — the removal of enmity and the restoration of fellowship between the offerer and God. Paul's exposition of reconciliation in Romans 5 is grounded in exactly this imagery.

section: The Sin Offering and Unknown Sins
text: The Sin Offering and Unknown Sins

section: The Sin Offering and Unknown Sins
text: The sin offering (

section: The Sin Offering and Unknown Sins
text: chattat, חַטָּאת) addressed unintentional sins — violations committed without awareness. It illustrated the provision for unknown sins that require divine handling, corresponding in Church Age terms to the rebound principle: naming known sins to God under the mechanism of 1 John 1:9, with the understanding that unknown sins are handled by Christ's advocacy before the Father. The priest's role in the sin offering made this provision visible.

section: The Trespass Offering and Rebound
text: The Trespass Offering and Rebound

section: The Trespass Offering and Rebound
text: The trespass offering (

section: The Trespass Offering and Rebound
text: asham, אָשָׁם) addressed specific, known transgressions against God or man, with a requirement of restitution where applicable. It illustrated the rebound principle in its full scope: acknowledgment of the specific sin, reliance on the atoning work of Christ as the basis of forgiveness, and restoration to fellowship with God. The trespass offering made rebound not merely a concept but a procedure the worshiper enacted with his own hands.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven
text: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven
text: 1. The participle hierourgounta governs the entire description of Paul's ministry: he ministers as a priest, not merely as a herald. The distinction is functional — the priest communicates doctrine through enacted and visible means, not verbal proclamation alone. This characterizes the mode of ministry Paul claims for himself in his Gentile mission.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven
text: 2. The present progressive tense of hierourgounta signals sustained, linear action: priestly ministry is not occasional but continuous. The priest-communicator does not offer a single dramatic presentation and withdraw; he maintains the discipline of consistent, sequential instruction using the full range of available aids.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven
text: 3. The direct object euangelion carries both technical and general force: the specific saving message and the entire body of doctrinal good news. Paul ministers the gospel of salvation, but the vehicle is the comprehensive revelation of God — the Levitical institutions, the prophetic writings, and their fulfillment in the person and work of Christ.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven
text: 4. The Levitical offerings were Israel's divinely designed curriculum: each offering taught a distinct doctrinal truth through a distinct sensory and procedural experience. The burnt offering illustrated propitiation; the food offering illustrated the person of Christ in hypostatic union; the peace offering illustrated reconciliation; the sin offering illustrated provision for unknown sins; the trespass offering illustrated rebound. Paul used these as training aids with Gentile audiences.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven
text: 5. The offering consisting of the Gentiles (prosphora tōn ethnōn) is Paul's characterization of his entire Gentile mission: every believer brought to faith and maturity through priestly instruction constitutes a living sacrifice presented to God. The priest-communicator's labor produces the offering. The offering is the congregation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven
text: 6. The distinction between prophet and priest maps onto two distinct modes of communication in the Church Age: the gift of pastor-teacher corresponds to the prophetic mode and is restricted to the male believer with that gift. The priestly mode belongs to every member of the royal family of God and is exercised by any believer — male or female — who possesses sufficient doctrine and the motivation to communicate it using training aids appropriate to the audience.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven
text: 7. Flexibility in method is not accommodation but fidelity to the priestly model: the Levitical system itself employed a wide range of materials, procedures, and sensory registers precisely because different doctrinal truths require different vehicles. The priest-communicator who insists on a single approved method impoverishes both the content and the reception of the doctrine he teaches.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven
text: 8. Doctrinal retention is maximized when verbal instruction is accompanied by visual and procedural elements: the Levitical worshiper who enacted the trespass offering internalized rebound at a level that verbal description alone could not produce. This principle governs any effective communication of doctrine across any dispensation.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven
text: 9. Effective priestly ministry requires the absence of arrogance in two forms: attachment to a preferred method that prevents adoption of a better one, and self-consciousness about appearing undignified that withholds aids the student needs. Neither the method nor the communicator's comfort is the standard — the doctrinal formation of the student is the standard.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Four Hundred Ninety-Seven
text: 10. The purpose clause (hina … prosphora … genētai euprosdektos) frames the entire ministry in terms of its eschatological goal: that the offering consisting of the Gentiles might be acceptable, sanctified by the Holy Spirit. The priest-communicator works toward an outcome that only the Spirit can complete. The human instrument provides the sustained, flexible, doctrinally grounded instruction; the Spirit produces the acceptability of the offering before God.
