section: Romans 16:5 — The Royal Family Honor Code: Personal and Impersonal Love, Morality and Integrity, Hope, Production, and the Dying Phase of Living
text: Romans 16:5 resumes the verse-by-verse exposition, but the immediate context is the continuing reorganization of the doctrine of the Royal Family Honor Code. This chapter addresses the final ten points of that doctrine — moving through impersonal love, morality and integrity, hope as motivation, the place of production, logistical grace, self-pity, self-righteousness, and the honor code's application even in the dying phase of living.

section: I. Point Six of the Honor Code: Personal Love and Impersonal Love
text: I. Point Six of the Honor Code: Personal Love and Impersonal Love

section: I. Point Six of the Honor Code: Personal Love and Impersonal Love
text: The command to love the brethren cannot be fulfilled until the believer understands the difference between the essential and the non-essential, and the difference between personal love and impersonal love. These two categories are not interchangeable; conflating them produces either hypocrisy or spiritual breakdown.

section: A. Defining the Two Categories
text: A. Defining the Two Categories

section: A. Defining the Two Categories
text: Impersonal love emphasizes the subject — the believer's own norms, standards, and mental attitude — and directs itself toward all persons within the believer's periphery. Personal love emphasizes the object and is directed toward only a few persons.

section: A. Defining the Two Categories
text: Three categories of personal love may be distinguished: (1) category one, directed toward the Lord Jesus Christ; (2) category two, directed toward right man or right woman; and (3) category three, directed toward a circle of close friends. Personal love assigns merit to the object and involves attraction, mutual interest, and emotional response. Impersonal love assigns no merit to the object whatsoever — its integrity derives entirely from the norms and standards residing in the subject.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: The following sub-points define the structure and function of impersonal love as a component of the Royal Family Honor Code.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 1. The command to love the brethren can never be fulfilled until the believer understands the difference between the essential and the non-essential, and between personal and impersonal love.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 2. Impersonal love emphasizes the subject; personal love emphasizes the object.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 3. Impersonal love depends on the norms and standards of the subject.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 4. Impersonal love directs itself toward all persons within the believer's periphery — both fellow believers (cf. John 15:12, 17; 1 John 3:23) and neighbors in the broader sense (cf. Romans 13:8–9; 1 Peter 2:17; 3:8).

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 5. Personal love is directed toward a few; impersonal love is directed toward all.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 6. The object of impersonal love is all believers and everyone within the believer's periphery.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 7. Impersonal love excludes emotion. Personal love has great emotional function, because emotion serves as an appreciator — it responds to what is valued. But when dealing with the human race in general, the subject's norms and standards govern, and emotion is excluded from the operational dynamic.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 8. Impersonal love emphasizes the integrity of the subject; personal love emphasizes the attractiveness of the object.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 9. Impersonal love cannot be reduced to the level of dog-eat-dog. When another person gossips, maligns, competes, or acts out of jealousy or vindictiveness, impersonal love prevents the believer from descending to that person's broken standards. To operate on the antagonist's standards is to share in their weakness rather than allowing them to benefit from the believer's strength.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 10. Impersonal love therefore excludes carrying a grudge.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 11. If wronged, the believer under impersonal love does not seek revenge. Retaliation would lower the believer to the standards of the antagonist.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 12. Impersonal love includes respect for the imputed righteousness of God residing in every other believer.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 13. Since the righteousness of God — one half of divine integrity — resides in every believer, impersonal love respects the other believer on that basis alone.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 14. The believer cannot hold a grudge against another believer. To do so is equivalent to bearing a grudge against the righteousness of God — which is blasphemous.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 15. Impersonal love is the relaxed mental attitude produced by the filling of the Spirit (Romans 5:5; Galatians 5:22), not overt friendliness or effusive hypocrisy. When Romans 5:5 and Galatians 5:22 speak of the Spirit producing love, the reference is to impersonal love, not personal love.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 16. Under impersonal love, the believer functions under his own doctrinal norms and standards rather than being influenced by flattery, attraction, attention, or reciprocity.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 17. Impersonal love not only excludes mental and verbal sins, but demands toleration, respect for privacy, and the avoidance of distracting others from doctrine.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 18. Flexibility is related to impersonal love.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: 19. Personal love, by contrast, emphasizes the object and demands learning to know that object — whether Christ, right man or right woman, or close friends. It demands genuine cognizance of the person involved.

section: B. The Nineteen Sub-Points of Impersonal Love in the Honor Code
text: Key passages for review in connection with this point: Romans 12:9; Romans 13:8–10.

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: The seventh major concept of the Royal Family Honor Code concerns the relationship between morality and the Christian way of life.

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: 1. Morality is designed for the fulfillment of the laws of divine establishment and is therefore designed for the entire human race, believers included.

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: 2. Since the unbeliever can produce morality, morality is not in itself a component of the Christian way of life.

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: 3. While the Christian way of life is not morality, it does not exclude morality. The Christian way of life is higher than morality.

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: 4. The honor code demands a standard superior to morality for the royal family of God.

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: 5. Christianity uses the morality of divine establishment as a base, but exceeds that base in the function of the honor code. Morality does not demand impersonal love; impersonal love is a higher standard than morality.

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: 6. Anything the unbeliever can do is not the Christian way of life. The Christian way of life is a supernatural way of life, which demands a supernatural means of execution — namely, the filling of the Holy Spirit. The unbeliever can fulfill morality without the Spirit. The filling of the Spirit is required to function under impersonal love. Hell is filled with moral people — the rich young ruler being the paradigm case: perfectly moral, yet an unbeliever (cf. Mark 10:17–22).

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: 7. Morality is not rejected as per antinomianism, nor is morality elevated to a saving or sanctifying mechanism as per legalism.

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: 8. Neither legalism nor antinomianism is the Christian way of life.

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: 9. The honor code demands that the believer live under establishment but exceed the morality of establishment through the perception of doctrine and the filling of the Holy Spirit.

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: 10. Both the morality of establishment and the integrity of the honor code support the believer's advance toward the maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: 11. The honor code demands patriotism, respect for governmental authority, military service, and respect for law and order in the believer's relationship with the civil government (cf. Romans 13:1–7).

section: II. Point Seven: Morality and Integrity in the Honor Code
text: Passage for review: Romans 13:1–7.

section: III. Point Eight: Hope as Motivation and Momentum in the Honor Code
text: III. Point Eight: Hope as Motivation and Momentum in the Honor Code

section: III. Point Eight: Hope as Motivation and Momentum in the Honor Code
text: Hope, defined as confident anticipation or confident expectation regarding the future, functions as both the motivation and the momentum in the believer's advance through the Protocol Plan of God. It is not wishful thinking but a category of certain expectation grounded in divine promises.

section: III. Point Eight: Hope as Motivation and Momentum in the Honor Code
text: Hope operates not only as the motivator in the advance toward maturity but as the motivator in the function of Christian integrity. The doctrine of hope, already treated in detail in prior chapters, bears directly on the honor code. Romans 15:13–14 specifically connects hope to the function of the honor code and should be reviewed in this connection.

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: The ninth major concept of the Royal Family Honor Code is the principle of production and its proper relationship to the priesthood and ambassadorship of every believer.

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: 1. A distinction must be maintained between the believer's royal priesthood and royal ambassadorship. Every believer holds both offices from the moment of salvation.

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: 2. As a royal priest, the believer advances through persistent perception of doctrine.

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: 3. As a royal ambassador, the believer produces as a result of spiritual growth — never as the means of spiritual growth. No legitimate production can exist apart from the ministry of the Spirit.

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: 4. The Royal Family Honor Code excludes all forms of Christian works — whether legitimate or illegitimate — as a means of blessing from God.

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: 5. Nothing accomplished in the areas of witnessing, praying, giving, worshiping, sacrificing, or church service can bring divine blessing as an earned reward.

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: 6. Neither morality, talent, personality change, asceticism, sacrificial giving, devotional worship, nor church work will elicit blessing from God as its cause.

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: 7. Blessing from God originates from doctrine resident in the soul, which produces capacity for life, which in turn triggers the imputation of divine blessing to the target — the imputed righteousness of God residing in the mature believer.

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: 8. Divine blessing is a real imputation from the justice of God to the imputed righteousness of God — the home address of divine blessing in the believer at the point of maturity.

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: 9. The attainment of maturity through maximum doctrine perceived is the only basis for the imputation of divine blessing. The advance from salvation to maturity, through the filling of the Spirit and doctrine in the soul, produces Christian production. But production is always the result of blessing, never its means. The means of blessing from God is in the priesthood; the result is expressed in ambassadorship.

section: IV. Point Nine: Production and the Honor Code
text: 10. What is often construed as blessing from God is either logistical grace or blessing by association.

section: A. Logistical Grace
text: A. Logistical Grace

section: A. Logistical Grace
text: Under logistical grace, God provides every support necessary for the believer to attain maturity. This support is individualized — no two believers receive the same allocation. The components include:

section: A. Logistical Grace
text: — Time: No two believers are given the same span of life.

section: A. Logistical Grace
text: — Food, shelter, clothing: All variable in kind and quantity.

section: A. Logistical Grace
text: — Transportation: The means by which the believer reaches the local assembly for doctrine intake — whatever that means may be.

section: A. Logistical Grace
text: — Financial provision: The believer's effective 'allowance' from God, determined by divine wisdom regarding what the believer can be trusted to handle.

section: A. Logistical Grace
text: — A right pastor-teacher and a local church: The assembly through which doctrine is communicated.

section: A. Logistical Grace
text: The variation in logistical support is not an index of spiritual status. The Apostle Paul died without material wealth and yet is the greatest believer of the Church Age. Philippians 4:11–12 records his statement: 'I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content. I know both how to be abased, and I know how to abound.' The honor code prohibits self-pity and envy arising from comparison of one believer's logistical support with another's.

section: B. Blessing by Association
text: B. Blessing by Association

section: B. Blessing by Association
text: Under blessing by association, a believer may receive material and providential blessing from God not because of his own maturity but because he is associated with a mature believer — a family member, colleague, or friend through whom the mature believer's imputed blessing overflows. This explains the apparent prosperity of some believers who have not yet attained maturity.

section: B. Blessing by Association
text: 13. The Royal Family Honor Code demands total dependence on the integrity of God rather than dependence on one's own ability or human achievement. This is not an excuse to cease productive effort; rather, the believer is motivated to work hard while understanding that the ultimate source of every provision is divine integrity.

section: B. Blessing by Association
text: 14. The purpose of the honor code is to provide the necessary privacy, protection from bullying, and survival in life during the advance to maturity.

section: B. Blessing by Association
text: 15. Works are the result of the advance, never the means of advance in Christianity. Production may be a manifestation of spiritual progress, but it is never the means of spiritual progress.

section: V. Point Ten: The Strong Believer and the Weak Believer
text: V. Point Ten: The Strong Believer and the Weak Believer

section: V. Point Ten: The Strong Believer and the Weak Believer
text: The Royal Family Honor Code demands more of the strong or mature believer than of the weak. Romans 15:1 states: 'Now we, the strong, are obligated under the honor code to keep bearing the weaknesses of the weak and not to accommodate ourselves.' As the believer advances toward maturity, he not only carries his own weight but assumes the burden of tolerating those who are ignorant of doctrine.

section: V. Point Ten: The Strong Believer and the Weak Believer
text: Bearing the weaknesses of the weak is the maximum utilization of impersonal love and total toleration in the area of the non-essentials. The strong believer who operates under maximum doctrine and the filling of the Spirit is able to tolerate the erroneous and inconsequential opinions formulated from ignorance, without being drawn down to that level. This is strength through flexibility.

section: V. Point Ten: The Strong Believer and the Weak Believer
text: The weak believer is weak because he has little understanding of doctrine and formulates inconsequential opinions about superficialities of life with maximum arrogance. The mature believer's function of impersonal love fulfills his honor code duty to the weak believer, placing all emphasis on his own doctrinal norms and standards rather than on the merit or demerit of the weak believer as an object.

section: V. Point Ten: The Strong Believer and the Weak Believer
text: Passage for review: Romans 15:1–4.

section: VI. Point Eleven: Authority Orientation and Momentum
text: VI. Point Eleven: Authority Orientation and Momentum

section: VI. Point Eleven: Authority Orientation and Momentum
text: The thrust of the honor code demands authority orientation as the basis for continued momentum in the Christian way of life. This encompasses the full structure of divinely ordained authority in the spiritual realm — pastor-teacher, local assembly, the canon of Scripture — and will be developed in subsequent treatment.

section: VII. Point Twelve: Reciprocity in the Honor Code
text: VII. Point Twelve: Reciprocity in the Honor Code

section: VII. Point Twelve: Reciprocity in the Honor Code
text: Reciprocity is a component of the honor code. The principle is found in Romans 15:26–27, where the Gentile churches' contribution to the Jerusalem saints is framed as the discharge of a spiritual debt — those who have received spiritual benefit are obligated to minister to those who provided it in material terms. This reciprocity is not legalism but honor-code obligation arising from genuine gratitude and impersonal love.

section: VIII. Point Thirteen: The Exclusion of Self-Pity
text: VIII. Point Thirteen: The Exclusion of Self-Pity

section: VIII. Point Thirteen: The Exclusion of Self-Pity
text: The Royal Family Honor Code demands the avoidance of self-pity and of any behavior designed to arouse pity from others. Self-pity is among the most powerful distractions from the spiritual life, because it directs the believer's attention inward and away from doctrine.

section: VIII. Point Thirteen: The Exclusion of Self-Pity
text: When another person takes an interest in a believer because they feel sorry for him, that interest is not genuine friendship but compassion. A relationship built on manufactured sympathy severs the believer from reality and produces a pattern of behavior — deliberate exhibition of vulnerability to elicit attention — that is incompatible with the honor code.

section: VIII. Point Thirteen: The Exclusion of Self-Pity
text: Romans 12:9 states that love must be non-hypocritical. Impersonal love is free from hypocrisy because it operates on the subject's own norms and standards, not on a calculated performance for the benefit of an observer. Romans 12:9–10 and 13:8 demand a response of impersonal love, not personal love, toward the general body of believers. Attempting to fulfill these impersonal-love commands through personal love will produce either spiritual breakdown or hypocrisy.

section: VIII. Point Thirteen: The Exclusion of Self-Pity
text: Since impersonal love depends upon doctrinal standards resident in the conscience, it excludes self-pity on the part of the subject and repudiates any operational pattern designed to arouse pity in others.

section: VIII. Point Thirteen: The Exclusion of Self-Pity
text: Passages for review: Romans 12:9–10; 13:8; 14:8; 15:5–7.

section: IX. Point Fourteen: Self-Righteousness Excluded by Imputed Righteousness
text: IX. Point Fourteen: Self-Righteousness Excluded by Imputed Righteousness

section: IX. Point Fourteen: Self-Righteousness Excluded by Imputed Righteousness
text: The imputation of divine righteousness at salvation eliminates the function of self-righteousness in the Christian way of life. The Royal Family Honor Code therefore excludes self-righteousness entirely.

section: IX. Point Fourteen: Self-Righteousness Excluded by Imputed Righteousness
text: 1. Divine justice can only bless divine righteousness, never self-righteousness. The self-righteous believer who presents his moral achievements to God as grounds for blessing misunderstands the nature of divine integrity.

section: IX. Point Fourteen: Self-Righteousness Excluded by Imputed Righteousness
text: 2. Self-righteousness functions in all three categories of the old sin nature's modus operandi. It produces arrogance, human good, and evil — including the ideological evil of statism and collectivism.

section: IX. Point Fourteen: Self-Righteousness Excluded by Imputed Righteousness
text: 3. Self-righteousness is a complex of evil eliminated by the function of the honor code.

section: IX. Point Fourteen: Self-Righteousness Excluded by Imputed Righteousness
text: 4. Self-righteousness plus sincerity guarantees the function of evil in the believer's life.

section: IX. Point Fourteen: Self-Righteousness Excluded by Imputed Righteousness
text: 5. Self-righteousness is not only excluded from the honor code, but its very presence in the believer's life constitutes an insult to the integrity and holiness of God and a blasphemous denial of the divine provision of logistical grace.

section: X. Point Fifteen: The Maximum Function of the Honor Code — Risking Life for Another
text: X. Point Fifteen: The Maximum Function of the Honor Code — Risking Life for Another

section: X. Point Fifteen: The Maximum Function of the Honor Code — Risking Life for Another
text: The maximum expression of the Royal Family Honor Code is to risk or give one's life for another member of the royal family. Romans 16:3–4 presents this in concrete historical terms: Priska and Aquila 'risked their own necks' for the Apostle Paul, and all the Gentile churches joined Paul in giving thanks for their sacrifice.

section: X. Point Fifteen: The Maximum Function of the Honor Code — Risking Life for Another
text: This principle is grounded in the Lord Jesus Christ's own statement in John 15:12–13: 'This is my commandment, that you love one another as I have loved you. Greater love has no one than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends.' See also Romans 5:7 and 1 John 3:16.

section: XI. Point Sixteen: The Honor Code Makes Dying a Part of Living
text: XI. Point Sixteen: The Honor Code Makes Dying a Part of Living

section: XI. Point Sixteen: The Honor Code Makes Dying a Part of Living
text: The final major concept of the Royal Family Honor Code addresses the dying phase of living. In human thinking, dying is categorized as the cessation of living. The honor code, however, refuses that equation: as long as the believer draws breath, the Christian way of life is fully operative.

section: XI. Point Sixteen: The Honor Code Makes Dying a Part of Living
text: A terminal diagnosis, confinement to a hospital bed, and isolation from the normal activities of life do not suspend the honor code. The dying phase of living is not the absence of life but one of its most demanding arenas. For the believer with maximum doctrine resident in the soul, the dying phase becomes the greatest challenge and the greatest opportunity for the application of that doctrine.

section: XI. Point Sixteen: The Honor Code Makes Dying a Part of Living
text: Philippians 1:20–21 captures the principle: 'According to my intense concentration on doctrine and resultant hope, that in nothing shall I be disgraced, but with integrity of the honor code, even now as always, Christ shall be exalted in my person, whether by living or by dying. For me, living is Christ and dying is gain.' The honor code therefore makes greater demands in the dying phase of living than in any living phase, because it requires that doctrine be applied under maximum pressure and minimum external support — a condition that only maximum doctrine in the soul and the filling of the Spirit can sustain.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two
text: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 1. Impersonal love and personal love are structurally distinct. Impersonal love is governed by the subject's norms and standards and directed toward all persons. Personal love is governed by attraction to a specific object and directed toward only a few. Collapsing these two categories produces either hypocrisy or psychological breakdown.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 2. The filling of the Holy Spirit produces impersonal love, not personal love. Romans 5:5 and Galatians 5:22 refer to the Spirit's production of impersonal love as a relaxed mental attitude — not to an emotion directed toward a specific person. The filling of the Spirit is required for impersonal love; it is not required for mere morality.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 3. Morality is not the Christian way of life but its foundation. Since the unbeliever can produce morality without the filling of the Spirit, morality is not a component unique to Christianity. The Christian way of life exceeds morality through the function of the honor code under the Spirit's control. The honor code is neither legalism nor antinomianism.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 4. Production is always the result of advance, never its means. All blessing flows from the justice of God to the imputed righteousness of God residing in the mature believer. Works, witnessing, giving, and moral achievement cannot produce divine blessing as their cause. Logistical grace supports the advance to maturity; blessing by association may benefit those not yet mature.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 5. Logistical grace is individualized. God provides precisely the resources — time, food, shelter, transportation, financial provision, and a right pastor-teacher — that each believer requires for the advance to maturity. Variation in logistical support is not an index of spiritual status. Self-pity arising from comparison with others violates the honor code.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 6. The mature believer bears the burdens of the weak. Romans 15:1 assigns to the strong the obligation to bear the weaknesses of the weak rather than accommodating themselves. This is maximum impersonal love in function — tolerance of the inconsequential opinions of doctrinally weak believers, executed through doctrinal norms and the filling of the Spirit, not through emotional forbearance.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 7. Self-pity is incompatible with the honor code. Impersonal love operates on the subject's own standards and assigns no merit to the object. It therefore excludes self-pity and any operational pattern designed to elicit pity from others. Relationships built on manufactured sympathy are incompatible with genuine honor-code function.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 8. Imputed righteousness eliminates self-righteousness. Divine justice blesses divine righteousness, not self-righteousness. Self-righteousness — a complex of arrogance, human good, and evil — is excluded by the honor code and constitutes an insult to divine integrity and a denial of logistical grace.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 9. Dying is a phase of living under the honor code. Philippians 1:20–21 establishes that Christ is exalted whether by living or by dying. The honor code remains fully operative in the terminal phase of physical life and makes greater demands there than in any other phase, because the application of maximum doctrine under maximum pressure is the highest expression of the Christian way of life.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Two
text: 10. The maximum expression of the honor code is self-sacrifice for a fellow believer. Romans 16:3–4, John 15:12–13, Romans 5:7, and 1 John 3:16 converge on the principle that the willingness to risk or give one's life for another member of the royal family is the apex of honor-code function.

Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three

section: Romans 16:5 — The Honorable Romans: Epinetus, First Convert from Asia
text: Romans 16:5 — The Honorable Romans: Epinetus, First Convert from Asia

section: Romans 16:5 — The Honorable Romans: Epinetus, First Convert from Asia
text: Romans 16:5 “Greet also the church in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who was the first convert to Christ in Asia.” (ESV)

section: Romans 16:5 — The Honorable Romans: Epinetus, First Convert from Asia
text: Corrected translation: Also pay my respects to the church in their home. Greet Epinetus, my beloved friend, who is the first convert to Christ from Asia — the Roman province of Asia.

section: Romans 16:5 — The Honorable Romans: Epinetus, First Convert from Asia
text: Romans 16 continues the honor roll of mature believers who assembled in the homes of Priska and Aquila and in two other house-churches in Rome. The chapter exhibits the royal family honor code — the operational standard of conduct for Church Age believers — as it was lived out by identifiable historical persons. Verses 1 through 4 introduced Phoebe, a mature single woman who served the church at Cenchreae, and the married couple Priska and Aquila, who risked their lives for Paul and hosted a local church in their home. Verse 5 introduces Epinetus, the first convert to Christ from the Roman province of Asia. The present chapter examines point sixteen of the royal family honor code — that dying is a part of living — and then turns to the grammatical and theological analysis of verse 5.

section: I. Point Sixteen of the Royal Family Honor Code: Dying as a Part of Living
text: I. Point Sixteen of the Royal Family Honor Code: Dying as a Part of Living

section: I. Point Sixteen of the Royal Family Honor Code: Dying as a Part of Living
text: The royal family honor code culminates in a principle without parallel in any human ethical system: dying is not assigned to the category of death but to the category of life. The dying phase of physical existence is as much a part of living as any other dimension of life. This principle is grounded in the dynamics of Bible doctrine resident in the soul and reaches its ultimate expression in Philippians 1:20–21.

section: A. The Anatomy of Physical Death
text: A. The Anatomy of Physical Death

section: A. The Anatomy of Physical Death
text: Every human body is a temporary dwelling — a tent — that houses both the human soul and, for the believer, the human spirit. Human life was imputed to the soul at physical birth; eternal life was imputed to the human spirit at regeneration. The believer therefore carries two categories of life simultaneously within a mortal frame. At physical death, soul and spirit depart from the body and the believer is immediately face to face with the Lord (2 Corinthians 5:8). The departure itself is not the problem. The problem is the dying — the days, weeks, or months of deterioration, pain, isolation, or sudden violence that precede the moment of departure.

section: A. The Anatomy of Physical Death
text: Dying is always a solitary act. No companion can share the experience. A person may enjoy a symphony, a meal, or a conversation with another; no one can die alongside another in the sense of bearing that death for him. Physical death is the one test in human existence that must be faced and executed entirely alone. This is the reason it constitutes the supreme test of the Christian life: it is the one arena where only the doctrine resident in the believer's own soul is available as a resource.

section: B. Doctrine as the Only Sufficient Resource for Dying
text: B. Doctrine as the Only Sufficient Resource for Dying

section: B. Doctrine as the Only Sufficient Resource for Dying
text: The mature believer who has accumulated maximum doctrine in the soul — through the consistent daily function of the Grace Apparatus for Perception (GAP) — carries that doctrine directly into the dying phase without interruption. Capacity for life in living, built on maximum doctrine resident in the soul, translates without diminution into capacity for life in dying. The dynamics are identical: right thinking produces right motivation; right motivation produces right action. This sequence operates in the dying phase precisely as it operates in the living phase.

section: B. Doctrine as the Only Sufficient Resource for Dying
text: Logistical grace — God's provision of everything necessary for the believer's physical existence — does not terminate at the onset of terminal illness or mortal danger. The same Lord, the same logistical support, the same indwelling Spirit, and the same doctrine are present in dying as in living. God has no intention of withdrawing His support from the positive believer at the moment of his greatest test.

section: B. Doctrine as the Only Sufficient Resource for Dying
text: Undeserved suffering, when handled with doctrine and without self-pity, functions as preparation for dying. The believer who can handle undeserved suffering with occupation with Christ and stability of soul has already demonstrated the inner resources that will carry him through the dying phase. The believer who panics at undeserved suffering has revealed that those inner resources are not yet in place.

section: C. The Contrast with the Unbeliever
text: C. The Contrast with the Unbeliever

section: C. The Contrast with the Unbeliever
text: For the unbeliever, dying typically represents the nadir of existence. Without eternal life imputed to a human spirit, without Bible doctrine in the soul, and without the indwelling Holy Spirit, the unbeliever faces dying with no inner resources. Beyond death lies the appointment with judgment (Hebrews 9:27). The unbeliever may achieve a degree of poise or dignity through the resources of human character — as certain historical figures have demonstrated at the point of execution — but these resources, however admirable, are of a different order entirely from the occupation with Christ that sustains the mature believer.

section: D. The Three-Hope Schema and Dying Grace
text: D. The Three-Hope Schema and Dying Grace

section: D. The Three-Hope Schema and Dying Grace
text: The theological framework that supports the dying-as-living principle is the three-hope schema developed earlier in the epistle. The first hope rests on the imputation of human life at birth and the judicial imputation of Adam's sin, which establishes the need for salvation. The gospel addresses that need, and faith in Christ replaces the hope with the reality of eternal salvation — the first adjustment to the justice of God.

section: D. The Three-Hope Schema and Dying Grace
text: The second hope rests on the two judicial imputations at the cross: all personal sins imputed to Christ and judged, and the righteousness of God imputed to the believer at salvation. This produces the second potential — the blessing of time, including dying grace as its ultimate expression. Consistent perception of doctrine advances the believer toward cracking the maturity barrier. The reality that replaces the second hope is the maturity adjustment to the justice of God.

section: D. The Three-Hope Schema and Dying Grace
text: The third hope rests on the imputation of eternal life to the human spirit at regeneration and on the blessings imputed at maturity, with dying grace as the final and greatest of those blessings. Undeserved suffering, handled with doctrine, functions as a rehearsal for the dying phase and contributes to the third hope — absolute confidence regarding the eternal future: the resurrection body, the judgment seat of Christ, the imputation of eternal reward and blessing, and the eternal state in which there is no more death, sorrow, tears, or pain.

section: E. Philippians 1:20–21 as the Ultimate Statement of the Honor Code
text: E. Philippians 1:20–21 as the Ultimate Statement of the Honor Code

section: E. Philippians 1:20–21 as the Ultimate Statement of the Honor Code
text: The scriptural anchor for point sixteen is Philippians 1:20–21. Paul writes from the vantage point of a believer who has advanced to ultra-supergrace and who faces the real possibility of execution. The passage reads:

section: E. Philippians 1:20–21 as the Ultimate Statement of the Honor Code
text: Philippians 1:20–21 “as it is my eager expectation and hope that I will not be at all ashamed, but that with full courage now as always Christ will be honored in my body, whether by life or by death. For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (ESV)

section: E. Philippians 1:20–21 as the Ultimate Statement of the Honor Code
text: Corrected translation: According to my intense concentration on doctrine and resultant hope that in nothing shall I be disgraced, but with the integrity of the honor code, even now as always, Christ shall be exalted in my person, whether by life or by death. For me, living is Christ; and dying — which is still a part of living — is gain.

section: E. Philippians 1:20–21 as the Ultimate Statement of the Honor Code
text: The phrase 'whether by life or by death' eliminates any categorical distinction between living and dying as spheres of Christian function. Both are arenas for the exaltation of Christ. The declaration 'living is Christ' marks the condition of maximum doctrine resident in the soul — occupation with the person of Christ as the organizing center of all thought and motivation. When living is Christ, dying is not loss but gain — profit — because the same occupation with Christ that generates capacity in living generates greater capacity in dying. Dying becomes the highest expression of the honor code, not the negation of it.

section: E. Philippians 1:20–21 as the Ultimate Statement of the Honor Code
text: The honor code is the only ethical system that assigns dying to the category of life and makes it the ultimate achievement of Christian existence. The mature believer does not have two modes — a living mode and a dying mode — because occupation with Christ is a continuous state that admits no interruption. The unbeliever and the immature believer are compelled to change modes; the mature believer is not.

section: II. Romans 16:5a — The Church in the Home of Priska and Aquila
text: II. Romans 16:5a — The Church in the Home of Priska and Aquila

section: II. Romans 16:5a — The Church in the Home of Priska and Aquila
text: Verse 5 opens with a continuation of Paul's greetings to the believers assembled in Rome. The first clause directs attention to the local church that met in the private residence of Priska and Aquila.

section: II. Romans 16:5a — The Church in the Home of Priska and Aquila
text: The conjunction kai (καί) functions here in its adjunctive sense: also. The corrected translation therefore begins: Also pay my respects to the church in their home. No verb for 'greet' appears explicitly in the Greek; the aorist active imperative of aspázomai (ἀσπάζομαι) is implied from the surrounding context. Aspázomai means to greet, to salute, to pay one's respects to a person of honor.

section: II. Romans 16:5a — The Church in the Home of Priska and Aquila
text: The local church is identified by the accusative singular of ekklēsía (ἐκκλησία), the standard term for the local assembly. The phrase kata plus oíkos (κατά + οἶκος) — prepositional phrase governing the genitive plural of the intensive pronoun autós used as a possessive — specifies the location: in their home. The genitive plural indicates that the home belongs jointly to Priska and Aquila.

section: II. Romans 16:5a — The Church in the Home of Priska and Aquila
text: The practice of assembling for church services in private residences was characteristic of the first century of the Church Age. Comparable references appear in Acts 12:17, 1 Corinthians 16:19, Colossians 4:15, and Philemon 2. The home of Priska and Aquila was large enough to serve as one of at least three such assembly points mentioned in Romans 16. The identity of the pastor of this particular congregation is not specified; it is possible that Aquila himself served in that capacity, given his demonstrated spiritual maturity.

section: III. Romans 16:5b — Epinetus: The First Convert from Asia
text: III. Romans 16:5b — Epinetus: The First Convert from Asia

section: A. Grammatical Analysis
text: A. Grammatical Analysis

section: A. Grammatical Analysis
text: The verse continues with the aorist active imperative of aspázomai (ἀσπάζομαι), here expressed explicitly. The aorist is a constantive aorist — it contemplates the action of the verb in its entirety and refers to a momentary, complete act: the uttering of a word of greeting or the gesture of a salute. The active voice indicates that Paul himself produces the action; the imperative mood is the imperative of entreaty, conveying a request rather than a command. Paul is asking the Roman believers to extend his personal respects to Epinetus.

section: A. Grammatical Analysis
text: The accusative singular direct object is the proper noun Epínetos (Ἐπαίνετος). This is an uncommon name; an inscription discovered in Rome records an individual named Epinetus the Ephesian, and the identification with the person named here is well supported.

section: A. Grammatical Analysis
text: Paul qualifies Epinetus with the accusative singular adjective agapētós (ἀγαπητός), meaning beloved — one who is the object of deep personal affection. The possessive genitive singular of egó (ἐγώ) — my — specifies that this is Paul's own expression of personal love. Epinetus is not merely the recipient of Paul's impersonal love for the brethren generally; he is Paul's beloved friend, the object of category-three personal love.

section: A. Grammatical Analysis
text: The relative clause that follows employs the nominative singular relative pronoun hós (ὅς), whose antecedent is Epinetus. With this is the present active indicative of eimí (εἰμί), the verb of being, functioning here as a historical present — a past event described with the vividness of a present occurrence. The predicate nominative is aparchḗ (ἀπαρχή), meaning first fruits or first convert.

section: A. Grammatical Analysis
text: The ablative of source governs the proper noun Asia (Ἀσία). The King James renders this 'Achaia,' but the best manuscripts read Asia — the Roman proconsular province of Asia, located in western Asia Minor (modern western Turkey). This province included the seven churches addressed in Revelation 2–3 and encompassed the sub-regions of Phrygia, Mysia, Caria, and Lydia. Ephesus was the administrative capital. The phrase eis Christón (εἰς Χριστόν) — to Christ — completes the clause.

section: A. Grammatical Analysis
text: Corrected translation of Romans 16:5b: Greet Epinetus, my beloved friend, who is the first convert to Christ from Asia — the Roman province of Asia.

section: B. Historical and Theological Profile of Epinetus
text: B. Historical and Theological Profile of Epinetus

section: B. Historical and Theological Profile of Epinetus
text: Epinetus was almost certainly the first person Paul led to faith in Christ during his ministry in Ephesus, the principal city of the Roman province of Asia. He subsequently relocated to Rome. By the time of Paul's letter, he had continued positive toward Bible doctrine, had advanced to spiritual maturity, and had become one of the recognized leaders in the house-church of Priska and Aquila. He represents what may be called the non-spectacular type of mature believer.

section: B. Historical and Theological Profile of Epinetus
text: Epinetus is not identified in the New Testament with any dramatic act, apostolic mission, or visible leadership role beyond what can be inferred from his presence on this honor roll. He is not a rocket — he is a horse. His advance to maturity was not accomplished through any single spectacular burst of spiritual energy but through the slow, steady, continuous intake of Bible doctrine over many years: plugging, persevering, maintaining positive volition regardless of setbacks, ostracism, failure, or the disappearance of encouraging companions.

section: B. Historical and Theological Profile of Epinetus
text: Even after Paul's direct ministry was no longer available to him, Epinetus continued to take in doctrine — possibly under the teaching of Aquila in Rome. He was consistent in his attendance at the assembly in the home of Priska and Aquila. He was diligent in concentration on the teaching of doctrine, making the function of GAP a daily habit. Self-determination and positive volition toward doctrine, maintained day by day, were the operative factors in his advance.

section: B. Historical and Theological Profile of Epinetus
text: The result was capacity for life in all its dimensions: capacity in living, and — according to the logic of point sixteen — greater capacity in dying. Epinetus had, through sustained doctrine intake, accumulated the inner resources that no external circumstance can supply and no external pressure can take away. He lived an honorable life that glorified the Lord Jesus Christ, and he died an honorable death that glorified the Lord Jesus Christ.

section: B. Historical and Theological Profile of Epinetus
text: Epinetus therefore stands as a fulfillment of Philippians 1:20–21. He is the ordinary believer who achieved the extraordinary through the one mechanism available to every member of the royal family of God: consistent, daily, positive volition toward the Word of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three
text: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three
text: 1. Point sixteen of the royal family honor code: The honor code is the only ethical system that assigns dying to the category of life. Dying is as much a part of living as any other dimension of human existence for the Church Age believer. This principle has no parallel in secular ethics and cannot be grasped apart from Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three
text: 2. Physical death is a solitary act: No companion, friend, or fellow believer can share the dying experience. Every believer must face and execute his own dying. This makes dying the supreme test of the Christian life, because it is the one arena where only the doctrine in the believer's own soul is available as a resource. The quality of that dying is a direct measure of the doctrine accumulated over a lifetime.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three
text: 3. Logistical grace does not terminate at the onset of dying: The same Lord, the same provision, the same indwelling Spirit, and the same Bible doctrine that sustained the believer in living are present in dying. God does not withdraw His support at the moment of the greatest test. The positive believer can therefore face dying with the same inner resources available in every prior circumstance of life.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three
text: 4. Undeserved suffering is preparation for dying: The believer who handles undeserved suffering with doctrine, without self-pity or bitterness, has demonstrated the inner resources that will sustain him through the dying phase. Conversely, the believer who is still shocked by what people do, or who collapses under undeserved suffering, has revealed that his doctrine intake has not yet produced the stability required for dying grace.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three
text: 5. The three-hope schema culminates in dying grace: The second hope includes the imputation of divine blessing in time, with dying grace as its ultimate expression. The third hope encompasses the full range of eternal blessing — resurrection body, judgment seat of Christ, eternal reward — beginning from the point of maturity. Dying grace is therefore the apex of time-blessing and the threshold of eternity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three
text: 6. Philippians 1:20–21 is the definitive statement of the honor code's ultimate: Intense concentration on doctrine produces the resultant hope that the believer will not be disgraced in dying. When living is Christ — when occupation with the person of Christ is the organizing center of the believer's inner life — dying is gain. The exaltation of Christ occurs in both spheres without distinction. There is no mode-shift for the mature believer.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three
text: 7. The kai in Romans 16:5a is adjunctive: The conjunction should be rendered 'also' rather than 'likewise.' The implied verb is the aorist active imperative of aspázomai — to greet, to salute, to pay one's respects. The local church assembling in the home of Priska and Aquila in Rome is one of at least three house-churches identified in Romans 16.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three
text: 8. The Roman province of Asia, not Achaia, is the correct reading in Romans 16:5b: The best manuscript tradition reads 'Asia' — the proconsular province in western Asia Minor comprising the seven churches of Revelation 2–3 and the sub-regions of Phrygia, Mysia, Caria, and Lydia, with Ephesus as the administrative capital. Epinetus was the first convert to Christ from this province, most likely led to faith by Paul during his Ephesian ministry.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three
text: 9. Agapētos with the possessive genitive of egó indicates personal love, category three: Paul does not describe Epinetus merely as a fellow member of the royal family who receives impersonal love. He calls him 'my beloved friend' — the object of personal affection. This is one of the marks of Paul's intimate circle of spiritual companions, distinct from the general command to love all members of the royal family with impersonal love.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Three
text: 10. Epinetus represents the non-spectacular, consistently positive believer: His profile illustrates that spiritual growth is not the trajectory of a rocket but the slow, steady trot of a horse. He is the ordinary Christian who achieves the extraordinary through self-determined, daily positive volition toward doctrine. He did not require spectacular encouragement, visible recognition, or the continuous presence of his original teacher. He plugged. He persevered. He advanced to maturity. He had capacity for life — and capacity for dying.

Chapter Five Hundred Twenty-Four

section: Romans 16:6 — Mary of Rome; Job 5:19–27 — Dying Grace and the Royal Family Honor Code
text: Romans 16:6 — Mary of Rome; Job 5:19–27 — Dying Grace and the Royal Family Honor Code

section: Romans 16:6 — Mary of Rome; Job 5:19–27 — Dying Grace and the Royal Family Honor Code

section: Romans 16:6 — Mary of Rome; Job 5:19–27 — Dying Grace and the Royal Family Honor Code
text: Corrected translation: Pay my respects to Mary, who bestowed much labor on us.

section: Romans 16:6 — Mary of Rome; Job 5:19–27 — Dying Grace and the Royal Family Honor Code
text: Job 5:19–27 “He will deliver you from six troubles; in seven no evil shall touch you. In famine he will redeem you from death, and in war from the power of the sword. You shall be hidden from the lash of the tongue, and shall not fear destruction when it comes. At destruction and famine you shall laugh, and shall not fear the beasts of the earth. For you shall be in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field shall be at peace with you.
