Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine

section: Romans 16:25–26 — The Mystery Doctrine, Dispensations, and the Decree of the Eternal God
text: Romans 16:25–26 — The Mystery Doctrine, Dispensations, and the Decree of the Eternal God

section: Romans 16:25–26 — The Mystery Doctrine, Dispensations, and the Decree of the Eternal God
text: Romans 16:25–26 “Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith.” (ESV)

section: Romans 16:25–26 — The Mystery Doctrine, Dispensations, and the Decree of the Eternal God
text: Corrected translation: Now to him, God the Father, who is able to support you in logistical grace, according to my gospel and the proclamation of Jesus Christ, according to the disclosure of the mystery which has been concealed with reference to past history — but now is revealed through the prophetic scriptures by decree of the eternal God, made known to all nations for the obedience of faith.

section: Romans 16:25–26 — The Mystery Doctrine, Dispensations, and the Decree of the Eternal God
text: We continue in the doxology that began at verse 25 and runs through verse 27 — the longest single doxology in the Pauline corpus. These verses are dense with theological freight: each phrase connects to a major doctrinal category. In verse 25, Paul anchored the doxology in logistical grace, in the gospel, in the proclamation of Jesus Christ, and in the disclosure of the mystery. Verse 26 now introduces the temporal contrast — the mystery that was concealed throughout all previous dispensations is now made manifest through the New Testament canon and by the decree of the eternal God. Understanding the phrase 'with reference to past history' requires a structured grasp of dispensational categories, which this chapter addresses comprehensively.

section: I. The Concealment of the Mystery Through Past History (Romans 16:25, concluded)
text: I. The Concealment of the Mystery Through Past History (Romans 16:25, concluded)

section: I. The Concealment of the Mystery Through Past History (Romans 16:25, concluded)
text: The perfect passive participle of the verb σιγάω (sigaō) — 'to conceal, to keep silent' — governs the phrase 'which has been concealed.' The perfect tense is a dramatic perfect, the rhetorical use of the intensive perfect, indicating a completed state with ongoing effect: this information was sealed and remained sealed across the whole of prior human history. The passive voice confirms that the mystery doctrine received this concealment; it was acted upon by divine decision. The circumstantial participle indicates the status quo of this information from the beginning of human history through all prior dispensations.

section: I. The Concealment of the Mystery Through Past History (Romans 16:25, concluded)
text: The phrase rendered 'since the world began' consists of two Greek nouns: chronois aiōniois — χρόνοις αιωνίοις. The dative plural of chronos (χρόνος) denotes elapsed time, a succession of events. The dative plural of aiōnios (αιώνιος) connotes that which is without beginning or end. Together, the idiom means with reference to long ages past, a technical expression for all dispensational history prior to the Church Age. In every one of those ages, Church Age doctrine was classified top secret — sealed, not to be opened until the Lord's first advent authorized its disclosure.

section: II. Dispensational Categories: The Vocabulary of Human History
text: II. Dispensational Categories: The Vocabulary of Human History

section: II. Dispensational Categories: The Vocabulary of Human History
text: A dispensation is a category of human history from the divine viewpoint — God's own interpretation of history organized according to His policy for each period. The believer's orientation to time and history is essential for understanding what God's plan requires at any given moment. Three Greek terms define the vocabulary of dispensations.

section: A. Chronos — Time as a Succession of Events
text: A. Chronos — Time as a Succession of Events

section: A. Chronos — Time as a Succession of Events
text: The noun chronos (χρόνος) denotes time as a linear sequence of events. In dispensational usage it portrays the chronological history of Israel: periods of national obedience and blessing, interrupted by the five cycles of discipline, followed by restoration, and interrupted again. Chronos is the timeline of Israel's covenant history.

section: B. Kairos — Time as a Dispensational Epoch
text: B. Kairos — Time as a Dispensational Epoch

section: B. Kairos — Time as a Dispensational Epoch
text: The noun kairos (καιρός) treats time as a discrete epoch or era, each dispensation regarded as a complete entity in itself. Used dispensationally in 1 Thessalonians 5:1, kairos encompasses the Age of the Gentiles, the Age of Israel, the Church Age, the conclusion of Israel's age (the Tribulation), and the Millennium — each a distinct kairos.

section: C. Aiōn — A Dispensation as a Period of Divine Administration
text: C. Aiōn — A Dispensation as a Period of Divine Administration

section: C. Aiōn — A Dispensation as a Period of Divine Administration
text: The noun aiōn (αιών) refers to a dispensation as a period of time constituting a divine category of human history, as in Ephesians 3:2 and Colossians 1:25. The corresponding noun oikonomia (οικονομία) — often translated 'dispensation' — is better rendered administration or household administration, since it includes the concept of divine policy for each era. A dispensation is God's administrative policy for a particular period of human history.

section: III. The Four Dispensations
text: III. The Four Dispensations

section: A. The Age of the Gentiles — Genesis 1–11
text: A. The Age of the Gentiles — Genesis 1–11

section: A. The Age of the Gentiles — Genesis 1–11
text: The first dispensation runs from the creation of Adam to the destruction of the Tower of Babel, approximately two thousand years. It is documented in the first eleven chapters of Genesis and encompasses three internal periods: (1) innocence — positive revelation with no established moral conscience; (2) conscience — the period following the fall, in which the knowledge of good and evil operates without written law; and (3) divine establishment — the institution of human government following the flood.

section: A. The Age of the Gentiles — Genesis 1–11
text: This dispensation is characterized by one language and one race, prior to the multiplication of languages and the separation of nations at Babel. There was no written canon of Scripture; God communicated through direct revelation. There was no missionary structure and no client nation. Believers advanced to maturity through doctrine as it was revealed to them, and salvation was by faith in Christ — though the specific content of the revelation of Christ differed from subsequent periods. The non-meritorious system of perception was identical to what operates in the Church Age.

section: A. The Age of the Gentiles — Genesis 1–11
text: The satanic attacks on divine establishment during this dispensation were systematic. The attack on human volition occurred in Genesis 3. The attack on marriage and the family occurred in Genesis 6. The attack on nationalism — the attempt to unify humanity under a single world government apart from God — occurred in Genesis 11:1–9. God's response to that attack was the confusion of languages and the dispersion of the nations, which establishes the divine principle of nationalism as the appropriate political structure for a fallen world under Satan's rule.

section: B. The Age of Israel — Patriarchs through the Tribulation
text: B. The Age of Israel — Patriarchs through the Tribulation

section: B. The Age of Israel — Patriarchs through the Tribulation
text: The second dispensation is the Age of Israel, encompassing the majority of the Old Testament. It is divided into three stages. The first stage is the period of the patriarchs, from Abraham to Moses: the origin of the Jewish race and its formation as a missionary people before becoming a nation. The second stage runs from Moses to Christ, the period commonly (if imprecisely) called the period of the Law, during which Israel functioned as the first client nation in history. The third stage is the conclusion of the age — the Tribulation, from the Rapture of the Church to the Second Advent — during which the age of Israel is completed after the intercalation of the Church Age.

section: B. The Age of Israel — Patriarchs through the Tribulation
text: The Jewish race itself emerged through a unique sequence determined by divine omniscience. Abraham and his brother Nahor were brothers; Abraham believed, Nahor did not. Abraham is a Jew, Nahor a Gentile. From Abraham came Isaac (a Jew) and Ishmael (a Gentile). From Isaac came Jacob (a Jew) and Esau (a Gentile). In each generation the believing son is the Jew; the unbelieving son is the Gentile. Jesus Christ carries the Old Testament title 'the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob' — the God of the living — because all three are believers with resurrection life, heirs of the unconditional covenants.

section: B. The Age of Israel — Patriarchs through the Tribulation
text: The Age of Israel introduced characteristics absent from the first dispensation: multiple languages, multiple races, a written canon of Scripture entrusted to Israel, an organized missionary agency (Israel itself, with Jonah as the representative illustration), and national security grounded in the unconditional covenants — the Abrahamic, Palestinian, Davidic, and New Covenants. National blessing was contingent on observation of the laws of divine establishment; failure to observe them triggered the progressive stages of national discipline culminating in the fifth cycle.

section: B. The Age of Israel — Patriarchs through the Tribulation
text: A client nation is a national entity that follows the laws of divine establishment, maintains freedom, represents God in the exercise of that freedom, supports evangelism, and enables believers to advance to maturity. It maintains a consistently pro-Semitic posture — never anti-Semitic. Freedom is the indispensable condition for all of these functions: for the exercise of individual volition toward doctrine, for the missionary enterprise, and for the proper treatment of the Jewish people.

section: C. The Church Age — The Dispensation of Intercalation
text: C. The Church Age — The Dispensation of Intercalation

section: C. The Church Age — The Dispensation of Intercalation
text: The Church Age is the dispensation of intercalation — an insertion into the Age of Israel. The term intercalation denotes a deliberate interruption and insertion. The Age of Israel was not completed but postponed. At the ascension of Christ, ten days before Pentecost, the Age of Israel came to a dead halt and the Church Age was inserted in order to call out the royal family of God.

section: C. The Church Age — The Dispensation of Intercalation
text: Jesus Christ had won the strategic victory of the angelic conflict through the cross, resurrection, ascension, and session. He is King of kings and Lord of lords, a new category of royalty without historical precedent — but at the moment of His session He had no royal family. The Church Age exists to form that royal family. The Age of Israel will resume and be completed when the royal family is removed at the Rapture.

section: C. The Church Age — The Dispensation of Intercalation
text: The Church Age is the most intensified stage of the angelic conflict in all of human history. It is characterized by features that are unique to this dispensation and will not recur. Every Church Age believer at the moment of salvation receives the baptism of the Holy Spirit, which enters the believer into union with Christ at His current position — seated at the right hand of the Father. This is current positional truth; it is the source of the believer's royalty. The universal priesthood of the believer, the universal indwelling of Christ, and the universal indwelling of the Holy Spirit are all unique to this age.

section: C. The Church Age — The Dispensation of Intercalation
text: The Church Age is further divided into two periods: the pre-canon period (AD 30 to 96), during which the New Testament was being composed and temporary spiritual gifts were in operation; and the post-canon period (AD 96 to the Rapture), during which all divine revelation is contained in the completed canon, and temporary gifts have ceased. The canon of Scripture is the exclusive means of divine communication in the post-canon period. There is no extrabiblical revelation — no dreams, visions, voices, or trances — because the written canon is complete and sufficient.

section: C. The Church Age — The Dispensation of Intercalation
text: Every Church Age believer is in full-time Christian service as an ambassador of Jesus Christ. The doctrine pertaining to the Church Age — the mystery — was entirely absent from the Old Testament. The Old Testament writers were not given any information about it. Wherever Church Age content would otherwise have appeared in the prophetic sequence, the text passes over it in silence: between Daniel 2:40–41; Daniel 7:23–24; Daniel 8:22–23; Daniel 11:35–36; Hosea 3:4–5; Hosea 5:15–6:1; and between Psalm 22:22–23. The gap between Isaiah 61:2a and 61:2b is the classic example: our Lord quoted only the first half of the verse in the synagogue at Nazareth (Luke 4:18–19) because the second half describes His second advent — the Church Age falls between the two clauses.

section: D. The Age of Christ — The Millennium
text: D. The Age of Christ — The Millennium

section: D. The Age of Christ — The Millennium
text: The fourth and final dispensation before the eternal state is the Age of Christ, commonly called the Millennium because it lasts one thousand years (Revelation 20). It begins with the Second Advent and concludes with the Gog Revolution described in Revelation 20:7–10, after which the present earth and heavens are dissolved and the new heavens, new earth, and New Jerusalem are created.

section: D. The Age of Christ — The Millennium
text: The Millennium is the one period of human history characterized by perfect environment: Satan is bound, demons are removed from the earth, and there is therefore no organized religion. Israel is restored as the client nation under the direct rule of Jesus Christ as the Son of David, reigning from Jerusalem. World peace and universal prosperity prevail. Creation itself is released from the effects of the fall: there are no deserts, plant life abounds, animal ferocity is removed (Isaiah 11:6–9), and human longevity is extended so that a person who dies at one hundred years of age is considered a child (Isaiah 65:20). Justice is administered with perfect objectivity (Isaiah 11:3–5; Psalm 72:12–14).

section: D. The Age of Christ — The Millennium
text: The millennial population includes survivors of the Tribulation in natural bodies, resurrected Old Testament and Church Age saints, and the population explosion that follows. The Gog Revolution at the end of the Millennium demonstrates the foundational principle: without regeneration and without doctrine, perfect environment produces no permanent change in human nature. The unbelieving population, given ideal conditions for one thousand years, requires only the release of Satan to launch an immediate global rebellion. Environment is never the solution to the sin problem. The only capacity for a life lived in accordance with the character of God comes from Bible doctrine resident in the soul.

section: IV. Romans 16:26 — The Revelation of the Mystery Through the Prophetic Scriptures
text: IV. Romans 16:26 — The Revelation of the Mystery Through the Prophetic Scriptures

section: IV. Romans 16:26 — The Revelation of the Mystery Through the Prophetic Scriptures
text: Verse 26 opens with the conjunctive particle δέ (de), used here to connect two clauses in contrast, followed by the temporal adverb νῦν (nyn), 'now.' The combination — 'but now' — brings us into the present dispensation, the Church Age, in explicit contrast to all previous ages covered by the phrase 'past history' in verse 25.

section: IV. Romans 16:26 — The Revelation of the Mystery Through the Prophetic Scriptures
text: The verb is the aorist passive participle of phaneroō (φανερόω) — 'to make manifest, to reveal, to disclose.' The aorist tense here is a dramatic aorist, stating a present reality with the certainty of a completed event: but now is revealed. The passive voice indicates that the mystery doctrine pertaining to the Church Age receives the action of the verb — it is being unveiled by divine initiative, not discovered by human investigation. The circumstantial participle confirms that the condition of concealment described in verse 25 has now been replaced by the condition of disclosure.

section: IV. Romans 16:26 — The Revelation of the Mystery Through the Prophetic Scriptures
text: The agency of disclosure is expressed by the prepositional phrase dia plus the genitive plural of graphē (γραφή) — 'through writings' — modified by the descriptive genitive plural of the adjective prophētikos (προφητικός). The adjective prophētikos does not refer primarily to predictive prophecy — the disclosure of future events — but to prophetic communication in the broader sense: proclamation, preaching, authoritative declaration. The prophetic scriptures are the New Testament writings — preaching committed to writing. The correct translation is through the prophetic scriptures, referring to the New Testament canon, which was in the process of formation when Paul wrote Romans in approximately AD 58. Paul anticipates the completion and permanent preservation of that canon — its function as the doctrinal heritage of the royal family of God throughout the Church Age.

section: IV. Romans 16:26 — The Revelation of the Mystery Through the Prophetic Scriptures
text: The Church Age is the dispensation of mentality in the fullest sense. Divine communication operates exclusively through the written Word, transmitted by careful analysis and received through the Grace Apparatus for Perception into the right lobe of the soul as ἐπίγνωσις (epignosis) — full, exact, operational knowledge. This process requires concentration, objectivity, and sustained academic discipline applied to the text. The canon of Scripture replaces all extrabiblical forms of communication: dreams, visions, audible voices, and ecstatic experiences are not operative in the post-canon period.

section: V. The Decree of the Eternal God
text: V. The Decree of the Eternal God

section: V. The Decree of the Eternal God
text: The disclosure of the mystery occurs 'by decree of the eternal God' — the prepositional phrase kata plus the accusative singular of epitagē (ἐπιταγή) — 'in accordance with the command' or 'by decree of.' With this is the possessive genitive of the adjective aiōnios (αιώνιος) with theos (θεός): by decree of the eternal God. The phrase 'by decree of the eternal God' opens directly onto the doctrine of the divine decrees — a comprehensive theological framework encompassing omniscience, the decrees, election, foreknowledge, predestination, retribution, and condemnation. These categories are to be carefully distinguished and related to one another.

section: V. The Decree of the Eternal God
text: The divine omniscience knew simultaneously and eternally every thought, every decision, and every action of every person who has ever lived or ever will live — together with all possible alternatives that could have occurred but did not. What actually occurred (the actual) and what could have occurred but did not (the probable) are both within the scope of omniscience. The divine decrees, by analogy, are the output of that omniscience applied to what actually happened. Facts go into the decree; facts come out. The omniscience of God determined what was decreed; the decrees record what will actually occur in history.

section: V. The Decree of the Eternal God
text: For believers, this generates two specific categories: election and predestination. Election and predestination are technical terms that apply exclusively to believers. Foreknowledge is not the cause of what is decreed but the acknowledgment of it: foreknowledge merely registers what is factual as over against the far greater number of probabilities. Predestination establishes what believers are destined to receive as a consequence of their position in Christ — including ultimate glorification. For unbelievers, the corresponding categories are retribution and condemnation — entirely different categories operating on entirely different principles.

section: V. The Decree of the Eternal God
text: The concept that any person is predestined to hell — or predestined to heaven apart from faith — is a confusion of these categories. Predestination pertains to the believer's destiny in time and eternity: the believer is predestined to heaven. Within time, the direction of the believer's spiritual life — whether toward maturity or reversionism — depends upon the believer's personal attitude toward doctrine. God knew which way every volition would move, billions of years ago, without coercing that volition. Divine foreknowledge, predestination, and the decrees involve no interference with human free will; they reflect God's eternal knowledge of what free will would in fact choose.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine
text: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine
text: 1. The dramatic perfect of sigaō establishes the theological weight of concealment: the mystery was not merely unknown but actively sealed by divine decision across the whole of prior human history. Its disclosure at the first advent was equally a divine decision, executed at the appointed moment.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine
text: 2. Three Greek terms — chronos, kairos, and aiōn — provide a precise vocabulary for dispensational history: chronos as the linear succession of Israel's covenant history; kairos as each dispensation regarded as a discrete epoch; and aiōn as a period of divine administrative policy. Oikonomia (administration) is the overarching term for the policy God implements in each era.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine
text: 3. The Age of the Gentiles demonstrates that sin is a volitional, not an environmental, problem: with one language, one race, and direct divine revelation available, Satan successfully attacked human volition (Genesis 3), the family (Genesis 6), and nationalism (Genesis 11). The dispersal of the nations at Babel is not a curse but a corrective — the divine institution of the balance of power as the appropriate political structure for a fallen world.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine
text: 4. The client nation concept is the central organizing institution of the Age of Israel: a national entity that maintains freedom, supports evangelism, enables doctrinal advance, and maintains a pro-Semitic posture. Without freedom there is no genuine volition, no missionary enterprise, and no authentic spiritual growth. Freedom through military preparedness and the laws of divine establishment are not incidental to the client nation concept but constitutive of it.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine
text: 5. The Church Age is the dispensation of intercalation — not a replacement of Israel but an insertion into Israel's suspended age: the Age of Israel was halted, not cancelled. It will resume at the Rapture and be completed through the Tribulation and Second Advent. The insertion exists for one purpose: to call out the royal family of God to accompany the Victor of the angelic conflict into His eternal reign.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine
text: 6. The unique features of the Church Age — baptism of the Spirit, universal priesthood, universal indwelling of Christ and the Holy Spirit, the completed canon, and universal ambassadorship — are without precedent in any prior dispensation and will not recur in any subsequent one. Their uniqueness reflects the unique status of the royal family and the intensified character of the angelic conflict during this intercalated age.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine
text: 7. The prophetic scriptures (dia tōn prophētikōn graphōn) denote the New Testament canon — preaching committed to writing: the term prophētikos here carries its broad sense of authoritative proclamation rather than its narrow sense of predictive prophecy. The Church Age is the dispensation of mentality: the Word written, analyzed, and transferred through academic discipline into the soul as epignosis.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine
text: 8. The Millennium demonstrates the definitive theological principle that environment is never the solution to the sin problem: a population living under perfect conditions for one thousand years — no Satan, no demons, no religion, no injustice, no poverty, no natural hostility — requires only the temporary release of Satan to launch an immediate global rebellion. The capacity for a life aligned with the character of God derives exclusively from Bible doctrine resident in the soul, not from the quality of one's circumstances.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Forty-Nine
text: 9. Election and predestination are technical categories that apply exclusively to believers; foreknowledge is the acknowledgment of what is decreed, not its cause: omniscience supplied the content of the decrees; the decrees record the actual. Predestination establishes the believer's destiny; the direction of the believer's spiritual life within time is determined by personal volition toward doctrine. God knew the outcome of every volition without coercing it — the eternal coexistence of divine omniscience and human freedom.

Chapter Five Hundred Fifty

section: Romans 16:25–27 — The Theology of God's Perfect Plan: Sovereignty, Omniscience, and the Divine Decrees
text: Romans 16:25–27 — The Theology of God's Perfect Plan: Sovereignty, Omniscience, and the Divine Decrees

section: Romans 16:25–27 — The Theology of God's Perfect Plan: Sovereignty, Omniscience, and the Divine Decrees
text: Romans 16:25–27 “Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith — to the only wise God be glory forevermore through Jesus Christ! Amen.” (ESV)

section: Romans 16:25–27 — The Theology of God's Perfect Plan: Sovereignty, Omniscience, and the Divine Decrees
text: Corrected translation: Now to Him — reference to God the Father — who is able to support you, according to my gospel and the public communication of Jesus Christ, according to the unveiling of the mystery, the mystery being church age doctrine which has been concealed with reference to past history, but now revealed through the prophetic scriptures by the decree of the eternal God — to the only wise God, glory through Jesus Christ forever. Amen.

section: Romans 16:25–27 — The Theology of God's Perfect Plan: Sovereignty, Omniscience, and the Divine Decrees
text: Romans 16:25–27 is the doxology that closes Paul's letter. Its closing phrase — 'by the decree of the eternal God' — introduces a theological category of the highest importance: the perfect plan of God, rooted in His eternal decrees. This doctrine serves not only as the exegetical key to the doxology itself, but as indispensable preparation for Romans 9–11, where election, foreknowledge, predestination, and divine sovereignty appear with concentrated frequency. The present chapter begins a systematic exposition of the theology of God's plan, covering its definition, the sovereignty of God, and the will of God as the foundational categories.

section: I. Definition and Description: A Perfect Plan for Imperfect Persons
text: I. Definition and Description: A Perfect Plan for Imperfect Persons

section: A. The Perfection of God Requires a Perfect Plan
text: A. The Perfection of God Requires a Perfect Plan

section: A. The Perfection of God Requires a Perfect Plan
text: The starting point for any theology of God's plan is the nature of God Himself. God is perfect — eternally, immutably, and infinitely perfect. A perfect God can only produce a perfect plan. It would be a logical and ontological contradiction for infinite perfection to generate anything less than a perfect result. The plan of God, therefore, cannot be separated from the perfect essence of God.

section: A. The Perfection of God Requires a Perfect Plan
text: The complication — and the occasion for all of divine genius — is that the recipients and beneficiaries of this perfect plan are imperfect. Three factors define the problem: God, perfect; the plan, perfect; the persons involved, imperfect. This is not a minor qualification. Total depravity means that human beings are imperfect not only in the category of sinfulness, but in every attempt to supplement the plan of God with human good, social action, self-righteousness, or religious works. The genius of the plan is precisely that it is perfect for imperfect persons.

section: B. The Plan Cannot Include Human Cooperation
text: B. The Plan Cannot Include Human Cooperation

section: B. The Plan Cannot Include Human Cooperation
text: Because the plan is perfect, any intrusion of human effort corrupts it. Imperfect persons cannot contribute to a perfect plan without introducing imperfection. This is why Paul writes in Ephesians 2:8–9 that salvation is by grace through faith, not of works, lest anyone should boast. The logic is not arbitrary — it follows directly from the nature of God. If the plan is perfect, and human effort is imperfect, then human effort must be excluded entirely from the mechanism of the plan. Grace is not merely a divine disposition of generosity; it is the structural requirement of a perfect plan designed for imperfect persons.

section: B. The Plan Cannot Include Human Cooperation
text: This exclusion extends beyond the moment of salvation. Worry, social crusades, human-viewpoint solutions to historical problems, and self-righteous religious activity all represent the same structural error: the attempt to introduce human imperfection into a plan that demands divine perfection at every point. The correct orientation is non-meritorious reception of what God provides, not the generation of works that appear to assist the plan.

section: C. The Function of the Plan Requires That God Does the Work
text: C. The Function of the Plan Requires That God Does the Work

section: C. The Function of the Plan Requires That God Does the Work
text: Three dimensions must be distinguished: the person of God is perfect, the plan of God is perfect, but those who function within the plan are imperfect. The problem is not simply that believers sin; it is that believers consistently want to work — to cooperate, improve the situation, correct the environment, demonstrate brotherly love through human effort. The plan of God calls for thought, specifically non-meritorious divine-viewpoint thinking received through consistent doctrine intake, not for human working. God does the thinking for the believer through revealed doctrine; God does the planning; God does the executing. The believer's role is reception, perception, and application under the filling of the Holy Spirit.

section: C. The Function of the Plan Requires That God Does the Work
text: The execution of the plan of God requires a summary of several supporting doctrines: the sovereignty of God, the will of God, the omniscience of God, and the divine decrees. These function together as the theological framework within which election, foreknowledge, predestination, reprobation, and retribution can be properly understood — and misunderstood categories corrected.

section: II. The Sovereignty of God
text: II. The Sovereignty of God

section: A. God as an Infinite Eternal Personality
text: A. God as an Infinite Eternal Personality

section: A. God as an Infinite Eternal Personality
text: Sovereignty begins with the nature of God as a person. God is not merely a force or principle; He is a personality — but an infinite, eternal personality. Eternal means that God never had a beginning; there was no moment at which God came into existence. Infinite means that the human mind cannot fully comprehend every dimension of the divine being. Because of this, Scripture describes God in terms drawn from human experience — God loves, God hates, God repents — but these descriptions are anthropopathisms and anthropomorphisms. They communicate divine policy in terms accessible to finite understanding; they do not describe God's inner nature directly.

section: A. God as an Infinite Eternal Personality
text: As an eternal infinite personality, God has self-consciousness — He has always been aware of His own existence — and self-determination — He has been making decisions throughout eternity. God recognizes Himself as a personality, and as such He thinks, decides, and acts in rational compatibility with His own integrity.

section: B. Sovereignty and the Divine Decrees
text: B. Sovereignty and the Divine Decrees

section: B. Sovereignty and the Divine Decrees
text: The sovereignty of God is bound up in His self-determination and in the divine decrees. The omniscience of God — the faculty by which God feeds facts into the computer of the divine decrees — operated simultaneously. God did not think through the history of the human race chronologically, event by event, as human beings think. In a single, instantaneous act of omniscience, God knew the entire history of the human race from the creation of Adam to the conclusion of the Millennium. Every thought every human being would ever think, every decision every human being would ever make, every action every human being would ever take — all of these were known simultaneously, and all were fed into the computer of the divine decrees as facts.

section: B. Sovereignty and the Divine Decrees
text: God's foreknowledge of a human decision does not cause that decision. The fact that God knew billions of years ago what a person would decide does not coerce the will of that person. Human volition remains genuinely free. The person is fully responsible for his own decisions. God is not the author of sin; superlapsarianism — the view that God decreed sin as a positive act — is an error. God knew sin would occur; He did not decree its occurrence as a causative act.

section: C. The Printouts of the Divine Computer
text: C. The Printouts of the Divine Computer

section: C. The Printouts of the Divine Computer
text: What the omniscience of God fed into the computer of the divine decrees prints out in several categories. For believers, the printouts include election, foreknowledge, and predestination (sometimes called foreordination). For unbelievers, the corresponding printouts are reprobation (total depravity), condemnation, and retribution. Dispensational categories also print out, organizing the facts of history under their respective economies.

section: C. The Printouts of the Divine Computer
text: A critical distinction governs these printouts. Predestination deals exclusively with believers. It does not deal with unbelievers. The Hegelian fallacy — if the believer is predestined to heaven, then the unbeliever must be predestined to hell — fails precisely because the antithesis is not stated in Scripture and is not a printout from the decrees. The unbeliever goes to the lake of fire because of his own personal refusal to believe in Jesus Christ as Savior, or because of sustained negative volition at the point of God-consciousness. This is not divine predetermination; it is divine justice responding to human negative volition. God as judge sentences; He is not the author of the outcome.

section: C. The Printouts of the Divine Computer
text: Foreknowledge (πρόγνωσις, prognōsis) must be carefully distinguished from the omniscience of God. Omniscience is the faculty by which God fed facts into the computer. Foreknowledge is a printout — it describes what God has decreed will occur, not the mechanism by which He knew it. The two operate at different points in the logical sequence of the divine decrees.

section: D. Sovereignty as Absolute Dominion
text: D. Sovereignty as Absolute Dominion

section: D. Sovereignty as Absolute Dominion
text: The sovereignty of God is His absolute dominion over created beings. Even when individual believers fail — through sin, distraction, subjectivity, or sustained reversionism — the plan of God is not damaged. A believer's failure results in divine discipline, which is itself an expression of the integrity of God maintaining the plan. But the plan itself continues without diminishment. Failure of individual participants does not hinder the inevitable victory of God. Human volition, whether positive or negative, serves the divine purpose rather than frustrating it.

section: D. Sovereignty as Absolute Dominion
text: The sovereignty of God operates across several spheres of relationship: as Creator, having authority over animate and inanimate creation; as Redeemer, having authority over all categories of believers; as the source of blessing, with the right to impute blessing in time and eternity under the conditions specified in Scripture; and as disciplinarian, with the right to punish those who fail in His plan. God has also delegated authority in both the spiritual and temporal realms — civil government, military authority, judicial authority, parental authority — and only delegated authority is legitimate authority.

section: E. Sovereignty over Possible and Actual Things
text: E. Sovereignty over Possible and Actual Things

section: E. Sovereignty over Possible and Actual Things
text: God's authority extends to both possible and actual things. Over possible things, God is sovereign in that He leaves them as only possible and does not convert them to actual. God does not intervene to prevent what He has permitted to remain within the category of human volition. He warned Adam and the woman repeatedly, but He did not physically prevent their sin. The sin moved from possible to actual through the exercise of their own volition. God did not make it actual; He permitted it to become actual through the operation of creature free will.

section: E. Sovereignty over Possible and Actual Things
text: Over actual things, God is the final and absolute authority. Representative passages include 1 Samuel 2:6–8; 1 Chronicles 29:11–12; Psalm 145; Matthew 6:13; and 1 Timothy 6:15. God renders no account to others but acts in agreement with His perfect being and His perfect plan.

section: III. The Will of God
text: III. The Will of God

section: A. One All-Inclusive Will and Purpose
text: A. One All-Inclusive Will and Purpose

section: A. One All-Inclusive Will and Purpose
text: There is one all-inclusive will and purpose of God concerning all that ever was or ever will be. This will and purpose originates within God Himself and is compatible with all of His attributes. Perfection produces perfection: the will of God is the expression of who God is, and because God is perfect, His will is perfect. The will of God is objectively designed for His glory, His pleasure, and His satisfaction, and it could not be otherwise given His perfect essence.

section: A. One All-Inclusive Will and Purpose
text: The only way a perfect plan can function for imperfect persons is for the perfect person to do all the work — all the planning, all the thinking, all the executing. Divine viewpoint thinking, received through the Grace Apparatus for Perception under the filling of the Holy Spirit, is God's provision of the thinking required for the believer to function within the plan. The believer's role is non-meritorious reception, not meritorious contribution.

section: B. Immanent and Transient Dimensions of the Will of God
text: B. Immanent and Transient Dimensions of the Will of God

section: B. Immanent and Transient Dimensions of the Will of God
text: Since there are three persons in the Trinity, the divine will and actions of God within the Godhead are immanent, intrinsic, and subjective — subjective here in the precise theological sense, meaning operating within the Godhead itself. The Father is generally identified as the author of the plan; the Son executes the plan of redemption; the Holy Spirit sustains the believer in the Church Age. These functional assignments do not imply any inferiority of person. The members of the Trinity are co-equal and co-eternal; assignments within the plan reflect function, not ontological rank.

section: B. Immanent and Transient Dimensions of the Will of God
text: The will of God related to creation is extrinsic — outside of God — in that creature volition was itself invented by God and operates outside of the divine being. It is transient, meaning it operates chronologically from the human vantage point, even though God knew all of it simultaneously in eternity past. And it is objective in the sense that the function of divine integrity moves toward the ultimate glory of God regardless of human performance.

section: C. The Comprehensive and Eternal Character of God's Will
text: C. The Comprehensive and Eternal Character of God's Will

section: C. The Comprehensive and Eternal Character of God's Will
text: Since God's will is all-comprehensive, not the slightest uncertainty can exist regarding even the smallest event without introducing confusion into the whole. The omniscience of God fed only facts into the computer of the divine decrees. Every thought, every decision, every action of every human being — individually and corporately — was fed in as fact. God knew how each person would think, decide, and act, and He incorporated all of it into the decrees without coercing any of it. Human responsibility for sin, negative volition, and failure remains intact precisely because God's foreknowledge does not cause human decisions.

section: C. The Comprehensive and Eternal Character of God's Will
text: The will of God is eternal: God has never gained knowledge. What God knows at any moment He has always known. He knew it all simultaneously in eternity past. Because nothing can occur unknown to God, His will is unchangeable and His plan is certain. Since nothing can occur unknown to God, His plan is victorious and perfect even when imperfect people within the plan fail.

section: C. The Comprehensive and Eternal Character of God's Will
text: The will of God as reflected in the divine decrees will be completed with regard to all His creatures — angelic and human — and with regard to creation in general, both animate and inanimate. Jesus Christ controls history. God is bound by His own integrity — His holiness, righteousness, justice, veracity, and faithfulness — to complete what He has begun. All events of history are interwoven and interdependent (Ephesians 1:11; 2:10).

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty
text: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty
text: 1. A perfect God can only produce a perfect plan. This is not merely a pious affirmation; it is a logical necessity rooted in the doctrine of divine immutability and infinite perfection. The plan cannot be partial, provisional, or dependent on human performance for its ultimate success.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty
text: 2. The genius of the plan is that it is perfect for imperfect persons. God does not wait for His creatures to achieve adequacy before including them in His plan. The plan is designed from the outset to function for those who are totally depraved, sinful, prone to human good, and given to reversionism. Grace is the structural mechanism that makes this possible.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty
text: 3. Human volition is genuinely free, and human beings are genuinely responsible. God's foreknowledge of every human decision — fed simultaneously into the computer of the divine decrees in eternity past — does not coerce those decisions. The person who rejects Christ goes to the lake of fire because of his own negative volition, not because God decreed his damnation as a causative act. Superlapsarianism, which makes God the author of sin and of reprobation in this sense, is an error.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty
text: 4. Predestination is a printout for believers only. The divine decrees print out election, foreknowledge, and predestination for the category of believers. There is no corresponding predestination to hell for unbelievers. Unbelievers are under reprobation, condemnation, and retribution — but these result from their own rejection of Christ, not from a divine decree of damnation independent of their volition.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty
text: 5. The failure of individual believers does not hinder the plan of God. Sovereignty means absolute dominion. Even when every participant fails, the plan of God continues unimpaired. Divine discipline maintains the integrity of God and addresses individual failure, but the plan itself is not blemished by human weakness or rebellion.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty
text: 6. The will of God is eternal, comprehensive, and certain. God is not gaining in knowledge. He knew all things simultaneously in eternity past. Because nothing can occur outside His knowledge, His will is unchangeable and His plan is certain of victory. Jesus Christ controls history, and the outcome of history — including the fulfillment of all promises to Israel — is secured by the integrity of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty
text: 7. Legitimate authority in both the spiritual and temporal realms is delegated authority. God is the only absolute authority. All other authority — civil government, military, judicial, parental, pastoral — is legitimate only insofar as it is delegated by God. Abuse of human authority does not invalidate the category; it reflects the imperfection of those to whom authority has been entrusted.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty
text: 8. The doctrine of God's perfect plan is the framework for understanding Romans 9–11. The categories of election, foreknowledge, predestination, the remnant, and God's faithfulness to Israel — which appear with concentrated frequency in Romans 9–11 — cannot be properly interpreted without this theological foundation. The present chapter establishes the framework within which those passages will be exegeted.

section: Romans 16:25–27 — The Theology of God's Perfect Plan: Divine Will, Omniscience, and the Decrees
text: Romans 16:25–27 constitutes the closing doxology of the epistle, and the phrase 'by the decree of the eternal God' opens into one of the most comprehensive doctrinal subjects in the New Testament: the theology of God's perfect plan. This chapter continues a multi-part exposition of that theology, resuming at Point Three — the will of God — and advancing through Point Four, the omniscience of God, and Point Five, the divine decrees. The goal is to provide the conceptual framework necessary for the detailed exegesis of Romans 9–11, where election, foreknowledge, predestination, and foreordination will demand exact definition.

section: I. The Will of God (Continued) — Points 13–19
text: I. The Will of God (Continued) — Points 13–19

section: I. The Will of God (Continued) — Points 13–19
text: The preceding sessions established that there is one all-inclusive will and purpose of God, that this will originated within God Himself and is perfectly compatible with His attributes, and that it is objectively designed for His glory, pleasure, and satisfaction. The following points complete the treatment of the divine will.

section: Point 13 — Providence
text: Point 13 — Providence

section: Point 13 — Providence
text: The work of God is called Providence, by which He molds all events into the fulfillment of His will and purpose. Providence is a precise theological term, largely displaced from contemporary usage but carried with full theological weight by such figures as Robert E. Lee and Thomas Jonathan Jackson, whose correspondence employs it extensively. Providence encompasses all events without exception: Satan's revolt, every act of reversionism, every sin, every expression of human good, every manifestation of evil — all are incorporated into the fulfillment of God's will without negating divine holiness or human volition.

section: Point 14 — Preservation and Direction
text: Point 14 — Preservation and Direction

section: Point 14 — Preservation and Direction
text: Two distinct but related divine operations govern creaturely existence. Preservation continues the existence of creatures, both animate and inanimate. Providence directs their progress. The distinction is important: God does not merely sustain existence passively; He actively directs the trajectory of history toward the fulfillment of His purpose.

section: Point 15 — Human History Programmed by the Dispensations
text: Point 15 — Human History Programmed by the Dispensations

section: Point 15 — Human History Programmed by the Dispensations
text: Human history is organized and programmed by the Dispensations. The divine objective within that history is revealed in the Seven Imputations, which together outline the glorification of God on the part of man — represented in doctrinal shorthand as the X-plus-Y-plus-Z framework of the believer's advance through salvation, rebound, and maturity adjustment.

section: Points 16–19 — The Will of God as Directive, Determinative, Permissive, and Preventative
text: Points 16–19 — The Will of God as Directive, Determinative, Permissive, and Preventative

section: Points 16–19 — The Will of God as Directive, Determinative, Permissive, and Preventative
text: Four characteristics complete the doctrine of the divine will. First, the will of God is directive: God has a plan for each life, and the believer's progress within that plan is the function of Providence. Second, the will of God is determinative: God has permitted non-meritorious positive volition to bring the believer to imputed blessing, and negative volition to bring cursing — the believer's attitude toward doctrine is the determining factor. Third, the will of God is permissive: negative volition is permitted, with consequences related to divine integrity that are severe. Fourth, the will of God is preventative: the laws of divine establishment, Bible doctrine, the royal family honor code, and divine discipline all function to keep human self-determination within the boundaries of God's plan.

section: II. The Omniscience of God — Point Four
text: II. The Omniscience of God — Point Four

section: II. The Omniscience of God — Point Four
text: Point Four in the theology of God's perfect plan addresses divine omniscience as it relates to the construction and content of the divine decrees.

section: Points 1–6 — The Scope and Character of Divine Knowledge
text: Points 1–6 — The Scope and Character of Divine Knowledge

section: Points 1–6 — The Scope and Character of Divine Knowledge
text: God knows perfectly and eternally all that is knowable — both actual and possible things. His perception is completely compatible with His essence: perfect essence entails perfect knowledge. Because God is eternal, His knowledge is eternal; He has always known everything He now knows. Because God is sovereign, His knowledge is superior to any creature knowledge and is not bounded by time or space. Because God is omnipotent, the application of that knowledge is far superior to any creaturely application. Every minute detail of both angelic and human creation is completely and perfectly in the mind of God at all times. Consequently, the future is as clearly comprehended by God as the past; time has no limiting effect on divine knowledge.

section: Point 7 — Knowledge of Alternatives
text: Point 7 — Knowledge of Alternatives

section: Point 7 — Knowledge of Alternatives
text: The omniscience of God knows not only the facts of history — every thought, every decision, every action — but also the alternatives to every thought, every decision, and every action. Every alternative to every historical event, down to the most minute particulars, has always been simultaneously and perfectly known by God. This is what distinguishes omniscience from foreknowledge as a technical category.

section: Points 8–9 — Knowledge of Counterfactuals
text: Points 8–9 — Knowledge of Counterfactuals

section: Points 8–9 — Knowledge of Counterfactuals
text: God knows all that would have been involved had He adopted any one of an infinite number of plans. He knows all that would have been involved in every case where any creature's decision might have been different from what it actually was — and He knows the downstream consequences of every alternative decision across every subsequent generation.

section: Point 10 — Three Categories of Divine Knowledge
text: Point 10 — Three Categories of Divine Knowledge

section: Point 10 — Three Categories of Divine Knowledge
text: Three distinct categories of divine knowledge must be distinguished for precise theological analysis.

section: Point 10 — Three Categories of Divine Knowledge
text: Category One is self-knowledge: omniscience includes God's perfect, eternal understanding of His own attributes, the co-equality, co-infinity, and co-eternity of all three persons of the Trinity, and all things comprehended within divine essence.

section: Point 10 — Three Categories of Divine Knowledge
text: Category Two is omniscience proper: the knowledge of all things in creation, both actual and possible. Omniscience is the comprehensive feeder of all facts into the computer of the divine decrees.

section: Point 10 — Three Categories of Divine Knowledge
text: Category Three is foreknowledge: a technical and more limited category. Foreknowledge has as its subject matter only what is decreed. It does not range across alternatives; it reads only the printout of the decrees. Logically, the decrees precede foreknowledge — foreknowledge is divine cognizance of what is already in the computer, not the basis on which the computer was loaded.

section: Points 11–22 — Omniscience, the Computer, and the Decrees
text: Points 11–22 — Omniscience, the Computer, and the Decrees

section: Points 11–22 — Omniscience, the Computer, and the Decrees
text: Omniscience feeds only facts into the computer of the divine decrees — every thought, decision, and action of every creature, together with full knowledge of every alternative. Foreknowledge reads only the printout; it does not encompass alternatives. The decrees contain only what has happened or will happen and guarantee their certain future occurrence.

section: Points 11–22 — Omniscience, the Computer, and the Decrees
text: The content of the decrees is classified categorically. Three categories are of particular importance to the believer: election, foreknowledge, and predestination. These are the governing terms in Romans 9–11. Election refers to what is in the decrees regarding the believer in the X-plus-Y-plus-Z advance — specifically Y and Z, the post-salvation phases. Foreknowledge deals with all people in the decrees. Predestination (also called foreordination or predetermination) covers only the thoughts, decisions, and actions of believers; unbelievers are never described in Scripture as predestined, predetermined, or foreordained. They are in the decrees under condemnation and reprobation, but not under predestination or election.

section: Points 11–22 — Omniscience, the Computer, and the Decrees
text: The logical sequence is: omniscience (perceiving all actuals and all alternatives) feeds facts into the computer; the decrees (also called foreordination, predestination, predetermination) establish the certain content of the computer; foreknowledge is divine cognizance of that content. Logically, the decrees precede foreknowledge, although the Infralapsarian position treats them as simultaneous and thereby avoids the need for careful logical analysis. The Sublapsarian position maintains the logical sequence and is to be preferred. Nothing was foreknown until it was first decreed — logically if not temporally, since to God all of this is one eternal, simultaneous act.

section: Points 11–22 — Omniscience, the Computer, and the Decrees
text: Foreknowledge is divine cognizance of what is in the decrees and does not produce or cause the events it recognizes. The decrees alone establish certainty; foreordination alone guarantees certain future occurrence.

section: III. The Divine Decrees — Point Five
text: III. The Divine Decrees — Point Five

section: Points 1–4 — Nomenclature and Scope
text: Points 1–4 — Nomenclature and Scope

section: Points 1–4 — Nomenclature and Scope
text: The facts in the computer of the divine decrees are designated by several terms, each emphasizing a different aspect of the same comprehensive divine act. The terms are: decree (or, collectively, the decrees), foreordination, predestination, predetermination, election, and foreknowledge. Each term will recur extensively in the exegesis of Romans 9.

section: Points 1–4 — Nomenclature and Scope
text: The decrees of God are the sum total of God's plan for the human race, anticipated through omniscience in eternity past and placed simultaneously into the computer — all facts entered at once, though they emerge chronologically within the time-space frame that God Himself invented.

section: Point 5 — The Single Comprehensive Intention
text: Point 5 — The Single Comprehensive Intention

section: Point 5 — The Single Comprehensive Intention
text: God's purpose relating to all events of every kind constitutes one single, all-comprehensive intention. Perceiving all events in omniscience — the free is free, the necessary is necessary — together with all their causes, conditions, and relations, as one indivisible system of things, every link of which is essential to the integrity of the whole. Human freedom is not negated by God's comprehensive knowledge; the free remains free precisely because omniscience perceived it as free. The necessary remains necessary because omniscience perceived it as necessary. The entire complex of causes, conditions, and relations constitutes one indivisible system whose integrity depends on every link.

section: Points 6–10 — The Eternal and Immutable Character of the Decrees
text: Points 6–10 — The Eternal and Immutable Character of the Decrees

section: Points 6–10 — The Eternal and Immutable Character of the Decrees
text: The decree of God is His eternal, holy, wise, and sovereign purpose, comprehending at once all things that ever were or will be — in their courses, conditions, successions, and relations — and determining their certain future occurrence. The decrees are eternal: there was never a time when they did not exist. They are holy: they are the product of perfect divine integrity, righteousness, and justice. They are wise: they reflect the omniscience of God. They are sovereign: they are subject to no external constraint.

section: Points 6–10 — The Eternal and Immutable Character of the Decrees
text: The decrees of God are His eternal and immutable will regarding the future existence of events which happen in time, together with the precise manner and order of their occurrence. By the decrees of God is meant that eternal plan by which God has rendered certain all events of human and angelic history. The omniscience of God placed in the computer every decision, every thought, every action of every person in the human race — simultaneously in eternity past, though they emerge chronologically within time and space, which God Himself created as the theater of their occurrence.

section: Points 6–10 — The Eternal and Immutable Character of the Decrees
text: The decrees are therefore the perception of eternal omniscience, the eternal purpose of God, the counsels of His will, and inevitably the promotion of His glory.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-One
text: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-One

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-One
text: 1. Providence is the technical theological term for God's governance of history. By Providence, God molds all events — including sin, failure, reversionism, and every expression of evil — into the fulfillment of His will and purpose, without compromising His holiness or overriding human volition.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-One
text: 2. The will of God operates in four modes simultaneously: directive (God has a specific plan for each life), determinative (volition is the operative factor in blessing or cursing), permissive (negative volition is not overridden, though its consequences are administered by divine integrity), and preventative (divine establishment, doctrine, and discipline provide boundaries).

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-One
text: 3. Omniscience and foreknowledge are not synonyms. Omniscience is comprehensive — it knows all actuals and all alternatives. Foreknowledge is technical and limited — it is divine cognizance only of what is in the decrees. Omniscience feeds facts into the computer; foreknowledge reads the printout.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-One
text: 4. The logical sequence of the divine decrees is critical for interpreting Romans 9–11. Omniscience perceives all facts and alternatives. The decrees (foreordination, predestination, predetermination) establish their certain occurrence. Foreknowledge and election are cognizance of what has been decreed. Nothing was foreknown until it was first decreed — logically, if not temporally.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-One
text: 5. Predestination applies exclusively to believers. Unbelievers appear in the decrees under condemnation and reprobation, not under predestination, foreordination, or election. The term 'decree' covers all humanity; predestination and foreordination cover only the believer's thoughts, decisions, and actions.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-One
text: 6. The entire plan of God constitutes one indivisible system. Every thought, decision, and action of every creature in all of human and angelic history is one single all-comprehensive intention of God, perceiving the free as free and the necessary as necessary, together with all their causes, conditions, and relations. Every link is essential to the integrity of the whole.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-One
text: 7. God's glory is the terminal objective of the entire system. God existed in perfect glory in eternity past, before any creature existed. At the conclusion of all angelic and human history, He will possess not only the same intrinsic glory He always possessed, but additional glory accrued through the entire course of creation, history, redemption, and the fulfillment of His plan. God can only increase in glory; He can never decrease.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-One
text: 8. The study of the divine decrees is prerequisite to Romans 9. Romans 9 is the most theologically concentrated chapter in the New Testament. The terms election, foreknowledge, predestination, and foreordination that govern that chapter cannot be exegeted responsibly without the conceptual framework developed here. The theology of the perfect plan of God is not background material — it is the necessary foundation.
