text: Corrected translation: Now to Him — God the Father — who is able to support you according to my gospel and the public communication of Jesus Christ, according to the unveiling of the mystery, Church Age doctrine, which has been concealed with reference to past history.

section: Romans 16:25 — The Theology of the Perfect Plan of God: Divine Decrees, Foreknowledge, and the Will of God
text: Romans 16:25 grounds its doxology in the phrase 'by the decree of the Eternal God' — a phrase that opens onto the full theology of the Protocol Plan of God. This chapter continues a sustained study of the divine decrees, foreknowledge, and the will of God as the framework within which Church Age doctrine operates. The treatment moves through points five through eight of a fourteen-point doctrinal outline on the theology of the perfect plan of God.

section: I. The Divine Decrees — Points Five through Twenty-One
text: I. The Divine Decrees — Points Five through Twenty-One

section: I. The Divine Decrees — Points Five through Twenty-One
text: The divine decrees are also designated foreordination, predetermination, and predestination. These terms are not synonyms for fatalism; they describe the eternal omniscient awareness of God regarding every thought, decision, and action of every creature, simultaneously apprehended in eternity past and placed into what may be called the computer of divine omniscience.

section: A. The Nature of the Decrees
text: A. The Nature of the Decrees

section: A. The Nature of the Decrees
text: The decrees of God are His eternal, holy, wise, and sovereign purpose, comprehending at once all things that ever were or will be — in their causes, conditions, successions, and relations — and determining their certain future occurrence. They constitute one single, all-comprehensive intention, receiving all events of history — free and necessary, sinful and righteous — into one indivisible system. Every link in that system is essential to the integrity of the whole.

section: A. The Nature of the Decrees
text: The sum total of God's plan for the human race was anticipated through omniscience in eternity past and placed into the divine decrees simultaneously — not sequentially. There was never a moment in which God arrived at new knowledge. The omniscience of God knew every cause for every effect, every thought before every decision, every decision before every action. This knowledge did not in any way override or manipulate the free agency of the creature. The free remains free; the necessary remains necessary.

section: A. The Nature of the Decrees
text: The glory of God that existed in eternity past will be even further magnified at the conclusion of history, when the divine decrees reach their full expression. No human failure, no accumulation of sin, no generation's reversionism, and no concentration of evil at any point in history alters the outcome: God is the winner, and God is glorified. The plan of God has never depended upon the success or failure of any creature. It depends on God.

section: B. Key Distinctions within the Decrees
text: B. Key Distinctions within the Decrees

section: B. Key Distinctions within the Decrees
text: Several distinctions are essential for accurate understanding of the decrees as a doctrinal category.

section: B. Key Distinctions within the Decrees
text: Point 12: The decrees deal only with what will happen, not with what will not occur. The omniscience of God did not enter a single probability, possibility, or alternative into the computer of divine decrees. Only actuality — what would in fact occur — was decreed. This eliminates all speculative 'what if' thinking as theologically meaningless: such speculation does not engage with what God has actually decreed, and therefore has no bearing on reality.

section: B. Key Distinctions within the Decrees
text: Point 14: No event or occurrence fed into the computer is directly affected or caused by the decree itself. The decree does not constitute fatalism. The omniscience of God anticipates the thought, decision, or action of the free agent; that anticipation is the decree. The execution of any thought, decision, or action on the part of the creature is not the decree — it is history, the fulfillment of the decree in time. The decree exists in eternity; its execution occurs in time.

section: B. Key Distinctions within the Decrees
text: Point 15: Omniscience distinguishes between the actual — which is fed into the computer — and the possible — which is never decreed. The alternatives to reality, though fully known to omniscience, were never placed into the decrees. This is why foreknowledge must be carefully distinguished from omniscience.

section: B. Key Distinctions within the Decrees
text: Point 17: Events in the decrees are affected by causes acting in a manner consistent with reality. Cause and effect in thoughts, decisions, and actions do not disturb the function of free agency. God knows what a free moral agent will think, decide, and do — but that knowledge does not influence the agent's self-determination.

section: B. Key Distinctions within the Decrees
text: Point 18: The antecedents of any act in the decrees are a part of the actuality. The thoughts that precede a decision — the full causal chain leading to an action — are included in the decree. Actuality does not disturb free agency; it encompasses it.

section: B. Key Distinctions within the Decrees
text: Point 19: God may desire the highest and best for every creature, but the creature can reject it. God knew what would be chosen and what would not. Only what would in fact occur was placed into the decrees. The printout is therefore absolute certainty — certain futurition.

section: B. Key Distinctions within the Decrees
text: Points 20–21: The decrees of God are efficacious in that they determine all that ever was, is, or will be. Efficacious decrees are distinguished from the permissive will of God, in which the free actions of creatures produce secondary causes — divine discipline, collective judgment, the five cycles of national discipline, and all forms of historical disaster to client nations. These secondary causes arise from the justice of God responding to the free volition of creatures whose decisions were known and decreed in eternity past.

section: II. The Foreknowledge of God
text: II. The Foreknowledge of God

section: II. The Foreknowledge of God
text: Foreknowledge is frequently misunderstood as the basis of the decrees. The reverse is true: the decrees are logically prior to foreknowledge. Foreknowledge is the divine cognizance of what has been decreed — it makes nothing certain but simply acknowledges what is certain.

section: A. Foreknowledge Defined
text: A. Foreknowledge Defined

section: A. Foreknowledge Defined
text: Foreknowledge belongs equally to God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit. It is not foresight — God does not learn or advance in knowledge. God knew everything simultaneously in eternity past. Foreknowledge is not the perception of future events as such; it is the cognizance of what is in the decrees.

section: A. Foreknowledge Defined
text: Point 1: No decree arises from the foreknowledge of God. Foreknowledge makes nothing certain but simply acknowledges what is certain. Omniscience places actuality into the decree; foreknowledge perceives only what is in the decree.

section: A. Foreknowledge Defined
text: Point 3: Foreknowledge is knowledge of what occurs in history — past, present, and future. Omniscience, by contrast, includes knowledge of what did not occur: all the alternative thoughts, decisions, and actions on the part of every member of the human race that could have occurred but did not.

section: A. Foreknowledge Defined
text: Point 4: The omniscience of God fed reality — what would happen — into the computer, while the foreknowledge of God knew all the events as certainly future, having decreed them.

section: A. Foreknowledge Defined
text: Point 6: God's foreknowledge does not produce or cause events, but recognizes events which have been fed into the computer.

section: A. Foreknowledge Defined
text: Point 8: God foreknows all events as certainly future because in eternity past He decreed them — He fed them into the computer and made them certainly future. The origin was sovereignty plus omniscience, not sovereignty plus foreknowledge. Foreknowledge followed the decrees logically, not before them.

section: B. Omniscience vs. Foreknowledge: A Critical Distinction
text: B. Omniscience vs. Foreknowledge: A Critical Distinction

section: B. Omniscience vs. Foreknowledge: A Critical Distinction
text: In rightly dividing the word of truth, one of the most important distinctions is between omniscience and foreknowledge. They are not synonymous.

section: B. Omniscience vs. Foreknowledge: A Critical Distinction
text: Omniscience encompasses all knowledge — actuality and probability, reality and alternative. Foreknowledge is restricted to actuality: what was decreed. When foreknowledge appears in Scripture, the subject is not the range of possibilities available to God, nor speculation about alternatives. The subject is the cognizance of reality as decreed.

section: B. Omniscience vs. Foreknowledge: A Critical Distinction
text: Point 10: Since the divine decrees alone establish certainty, nothing can be foreknown until it is first decreed. The logical order is: omniscience feeds actuality into the decrees → the decrees establish certain futurition → foreknowledge acknowledges what is decreed. Foreknowledge placed before the decrees would imply that God was aware but not the original cause — a theologically untenable position.

section: B. Omniscience vs. Foreknowledge: A Critical Distinction
text: Point 11: Omniscience only decreed what would happen. Therefore omniscience only fed reality into the computer. Human life is designed by divine provision to deal with reality — the reality of blessing and suffering, prosperity and adversity, life and death. Doctrine is the divinely provided means of coping with every form of reality. Speculation about alternatives — worry, regret, foreboding — is not engagement with what God has decreed; it is a departure from reality.

section: B. Omniscience vs. Foreknowledge: A Critical Distinction
text: Points 13–14: Omniscience precedes the decrees logically; foreknowledge is technically simultaneous with the decrees but logically follows them. Foreknowledge cannot be placed before the decrees without implying that God was reactive rather than originative. Foreknowledge makes nothing certain. The decrees are certainty, and foreknowledge acknowledges the reality in the computer.

section: III. The Will of God
text: III. The Will of God

section: III. The Will of God
text: Having established the nature of the decrees and the proper relationship of foreknowledge to omniscience, the study moves to the will of God as the volitional expression of the perfect plan.

section: A. Consistency with Divine Essence
text: A. Consistency with Divine Essence

section: A. Consistency with Divine Essence
text: Point 1: The will of God must be consistent with His perfect attributes and His eternal essence. There can be no inconsistency in a perfect God. A perfect God produces a perfect plan for imperfect people. All inconsistency arises from the old sin nature and the free volition of the creature — never from the plan itself.

section: A. Consistency with Divine Essence
text: Point 2: God cannot compromise His essence — nor any part of it. Not one divine attribute is subject to compromise. Immutability secures this. God cannot suspend His righteousness to accommodate human failure, nor override His justice to accommodate human sentiment.

section: A. Consistency with Divine Essence
text: Point 5: God did not decree Himself to be. God decreed from His omniscience all that would ever happen in human history. The divine existence is not a product of the decrees; the decrees are a product of divine existence and omniscience.

section: B. The Scope and Origin of the Divine Will
text: B. The Scope and Origin of the Divine Will

section: B. The Scope and Origin of the Divine Will
text: Point 7: The decree of God is His eternal, holy, wise, and sovereign purpose, comprehending at once — simultaneously — all things that ever were, are, or will be in their causes, conditions, successions, and relations, and determining their certain future. This definition must be kept in view throughout any discussion of election, foreordination, predestination, or predetermination.

section: B. The Scope and Origin of the Divine Will
text: Point 8: Because of the limitations of human mentality, the several contents of this one eternal decree and purpose are necessarily perceived by us in partial aspects — categories. This is why doctrinal study proceeds systematically, category by category. The difficulty of any particular category — including Romans 9 — is not inherent in the text but reflects inadequate preparation and sustained negative volition toward the doctrinal process.

section: B. The Scope and Origin of the Divine Will
text: Points 12–13: There is one all-inclusive will and purpose of God concerning all that ever was or will be. This will and purpose originate within God Himself. Being objective, the will and plan of God are designed for His glory, His pleasure, and His satisfaction. Divine blessing to the creature flows from divine glory — never from creature merit.

section: B. The Scope and Origin of the Divine Will
text: Point 15: The simultaneous decrees of God result in divine action both within the Godhead and related to creation. Action within the Godhead is intrinsic and subjective. Action related to creation is extrinsic and objective.

section: B. The Scope and Origin of the Divine Will
text: Point 16: A distinction must be maintained between the decree of God in eternity past and the action of God in time. The action of God in time is the execution of the decree of eternity past. The execution is not the decree but logically follows from it. What we observe in history is not the decree itself but the certain futurition of what was decreed — that is, history.

section: C. The Axle of Divine Righteousness
text: C. The Axle of Divine Righteousness

section: C. The Axle of Divine Righteousness
text: The practical application of this entire doctrinal section centers on a single choice that every believer makes: the axle on which the wheel of the Christian life will turn. Two axles are available. The first is the righteousness of God, imputed to the believer at salvation by the justice of God — permanent, perfect, entirely non-meritorious. The second is self-righteousness — the believer's own system of morality, religious performance, or personal standards, substituted for the divine standard.

section: C. The Axle of Divine Righteousness
text: The wheel of the Protocol Plan of God was designed to run on the axle of divine righteousness. Self-righteousness is a square axle on a round wheel. The friction it generates is not progress; it is a symptom of fundamental misalignment with the plan of God. The corrective is not moral improvement but doctrinal orientation — daily intake of Bible doctrine through the Grace Apparatus for Perception, sustained over time until the axle of divine righteousness becomes the operating base for every category of spiritual function.

section: C. The Axle of Divine Righteousness
text: Adjustment to the justice of God at salvation includes the imputation of divine righteousness. That imputed righteousness signals from the outset that the believer's own righteousness is not adequate — was never designed to be adequate — and that the entire Christian way of life rests on what God has provided, not on what the believer can produce.

section: IV. Reality, Speculation, and the Doctrinal Mandate
text: IV. Reality, Speculation, and the Doctrinal Mandate

section: IV. Reality, Speculation, and the Doctrinal Mandate
text: The theological content of the divine decrees has direct application to how the believer engages with his own life. Since God fed only actuality into the decrees — never probability, possibility, or alternative — every form of speculation is a departure from the operational reality God has designed the believer to inhabit.

section: IV. Reality, Speculation, and the Doctrinal Mandate
text: Worry is speculation about alternatives to what God has decreed. Regret is speculation about a past that cannot be changed and was, in fact, decreed. Foreboding is speculation about a future that is already certain in the mind of God. Guilt reaction — one of the most corrosive manifestations of this pattern — is the refusal to accept the provision God has made for sin (rebound) and the substitution instead of self-generated condemnation. None of these mental operations engages with what God has decreed. All of them divert cognitive resources from doctrine, which is the only resource designed to cope with reality.

section: IV. Reality, Speculation, and the Doctrinal Mandate
text: Doctrine is designed to care for reality — the reality of prosperity and adversity, blessing and suffering, social flourishing and national decline. The believer cannot die well without doctrine, cannot live well without doctrine, cannot face suffering without doctrine, and cannot enjoy prosperity without doctrine. Every form of reality that appears in the printout of the divine decrees is a reality for which God has provided doctrinal resources.

section: IV. Reality, Speculation, and the Doctrinal Mandate
text: Historical disaster — whether personal catastrophe, the discipline of a client nation, or the five cycles of national collapse — is not evidence that God has failed or abandoned the plan. It is the certain futurition of what was decreed in eternity past, executed through secondary causes arising from the justice of God in response to the sustained negative volition of creatures whose free decisions were fully known. The believer oriented to the decrees does not panic at historical crisis. The believer who has neglected doctrine has no framework within which to process it and will respond with the full range of emotional instability that characterizes spiritual immaturity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two
text: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two
text: 1. The divine decrees are one simultaneous, all-inclusive eternal purpose. In eternity past, the omniscience of God apprehended every thought, decision, and action of every creature simultaneously, and that omniscient apprehension of actuality constitutes the decrees. There was no sequential deliberation; the decrees are eternal and immutable.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two
text: 2. Only actuality was fed into the decrees — never probability, possibility, or alternative. The omniscience of God knows all alternatives to reality; the decrees contain only reality. This is why foreknowledge deals exclusively with actuality, and why speculation about alternatives has no bearing on the theological reality of the plan of God.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two
text: 3. Foreknowledge is logically posterior to the decrees, not prior. The decrees establish certain futurition; foreknowledge acknowledges what has been decreed. Placing foreknowledge before the decrees would make God reactive rather than originative — a position inconsistent with divine omniscience and sovereignty.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two
text: 4. Omniscience and foreknowledge are not synonymous. Omniscience encompasses all knowledge — actuality and probability alike. Foreknowledge is restricted to the printout of the decrees: actuality only. This distinction is essential for the exegesis of Romans 9 and any passage treating election, predestination, or predetermination.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two
text: 5. The decrees do not constitute fatalism and do not override free agency. God's anticipation of a free decision does not cause that decision. The cause remains the creature's own self-determination. The decree is the eternal record of that self-determination in the omniscience of God. Free will is fully operational within the framework of the decrees.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two
text: 6. The execution of the decree in time is history — not the decree itself. The decree exists in eternity past. What is observed in human history is the certain futurition of what was decreed. Secondary causes — including divine discipline, national judgment, and personal adversity — are the outworkings of the justice of God responding to the free decisions of creatures whose choices were known and decreed.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two
text: 7. The will of God is consistent with and inseparable from His perfect essence. No attribute of God is subject to compromise. The plan God designed for imperfect creatures is itself perfect, because its author is perfect and immutable. All inconsistency in the execution of the plan arises from the old sin nature and the free volition of the creature.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two
text: 8. The imputation of divine righteousness at salvation defines the operational base of the Christian life. The righteousness of God imputed to the believer at salvation signals that the believer's own righteousness is permanently and categorically inadequate. The Protocol Plan of God is designed to run on the axle of divine righteousness — not self-righteousness. Every attempt to substitute self-righteousness for divine righteousness misaligns the believer with the plan.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two
text: 9. Doctrine is the only provision designed to cope with every form of reality. Because the decrees deal exclusively with actuality, and because actuality is the only domain in which the believer lives, doctrine — which addresses every category of reality — is the believer's indispensable resource. Worry, regret, guilt reaction, and foreboding are forms of speculative thinking that divert from doctrine and disqualify the believer from engaging with reality as God has decreed it.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Two
text: 10. The plan of God does not depend on any creature's success or failure. The plan depends on God. This is not a peripheral observation but the defining principle of the doctrinal section introduced in Romans 16:25. The sooner the believer understands and accepts this, the sooner doctrine — not performance, personality, or self-generated spiritual systems — becomes the governing reality of the spiritual life.

text: Romans 16:25 — The Theology of the Perfect Plan of God: Divine Decrees, Election, Predestination, and the Glory of God

section: Romans 16:25 — The Theology of the Perfect Plan of God: Divine Decrees, Election, Predestination, and the Glory of God
text: Romans 16:25 “Now to him who is able to strengthen you according to my gospel and the preaching of Jesus Christ, according to the revelation of the mystery that was kept secret for long ages but has now been disclosed and through the prophetic writings has been made known to all nations, according to the command of the eternal God, to bring about the obedience of faith—” (ESV)

section: Romans 16:25 — The Theology of the Perfect Plan of God: Divine Decrees, Election, Predestination, and the Glory of God
text: Corrected translation: Now to Him — God the Father — who is able to support you by logistical grace, according to my gospel, the good news of salvation, and the public communication of Jesus Christ, according to the unveiling of the mystery — Church Age doctrine — which has been concealed with reference to past history, but now in the Church Age is revealed through the prophetic scriptures by the decree of the eternal God.

section: Romans 16:25 — The Theology of the Perfect Plan of God: Divine Decrees, Election, Predestination, and the Glory of God
text: Romans 16:25 concludes the epistle with a doxology anchored in the phrase 'the decree of the eternal God.' That phrase opens into the full theology of the divine plan — a subject that also serves as the necessary foundation for Romans 9, where the doctrines of election, foreknowledge, predestination, and condemnation are applied to Israel and the church. This chapter continues the doctrinal series on the perfect plan of God, resuming at point eight of a twenty-three-point outline and completing it through point fourteen. The organizing principle throughout is the adjustment to the justice of God — the mechanism by which all divine blessing is received, both in time and in eternity.

section: I. The Characteristics of the Will of God (Point Eight)
text: I. The Characteristics of the Will of God (Point Eight)

section: I. The Characteristics of the Will of God (Point Eight)
text: The will of God, as it operates within the divine decrees, possesses a cluster of defining characteristics that together explain how a perfect God can devise and execute a perfect plan for imperfect creatures without violating either His own integrity or human freedom.

section: A. The Will of God Is All-Comprehensive
text: A. The Will of God Is All-Comprehensive

section: A. The Will of God Is All-Comprehensive
text: God understood simultaneously, in eternity past, every act, every decision, and every thought of every human being who would ever live. No event, however small, could occur unknown to Him. Not the slightest uncertainty could exist regarding even the smallest occurrence without introducing confusion into the entire structure of history. Therefore, all events of history are interwoven and interdependent — each cause connected to its conditions, successions, and relations, all of them determining a certainly future outcome.

section: B. The Will of God Is Eternal and Unchangeable
text: B. The Will of God Is Eternal and Unchangeable

section: B. The Will of God Is Eternal and Unchangeable
text: God is not gaining knowledge incrementally. What He knows at any given moment in time He has always known. There never was a moment when God did not know everything that would occur, long before it occurred. Because nothing can take place unknown to Him, His will is both unchangeable and certain. This immutability of the divine will is not a constraint on God but an expression of His perfect character. It is the basis for confidence in a world where human institutions visibly decay and historical events appear chaotic. The principle that Jesus Christ controls history is not a pious sentiment but a logical entailment of divine omniscience and the eternal character of the divine decrees.

section: C. The Will of God Is Perfect
text: C. The Will of God Is Perfect

section: C. The Will of God Is Perfect
text: Since God is perfect, His will is perfect. The divine sovereignty reflected in the decrees will be completed regardless of the failures of creatures. The plan of God does not depend upon human performance. It depends upon who and what God is. Believers have the privilege of moving with that plan and receiving the imputation of divine blessing in time and eternity. The alternative is to reject Bible doctrine and construct a substitute system — a form of self-righteousness that cannot serve as the axle on which the wheel of the divine plan runs.

section: C. The Will of God Is Perfect
text: God is bound by His own integrity — His holiness, comprising righteousness and justice, plus His truth and the infinite faithfulness of His immutable character — to complete everything He has begun. The divine policy by which this completion is accomplished is grace: the justice of God blessing mankind totally apart from any human merit or ability.

section: D. The Will of God Is Directive, Determinative, Permissive, and Preventative
text: D. The Will of God Is Directive, Determinative, Permissive, and Preventative

section: D. The Will of God Is Directive, Determinative, Permissive, and Preventative
text: God has a plan for every life. That plan is expressed as: human life imputed at birth, plus the imputation of Adam's original sin, establishing the universal condition of spiritual death and the universal need for salvation. This equals the first potential: salvation, available to every member of the human race. The pertinent doctrine at this stage is the gospel, producing the first hope — absolute confidence that whoever believes in Jesus Christ has eternal life. That hope becomes reality through salvation adjustment to the justice of God: non-meritorious faith in Christ.

section: D. The Will of God Is Directive, Determinative, Permissive, and Preventative
text: The plan then advances through the intermediate stage: judicial imputation of all personal sins to Christ on the cross, and judicial imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at salvation. This righteousness — the divine axle — is what the wheel of the plan of God runs upon. The second potential is divine blessing in time that glorifies God. The second hope is absolute confidence that maturity attained through the daily intake of Bible doctrine will result in the imputation of divine blessing from the justice of God. That hope becomes reality through maturity adjustment to the justice of God: maximum doctrine resident in the soul.

section: D. The Will of God Is Directive, Determinative, Permissive, and Preventative
text: The final stage of the plan involves the imputation of eternal life at salvation plus the imputation of blessing in time at maturity, producing the third potential: great blessing and reward in eternity that glorifies God forever. The third hope is absolute confidence that at the judgment seat of Christ, the believer in resurrection body will receive eternal rewards. Undeserved suffering, endured in the orientation of eternity, focuses and intensifies this hope.

section: D. The Will of God Is Directive, Determinative, Permissive, and Preventative
text: The will of God is also determinative: God has permitted non-meritorious volition to bring the believer to blessing or cursing. The omniscience of God, which fed the facts of every free decision into the computer of divine decrees, does not thereby coerce the will. God never tampers with free will. The will of God is permissive with respect to negative volition toward doctrine — such volition is allowed, but divine justice provides discipline as the consequence in time. The will of God is also preventative: through doctrine, divine establishment, the royal family honor code, and discipline, God legitimately influences — but never coerces — human volition to remain within His plan. Influence is legitimate; coercion is not.

section: D. The Will of God Is Directive, Determinative, Permissive, and Preventative
text: The will of God operates in three modes: what He directly causes (as in the work of Christ on the cross and the act of creation), what He permits (including sin and human good), and the overruling will of God, by which a pivot of spiritually mature believers can preserve a nation, a military organization, or any other human institution from destruction.

section: II. The Extent of the Divine Decrees (Point Nine)
text: II. The Extent of the Divine Decrees (Point Nine)

section: II. The Extent of the Divine Decrees (Point Nine)
text: God has decreed ends as well as means, causes as well as effects, conditions and instrumentalities as well as the events that depend upon them. The omniscience of God, knowing simultaneously every thought, decision, and action in all of human history, fed only facts into the computer of divine decrees. Facts, and only facts, print out of that computer. History is the printout. Historical causation — the sequence of decisions and actions that produces a given outcome — was known to God in eternity past in all of its details. The causes are as much a part of the decrees as the outcomes, because causes are themselves facts.

section: II. The Extent of the Divine Decrees (Point Nine)
text: Some things God decreed to accomplish directly: creation is the paradigm case. Other things God accomplishes through secondary causes operating under the laws of necessity — the laws of divine establishment. When those laws are violated, the consequences built into them follow with the same certainty as any other decreed outcome. Still other things God has decreed to permit free moral agents to determine through the exercise of their own volition. Salvation belongs to this category: every person who has believed in Jesus Christ did so through a genuinely free decision that God neither caused nor coerced, but foreknew as fact and incorporated into the decrees.

section: II. The Extent of the Divine Decrees (Point Nine)
text: All categories of events — directly caused, secondarily caused, and freely chosen — are certainly future from the standpoint of the divine decrees. The extent of the decrees gives no basis for attributing any historical disaster to God's negligence. God has been faithful to provide opportunity, logistical grace, doctrine, and the freedom necessary for positive volition to function. What creatures do with those provisions is the product of their own free will.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: The members of the Godhead — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — are co-equal and co-eternal. Each possesses in identical measure the same sovereignty, holiness, righteousness, justice, truth, immutability, omniscience, omnipresence, and omnipotence. These attributes exist in three separate and distinct persons. When Scripture speaks of God as one, it speaks from the standpoint of His attributes — the same in quantity, quality, and duration in each member of the Trinity. When the author of the divine decrees is identified, it is God the Father who functions as the architect of the plan for the human race, feeding the facts of His omniscience into the decrees.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: Before any creature existed, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit possessed co-equal, co-eternal, infinite glory. The creation of angels and mankind, time and space, was designed to demonstrate that the divine plan — even when executed through free creatures who repeatedly fail — will ultimately glorify God. The following propositions summarize the relationship between the divine decrees and the glory of God:

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 1. The decrees unite in one all-inclusive final objective: the glory of God. The purpose for the creation of angels, mankind, time, and space is the glorification of God (Proverbs 16:4; Romans 11:36; Hebrews 2:10; Revelation 4:11).

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 2. Before all creation, the decrees concerned only the members of the Trinity. God's glory — what He is in His essence, person, and attributes — was the only referent.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 3. Being eternal and infinite, each member of the Godhead is worthy of glory. God's glory is identical with His essence.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 4. As the subject of the divine decrees, it is logical and inevitable that God will be glorified both in what He is and in what He has decreed. The facts fed into the computer by omniscience will, without exception, glorify God in their printout.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 5. The manifestation of God's glory secures the highest possible good for creatures: maturity adjustment to the justice of God and the resultant imputation of divine blessing. It is the attainment of spiritual maturity through maximum doctrine resident in the soul — not human activity or social engagement — that glorifies God and constitutes the believer's highest function on earth.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 6. God is pleased and glorified by advance and continued momentum in His plan. The believer whose life is characterized by operation in the advanced stage of the plan glorifies God both now and forever.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 7. The divine decrees are executed through the imputations from the justice of God. God designed His plan around seven imputations, six of which balance the equation of the plan, and the seventh of which is the eternal result.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 8. The seven imputations are: (1) human life at physical birth; (2) Adam's original sin at physical birth; (3) judicial imputation of all personal sins to Christ on the cross; (4) judicial imputation of divine righteousness to the believer at salvation; (5) imputation of eternal life at salvation; (6) imputation of divine blessing in time at maturity; and (7) imputation of divine blessing in eternity. These seven constitute the tactical victory of the angelic conflict.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 9. Each advance in the plan of God provides divine blessing that glorifies God. Advance occurs only through knowledge of doctrine.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 10. Blessing from God and glorification of God are always a potential based on positive volition — positive motivation toward Christ at salvation and positive volition toward doctrine after salvation. This is the plan of God reduced to its simplest expression.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 11. Only what actually occurs is fed into the decrees. The computer takes facts only and prints out facts only. Alternatives are not in the decrees and do not appear in the printout, even though omniscience knows them.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 12. Omniscience knows both the actual and the potential; foreknowledge knows only the actual — what is in the computer of divine decrees.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 13. God knew in eternity past what thoughts, motivations, decisions, and actions would carry one believer to maturity and another to reversionism. God knew every person who would crack the maturity barrier and has special provisions for them in time and eternity. The omniscience of God is also the basis of divine fairness toward believers who die shortly after salvation: God knows what a life perpetuated to full length would have produced, and eternal reward or its absence is assigned accordingly.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 14. Omniscience knows both the factual and the potential. Foreknowledge knows only the factual — only what is in the computer of divine decrees.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 15. The plan of God is consistent with human freedom and self-determination. God does not limit or coerce human volition.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 16. Distinctions must be maintained between what God causes directly — such as the cross — and what He permits indirectly — such as sin and human good.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 17. God created man with volition of the soul and therefore permits human self-determination to function. This is the origin of sin. Adam sinned from his own free will.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 18. God is not the author of sin. Human free will and self-determination are the cause of sin. This is the position called sublapsarianism.

section: III. The Divine Decrees and the Glory of God (Point Ten)
text: 19. Both sin and the cross are fed into the computer of divine decrees because both are facts. They have different sources — God directly causes the cross; man causes sin — but both are facts, and all facts, regardless of their cause, are fed into the decrees along with their causes, conditions, successions, and relations. While God warned Adam about sin and its consequences in perfect environment, He did not coerce Adam's will to avoid sin. God did directly cause the cross, by which every human being can believe in Christ for eternal salvation rather than reject Him.

section: IV. The Principle of Election (Point Eleven)
text: IV. The Principle of Election (Point Eleven)

section: IV. The Principle of Election (Point Eleven)
text: Election is not a selection of certain individuals for salvation to the exclusion of others. It is the printout of the computer of divine decrees dealing exclusively with believers — every person throughout human history who would believe in Jesus Christ. Condemnation is the corresponding printout dealing exclusively with unbelievers. Election and condemnation are thus two separate categories in the decrees, never to be conflated.

section: IV. The Principle of Election (Point Eleven)
text: The history of Israel illustrates the operation of election with clarity. The omniscience of God fed into the decrees the fact that Abraham would believe in God — Genesis 15:6, 'Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness' — and would advance to maturity in the supergrace stage. On that basis, Abraham ceased to be an Akkadian Gentile and became the first Jew. His brother Nahor was an unbeliever; he remained a Gentile. Abraham's firstborn son Ishmael was an unbeliever; he could not inherit the Abrahamic covenant, which requires both imputed divine righteousness and eternal life — neither of which an unbeliever possesses. Abraham's second son Isaac was a believer and therefore stands in the line of the Jewish nation. In the following generation, Esau and Jacob were twins. Esau, though the firstborn, was an unbeliever and therefore not in the Abrahamic line. Jacob was a believer and is therefore included.

section: IV. The Principle of Election (Point Eleven)
text: The critical inference is this: a true Jew is not defined by physical descent from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob but by spiritual descent — by sharing the faith that characterized the patriarchs. Abraham was a believer. Isaac was a believer. Jacob was a believer. Each had imputed divine righteousness and eternal life. Only those in the Abrahamic line who are likewise born again — who have both imputed righteousness and eternal life — are true Jews in the biblical sense. This is what Paul means in Romans 9:6: 'Not all who are descended from Israel belong to Israel.' The election of Israel is the election of believers within the physical line of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Romans 9–11 is the full printout of this category from the computer of divine decrees.

section: IV. The Principle of Election (Point Eleven)
text: Two major elections organize all of human history from the standpoint of the decrees: the election of Israel and the election of the church. Both pertain exclusively to believers. Both are to be understood in the framework of the justice of God blessing those who possess imputed divine righteousness and eternal life.

section: V. The Principle of Predestination (Point Twelve)
text: V. The Principle of Predestination (Point Twelve)

section: V. The Principle of Predestination (Point Twelve)
text: Predestination — also called predetermination and foreordination — is the divine preconceived and pre-designed plan for believers. Like election, it applies only to believers. Unbelievers are never said in Scripture to be predestined or elected. They are said to be condemned, judged, under retribution, and in the status of reprobation. These are the categories that apply to unbelievers in the decrees; election and predestination do not.

section: V. The Principle of Predestination (Point Twelve)
text: A common theological error imports the Hegelian dialectic into the interpretation of predestination: if Scripture states that God predestined believers to heaven (thesis), then the antithesis — that God predestined unbelievers to hell — must also be true, and the synthesis is a double predestination. This is both logically and hermeneutically invalid. A foundational principle of biblical hermeneutics requires that if a thesis is stated in Scripture but the antithesis is not, the antithesis does not exist. Double predestination is not taught in Scripture and is a form of fatalism incompatible with the biblical data.

section: V. The Principle of Predestination (Point Twelve)
text: Predestination deals with how far a believer will advance in the plan of God. Every believer has entered the plan of God at salvation adjustment to the justice of God. From that point, the question is the believer's attitude toward Bible doctrine. Positive volition toward doctrine leads through the GAP — the grace apparatus for perception — to the maturity barrier, and beyond it to supergrace and ultra-supergrace. Negative volition leads to warning discipline, intensified discipline, and potentially the sin unto death — a miserable life in time, though not misery in eternity, since all believers regardless of their spiritual condition at death enter a state in which there is no sorrow, tears, pain, or death. Those who advance to the ultra-supergrace stage live in the imputation of divine blessing and die magnificently, with great eternal reward to follow.

section: V. The Principle of Predestination (Point Twelve)
text: God knew in eternity past exactly how far each believer would advance in the plan — which thoughts, motivations, decisions, and actions would carry a given individual to maturity or to reversionism. He knew every person who would crack the maturity barrier. He has designed specific provisions in time and eternity for those who do. This is predestination: the predetermined plan of God as it relates to the believer's own volition, motivation, and momentum in the divine plan.

section: VI. The Integrity of God (Point Thirteen)
text: VI. The Integrity of God (Point Thirteen)

section: VI. The Integrity of God (Point Thirteen)
text: The integrity of God is that aspect of divine essence identified as holiness, consisting of righteousness and justice. It is the attribute-complex that governs all divine action toward creatures. In the context of Romans 9, several further dimensions of the integrity of God will require detailed treatment: the distinction between the attribute of divine love and the anthropopathism of love; the significance of Romans 9:13, 'Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated'; the relationship between human failure and divine faithfulness; and the way in which the integrity of God inevitably produces the glorification of God. These subjects will be developed in detail when the commentary reaches Romans 9.

section: VII. The Computer of Divine Decrees and Condemnation (Point Fourteen)
text: VII. The Computer of Divine Decrees and Condemnation (Point Fourteen)

section: VII. The Computer of Divine Decrees and Condemnation (Point Fourteen)
text: Election, foreknowledge, and predestination are information categories in the computer of divine decrees that deal exclusively with believers. The omniscience of God also feeds into that computer information regarding unbelievers. That information is filed under a single category: condemnation. The justice of God condemns the unbeliever both in time and in eternity.

section: VII. The Computer of Divine Decrees and Condemnation (Point Fourteen)
text: Condemnation and election are therefore separate files in the decrees. Condemnation is not a subcategory of predestination; it is an entirely distinct category with its own logic. Unbelievers are excluded from the plan of God for believers — election, foreknowledge, predestination — and are instead under condemnation. This means that physical descent from Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob confers no exemption from condemnation. The racial Jew who rejects Jesus Christ as Savior is not under election but under condemnation, as Romans 9:8 will make explicit: 'The children of the flesh — these are not the children of God.'

section: VII. The Computer of Divine Decrees and Condemnation (Point Fourteen)
text: The unbeliever is never predestined to the lake of fire. He arrives there by his own free will — by rejecting Christ at the point of gospel hearing, or by remaining negative at God-consciousness such that the gospel never reaches him, which is tantamount to rejection. The lake of fire was prepared for the devil and his angels (Matthew 25:41); human beings arrive there only through their own self-determination. The computer of divine decrees records this as a fact — not as a divine sentence imposed on individuals apart from their own choice.

section: VIII. The Ultimate Issue: God's Axle or Man's
text: VIII. The Ultimate Issue: God's Axle or Man's

section: VIII. The Ultimate Issue: God's Axle or Man's
text: The fundamental option confronting every believer reduces to a single question: will the believer use the system God has designed, or attempt to construct an alternative? God invented both the wheel — the plan of God — and the axle on which it runs: imputed divine righteousness, received through non-meritorious faith in Jesus Christ at salvation. The believer who chooses self-righteousness as the operating principle — whether expressed through morality, religious works, social action, or any other form of human good — is attempting to run the wheel of the divine plan on a self-made axle. The result is not a functioning wheel but a stationary, non-rotating system that cannot advance in the plan of God.

section: VIII. The Ultimate Issue: God's Axle or Man's
text: The error of first-century Judaism illustrates this at the national level. Many within racial Israel took the Mosaic Law and distorted its function, using it as a system of self-righteousness for salvation rather than as the divine standard pointing to Christ. They reinvented the wheel. The same error appears in every generation of believers who substitute human effort, community engagement, or moralistic achievement for the intake of Bible doctrine and the resultant adjustment to the justice of God. The plan of God does not advance through what believers do in the arena of human activity. It advances through what believers think — specifically, through the epignosis knowledge of doctrine resident in the soul that enables the justice of God to impute divine blessing in time and eternity.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three
text: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three
text: 1. The will of God is all-comprehensive: God understood simultaneously, in eternity past, every thought, decision, and action of every human being. Not the slightest uncertainty could exist regarding even the smallest event without introducing disorder into the entire structure of history.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three
text: 2. The plan of God does not depend on human performance: God is bound by His own integrity to complete what He has begun. The failure of any individual believer or of any generation does not alter the outcome of the divine plan, because the plan depends on who and what God is, not on the quality of creaturely response.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three
text: 3. Grace is the divine policy: Grace is the justice of God blessing mankind totally apart from human merit or ability. It is not a supplement to human effort but the exclusive channel through which all divine blessing flows.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three
text: 4. The seven imputations constitute the tactical victory of the angelic conflict: The imputation of human life and Adam's sin at physical birth; the judicial imputation of all sins to Christ and of divine righteousness to the believer at salvation; the imputation of eternal life at salvation; the imputation of blessing in time at maturity; and the imputation of blessing in eternity — these seven form the complete structure of the divine plan and demonstrate the justice of God to all angelic observers.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three
text: 5. Election and predestination apply exclusively to believers: These are categories in the computer of divine decrees that deal with those who believe in Jesus Christ. Unbelievers are not predestined to hell; they arrive there through their own free self-determination. The biblical categories for unbelievers are condemnation, reprobation, and retribution — never election or predestination.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three
text: 6. A true Jew is defined by the new birth, not by physical descent: The patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were each believers who possessed imputed divine righteousness and eternal life. Only those who share this spiritual condition stand in the true line of Israel. Physical descent from the patriarchs without regeneration places an individual under condemnation, not election — as Romans 9:8 states, 'The children of the flesh are not the children of God.'

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three
text: 7. Predestination concerns how far a believer advances in the plan of God: God knew in eternity past what thoughts, motivations, decisions, and actions would carry each believer to maturity or to reversionism. He has designed specific blessing in time and eternity for those who crack the maturity barrier and advance to supergrace and ultra-supergrace.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three
text: 8. God is not the author of sin: The sublapsarian position correctly identifies human free will and self-determination as the cause of sin. God warned Adam, but He did not coerce his will. God directly caused the cross — the solution to sin — while permitting the function of human freedom that produced sin in the first place.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three
text: 9. The glory of God is the single unifying objective of the divine decrees: Every decree, every imputation, every advance in the plan of God, every creaturely success and failure that is overruled by divine grace — all of it converges on the glorification of God as its final and inevitable outcome.

section: Conclusions from Chapter Five Hundred Fifty-Three
text: 10. The ultimate issue for every believer is the choice between the divine axle and a self-made substitute: Imputed divine righteousness, received through faith in Christ, is the axle on which the wheel of the divine plan turns. Any system of self-righteousness — moral, religious, or social — is an attempt to replace that axle with a human substitute. The result is the inability to advance in the plan of God and the forfeiture of the imputation of divine blessing in time and eternity.
